Protein folding and misfolding

1TA ×1
Normal prion protein (PrPC, mostly α-helix) refolds into PrPSc (mostly β-sheet) with no change in its amino acid sequence. Which bonds are rearranged in this change?
  1. A. Hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl and amide groups
  2. B. Hydrophobic interactions between nonpolar side chains
  3. C. Ionic bonds between charged side chains
  4. D. Peptide bonds between adjacent residues
  5. E. Disulfide bonds between cysteine side chains
AnswerA. Hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl and amide groups
WhyThe α-helix and the β-sheet are both secondary structure, held by backbone C=O···H–N hydrogen bonds: within one chain (n to n + 4) in the helix, between strands in the sheet. Switching one for the other rearranges those H-bonds. The unchanged sequence shows the peptide bonds are intact; disulfide, ionic and hydrophobic forces are tertiary.
Key factSecondary structure = local folds held by H-bonds between backbone C=O and N–H (not side chains).
α-helix: right-handed, 3.6 residues per turn; the C=O of residue n bonds the N–H of residue n + 4 → intrachain H-bonds running parallel to the axis; R groups point outward.
β-sheet: H-bonds between adjacent strands (separate chains or distant parts of one chain), parallel or antiparallel; R groups above and below the sheet.
A helix ↔ sheet switch (amyloid or prion β-sheet ↔ α-helix) only rearranges these H-bonds; peptide and disulfide bonds are untouched.
What it unlocks: 1 question

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Alzheimer vignette: a drug turns a β-sheet protein into α-helix → which interaction is reorganized (hydrogen bonds)
  • TA style: "α-helices and β-sheets are stabilized by hydrogen bonding; which interaction maintains this level?" → H-bonds between backbone carbonyl and amide groups
  • Fill-in or "true only for the β-sheet": helix H-bonds within the same chain, sheet H-bonds between strands (interchain)
  • α-helix features: 3.6 residues per turn, n to n + 4, R groups outward; labeled-atom figure → the C=O and N–H one turn apart

What it lets you eliminate

  • "β-sheets are held by H-bonds but α-helices are not" (both are)
  • Peptide, disulfide, ionic or hydrophobic bonds as the secondary-structure bond
  • R groups pointing into the helix core; a left-handed helix; H-bond to the adjacent (n + 1) residue

Straight-recall questions it answers (1)

  • TA1 A researcher analyzes a protein and finds that its α-helices and β-pleated sheets are stabilized by hydrogen bonding. Which of the following interactions is primarily res… → B. Hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl and amide groups

2unlocks 193 not obvious
A newly imported mitochondrial matrix protein is enclosed in a barrel-shaped, ATP-dependent complex capped by a lid protein, where it folds in isolation. Which protein forms this barrel?
  1. A. Ubiquitin
  2. B. Peptidyl transferase
  3. C. Signal recognition particle
  4. D. Hsp70
  5. E. Hsp60
AnswerE. Hsp60
WhyHsp60 (a chaperonin, with Hsp10 as the lid) is the barrel that folds proteins, mainly in mitochondria. Hsp70 is the tempting choice: it is the most abundant chaperone, but it binds exposed hydrophobic stretches and holds proteins unfolded for translocation rather than enclosing them.
Key factChaperones = heat shock proteins (HSPs): recognize exposed hydrophobic regions of new or misfolded proteins and help them fold correctly; they hydrolyze ATP (ATPase domain); induced by stress.
  • Hsp70: the most abundant chaperone; binds and stabilizes hydrophobic regions, keeping proteins unfolded until they reach their destination (translocation).
  • Hsp60 (chaperonin, + Hsp10 lid): barrel that encloses the protein and folds it, contacting it through hydrophobic (not hydrophilic) patches; main site mitochondria.
  • Proteins chaperones cannot rescue are tagged with ubiquitin → proteasome (e.g., ΔF508 CFTR); enhancing this pathway clears toxic aggregates. Failed chaperone folding underlies misfolding diseases such as Alzheimer.
What it unlocks: 19 questions

The 3 questions you might not expect it to answer are in the dropdown at the bottom.

How it shows up

  • Direct: which Hsp forms a barrel, stabilizes unfolded proteins, or is most abundant; Hsp60 vs Hsp70 contrast
  • Organelle: barrel-shaped chaperones are abundant in which organelle → mitochondria
  • Function: what do HSPs do → help fold/refold using ATP; which enzyme activity is in all HSPs → ATPase
  • Drug or fate: Parkinson drug that reduces aggregates → enhances the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway; ubiquitinated ΔF508 CFTR → proteasome

What it lets you eliminate

  • Cross out release factors, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, SRP and peptidyl transferase: translation machinery, not folding.
  • Cross out 'tags proteins with ubiquitin' as an HSP function: that is the degradation system.
  • Cross out 'binds hydrophilic patches', 'forms disulfide bonds' and 'substitutes amino acids'.

Questions it helps you answer (3)
Practice Q336Looks like another topic
A 70-year-old man presents with progressive memory loss, confusion, and difficulty performing daily activities. A brain biopsy reveals intracellular neurofibrillary tangles and extracellular amyloid plaques. Which of the following molecular processes is most directly implicated in the pathogenesis of this patient’s disease?
  1. A) Defective ubiquitination
  2. B) Impaired chaperone-mediated protein folding
  3. C) Impaired N-linked glycosylation
  4. D) Defective ribosomal scanning
AnswerB. Impaired chaperone-mediated protein folding
WhyNeurofibrillary tangles plus amyloid plaques mean Alzheimer disease, a protein-misfolding disorder: Aβ and tau adopt abnormal β-sheet conformations and aggregate. Chaperones (heat shock proteins) normally prevent this, so failed chaperone-mediated folding is most directly implicated.
Explanation from the source
The patient likely has Alzheimer’s disease, which is associated with the accumulation of misfolded amyloid-β proteins. Chaperone proteins such as heat shock proteins (Hsp) play a role in proper protein folding, and their dysfunction can contribute to neurodegenerative diseases.
How it follows from the main questionPlaques + tangles are misfolded aggregates, and chaperones (HSPs) are what normally prevent misfolding → impaired chaperone-mediated folding. Ubiquitination is the cleanup step, not the folding failure.
Practice Q417Asked from the other direction
An investigational drug for Parkinson’s disease is found to reduce the accumulation of toxic mutant protein aggregates within the cell. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of action of this investigational drug?
  1. A. Enhances the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway
  2. B. Inhibits formation of native conformation
  3. C. Enhances formation of beta pleated sheets in mutant protein
  4. D. Inhibits binding of mutant protein with heat shock proteins (HSP)
  5. E. Inhibits alpha helix formation in mutant protein
AnswerA. Enhances the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway
WhyMisfolded α-synuclein that chaperones can't rescue is tagged with ubiquitin and destroyed by the proteasome; enhancing this pathway clears the toxic aggregates. Promoting β-sheets, blocking HSP binding or blocking the native fold would worsen aggregation.
How it follows from the main questionProteins chaperones cannot rescue get ubiquitin → proteasome, so boosting that clears aggregates → enhances the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. More β-sheet, blocking HSP binding or blocking the native fold all worsen aggregation.
Practice Q489Asked from the other direction
130. An investigational drug for Parkinson's disease is found to reduce the accumulation of toxic mutant protein aggregates within the cell. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of action of this investigational drug?
  1. A. Inhibits alpha helix formation in mutant protein
  2. B. Enhances formation of beta pleated sheets in mutant protein
  3. C. Inhibits binding of mutant protein with heat shock proteins (HSP)
  4. D. Enhances the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway
  5. E. Inhibits formation of native conformation
AnswerD. Enhances the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway
WhyMisfolded proteins that chaperones cannot rescue are tagged and destroyed by the ubiquitin–proteasome pathway, so boosting it lowers aggregate load; the other options would worsen aggregation.
Explanation from the source
Misfolded proteins that chaperones cannot rescue are tagged with ubiquitin and destroyed by the proteasome, so a drug that strengthens this pathway lowers aggregate load. Promoting beta-sheets, blocking binding to Hsps, or preventing the native conformation would all make aggregation worse. Blocking alpha-helix formation does not lead to correct folding. Big picture: Cells have two answers to misfolding: refold it with chaperones, or destroy it through ubiquitin-proteasome degradation. Therapy for aggregate diseases boosts one of these two arms. CF uses both ideas: the cell degrades misfolded CFTR, and correctors act as chaperones. SGA drive (MSK 2) — 2021-2025 Self-assessments compiled by AI in 2026 - genetic code, proteoglycans, glycoprot · this fact is asked in 4 sources
How it follows from the main questionFailed-folding proteins go ubiquitin → proteasome; enhancing it lowers aggregate load → enhances the ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. Every other option promotes misfolding.

Protein folding and misfolding

3unlocks 20TA ×25 not obvious
A neurodegenerative disease is characterized by intracellular Lewy bodies made of a misfolded protein. Which disease–protein pairing is correct?
  1. A. ALS – amyloid-β
  2. B. Alzheimer disease – huntingtin
  3. C. Parkinson disease – α-synuclein
  4. D. Huntington disease – SOD1
  5. E. Parkinson disease – amyloid-β
AnswerC. Parkinson disease – α-synuclein
WhyParkinson = α-synuclein (Lewy bodies). Every other option swaps a protein between diseases: amyloid-β is Alzheimer, SOD1 is ALS, huntingtin (polyQ) is Huntington.
Key factMisfolded proteins tend to form β-sheet-rich amyloid fibrils and aggregates:
  • Alzheimer: amyloid-β (cleaved from APP; normal sequence, misfolded) → extracellular β-sheet plaques + intracellular hyperphosphorylated tau tangles. ApoE4 = risk (more plaques), ApoE2 = protective. Therapy idea: slow Aβ aggregation.
  • Parkinson: α-synuclein (Lewy bodies).
  • Huntington: expanded CAG → polyglutamine tract in huntingtin → misfolding and aggregation, a toxic gain of function (autosomal dominant; midlife chorea, personality change).
  • ALS: SOD1.
The interactive-session slide lists ALS with TDP-43; every practice question keys SOD1.

  • Amyloid-β has a normal sequence (misfolded, not mutated); Huntington is not a deletion or loss of function.

Practice Q306Answered by elimination
Q2: A 43-year-old patient presents with progressive movement disorder and family history of neurodegeneration. Genetic testing reveals a polyglutamine (polyQ) expansion in the huntingtin protein. Which of the following best explains the cellular pathology?
  1. A) Loss of heme group incorporation prevents normal protein function
  2. B) Reduced proteasome degradation increases α-synuclein accumulation
  3. C) β-sheet rich amyloid plaques accumulate extracellularly in cerebral cortex
  4. D) Excessive chaperone activity stabilizes abnormal folding intermediates
  5. E) Increased hydrophobic interactions cause protein aggregation and misfolding
AnswerE. Increased hydrophobic interactions cause protein aggregation and misfolding
WhyAn expanded CAG repeat adds a long polyglutamine tract to huntingtin, which misfolds and exposes sticky surfaces that drive aggregation into toxic neuronal inclusions. α-synuclein is Parkinson disease and extracellular amyloid plaques are Alzheimer disease.
Explanation from the source
Explanation: Polyglutamine (CAG repeat) expansions cause abnormal protein folding → hydrophobic aggregation → toxic neuronal inclusions (Huntington disease).
How it follows from the main questionHuntington = polyQ huntingtin misfolds and aggregates. Cross out α-synuclein (Parkinson), extracellular plaques (Alzheimer), heme and 'excess chaperones' → increased hydrophobic interactions cause aggregation and misfolding.
Practice Q573Trap: the obvious answer is wrong
An 80-year-old man presented with impairment of higher intellectual function and alterations in mood and behavior. His family reported progressive disorientation and memory loss over the last 6 months. There is no family history of dementia. The patient was tentatively diagnosed with Alzheimer disease. Which one of the following best describes Alzheimer disease?
  1. A. It is associated with β-amyloid, an abnormal protein with an altered amino acid sequence.
  2. B. It results from accumulation of denatured proteins that have random conformations.
  3. C. It is associated with the accumulation of amyloid precursor protein.
  4. D. It is associated with the deposition of neurotoxic amyloid β peptide aggregates.
  5. E. It is an environmentally produced disease not influenced by the genetics of the individual.
  6. F. It is caused by the infectious β-sheet form of a host-cell protein.
AnswerD. It is associated with the deposition of neurotoxic amyloid β peptide aggregates.
WhyAlzheimer disease involves deposition of neurotoxic amyloid-β aggregates, cleaved from normal APP and misfolded into β-sheet fibrils; the peptide sequence is normal, the deposits are ordered, genetics (ApoE4, APP, presenilins) matter, and infectious β-sheet proteins are prions.
Explanation from the source
Amyloid-beta has a normal amino acid sequence. It is cut out of the normal amyloid precursor protein and then misfolds into neurotoxic beta-sheet aggregates, which make the deposits. The deposits are ordered fibrils, not random denatured protein or intact APP, and genetics plays a part (APP, presenilins, ApoE4). The infectious beta-sheet form of a host protein describes prions, not Alzheimer.
How it follows from the main questionAβ has a normal sequence (kills 'altered sequence'), is cleaved from APP (kills 'APP accumulates'), and infectious β-sheet is prion → deposition of neurotoxic amyloid-β aggregates.
Practice Q246Vignette never names it
16. A 69-year-old former bank president cannot tell you the name of the current president and has difficulty identifying the woman sitting next to him (his wife). He began having memory problems 3 years ago. The postmortem brain biopsy or this patient is most likely to show
Show figure
  1. (A) increased 3-methoxy-4- hydroxyphenylglycol (MHPG)
  2. (B) right frontal hypertrophy
  3. (C) decreased calcium levels
  4. (D) decreased homovanillic acid (HVA)
  5. (E) deposition of β-amyloid
AnswerE. deposition of β-amyloid
WhyGradual memory loss over years, progressing to failure to recognize family (prosopagnosia), is Alzheimer disease. Its pathology is extracellular β-amyloid plaques (misfolded Aβ from APP) plus intracellular tau neurofibrillary tangles. HVA and MHPG are dopamine and norepinephrine metabolites.
How it follows from the main questionSlow, years-long memory loss is Alzheimer, never named → β-amyloid deposition. HVA and MHPG are dopamine and norepinephrine metabolites, not misfolding.
Practice Q561Vignette never names it
A patient has midlife onset of the following symptoms: abnormal, involuntary jerking body movements, an unsteady gait, personality changes, and chewing and swallowing difficulty, which has led to a gradual weight loss. The patient’s father had similar symptoms before his death at the age of 45. Cellular analysis indicated precipitated proteins in the nucleus. This disease has, at its origins, which biochemical problem?
  1. A. An exonic deletion
  2. B. A polyglutamine tract in an exon of the defective gene
  3. C. A nonsense mutation leading to the production of a truncated protein
  4. D. A splicing mutation, leading to the insertion of intronic sequences into the mature protein
  5. E. Production of an unstable mRNA, leading to reduced protein production
AnswerB. A polyglutamine tract in an exon of the defective gene
WhyMidlife chorea, personality change, dysphagia, an affected father and nuclear aggregates indicate Huntington disease: an expanded CAG repeat in an exon of HTT encodes a polyglutamine tract that makes huntingtin misfold and aggregate.
How it follows from the main questionMidlife chorea + personality change + affected parent = Huntington → expanded CAG → polyglutamine tract in an exon. Not a deletion, nonsense or splicing loss.

Protein folding and misfolding

4unlocks 7TA ×13 not obvious
A 77-year-old dies after years of progressive memory loss. The cortex shows extracellular deposits of a peptide cut from amyloid precursor protein (APP). Which statement best describes these deposits?
  1. A. An infectious protein that converts the host's normal copies into its own shape
  2. B. Intact APP that piles up because it is never cleaved
  3. C. A peptide with an abnormal amino acid sequence, folded mainly as α-helix
  4. D. Ordered fibrils of a normal-sequence peptide, rich in β-pleated sheet
  5. E. Randomly coiled, denatured protein whose peptide bonds have been cleaved
AnswerD. Ordered fibrils of a normal-sequence peptide, rich in β-pleated sheet
WhyAmyloid-β is cut from normal APP by secretases and spontaneously adopts β-sheet, stacking into ordered, insoluble amyloid fibrils (plaques). The sequence is normal and no peptide bonds are broken; only the fold changes. 'Infectious' describes prions, and the deposit is the cleaved Aβ peptide, not intact APP.
Key fact
  • Misfolded proteins tend to adopt β-pleated sheet, oligomerize and stack into insoluble amyloid fibrils: Alzheimer amyloid-β, Parkinson α-synuclein, ALS, polyQ huntingtin, prion PrPSc.
  • Alzheimer: Aβ is cut from APP by secretases; the peptide's sequence is normal, it spontaneously folds into β-sheet and aggregates into extracellular plaques (hyperphosphorylated tau tangles are the intracellular lesion). Therapy idea: compounds that slow Aβ aggregation into fibrils.
  • What changes is conformation, not sequence: peptide and other covalent bonds stay intact; the fibrils are ordered (not random coils) and resist proteases (PrPSc), so they accumulate.
  • Only prions are infectious.
TA2 is listed in J1_ta.md (shared TA numbering); J2 item 1 already carries it. q355 keys Alzheimer, though Parkinson α-synuclein also forms β-sheet fibrils; Alzheimer amyloid is the classic answer.
What it unlocks: 8 questions

The 3 questions you might not expect it to answer are in the dropdown at the bottom.

How it shows up

  • TA: Alzheimer plaques derived from APP → which structural feature? → predominantly β-pleated sheet (distractors: α-helix, peptide-bond cleavage, loss of all covalent bonds, extra normal subunits)
  • 'High content of which feature in amyloid plaques?' or 'characteristic feature of Alzheimer?' → β-pleated sheets (distractors: CAG repeats, prions, α-synuclein, disulfide bonds)
  • Reverse: 'which disease comes from β-sheet-rich fibrils in neural tissue?' → Alzheimer; 'promising therapy strategy?' → slow Aβ aggregation into fibrils
  • Lippincott 'best describes Alzheimer disease': Aβ peptide aggregates, not an altered sequence, random denatured coils, APP accumulation or an infectious β-sheet protein

What it lets you eliminate

  • Cross out α-helix as the structure of aggregates, and any option saying peptide bonds are cleaved or all covalent bonds are lost.
  • Cross out 'altered amino acid sequence', 'random conformation' and 'APP accumulation' for Aβ.
  • Cross out 'infectious' unless the case is a prion disease (cadaver tissue, kuru, dementia killing within a year).
  • Sickle cell polymer is not amyloid; Marfan syndrome is fibrillin.

Practice Q548Asked from the other direction
A clinical study was conducted to develop a promising therapeutic strategy for treatment of Alzheimer disease. Which of the following strategies was utilized in this study?
  1. A. Surgical removal of selective regions of the cerebral cortex
  2. B. Administration of serotonergic agonists that act specifically on cerebral cortical neurons
  3. C. Administration of cholinergic antagonists directed against nicotinic receptors in the cerebral cortex
  4. D. Administration of noradrenergic agonists directed against α 2 receptors in the cerebral cortex
  5. E. Administration of compounds that slow aggregation of amyloid-β peptide into its fibrillar form
AnswerE. Administration of compounds that slow aggregation of amyloid-β peptide into its fibrillar form
WhyAmyloid-β misfolds into β-sheet fibrils that form plaques, so slowing its aggregation targets the disease mechanism. Cortical resection makes no sense, and cholinergic antagonists would worsen the existing cholinergic deficit.
How it follows from the main questionThe disease step is Aβ misfolding into β-sheet fibrils, so therapy targets that step → compounds that slow Aβ aggregation into fibrils.
Practice Q355Answered by elimination
Which of the following diseases results from abnormal protein misfolding and aggregation of β-pleated sheet–rich fibrils in neural tissue?
  1. A. Alzheimer’s disease
  2. B. Sickle cell anemia
  3. C. Parkinson’s Disease
  4. D. Marfan syndrome
AnswerA. Alzheimer’s disease
WhyIn Alzheimer disease, Aβ peptide cleaved from APP misfolds into β-pleated sheet-rich amyloid fibrils that form extracellular plaques in cortex. Sickle cell is HbS polymerization in RBCs, and Marfan syndrome is a fibrillin defect. Note: Parkinson α-synuclein (Lewy bodies) also forms β-sheet fibrils, but Alzheimer amyloid is the classic answer.
Explanation from the source
Alzheimer’s disease involves misfolding and aggregation of β-amyloid peptides into amyloid fibrils rich in β-sheet structure. There are other protein-misfolding diseases like prion diseases (Creutzfeldt-Jakob) and Parkinson’s disease (α-synuclein aggregates), but they don’t form this characteristic structure. Chaperone proteins normally help ensure proper folding; failure leads to aggregation, ER stress, and cell death.
How it follows from the main questionβ-sheet fibrils = amyloid; the classic plaque disease is Alzheimer. Sickle cell is deoxyHbS polymer in RBCs, Marfan is fibrillin; Parkinson also fits but Alzheimer is keyed.

Protein folding and misfolding

5unlocks 92 not obvious
A pathologist cuts a finger during the autopsy of a patient who died of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. What kind of agent could transmit the disease?
  1. A. An RNA polynucleotide
  2. B. A misfolded protein containing no nucleic acid
  3. C. A DNA virus
  4. D. A lipid
  5. E. A bacterium
AnswerB. A misfolded protein containing no nucleic acid
WhyPrions are infectious proteins without nucleic acid: PrPSc has the same amino acid sequence as normal PrPC but a different fold, and it templates normal PrP into more PrPSc. A virus is the tempting answer only because the disease is transmissible.
Key factPrion = misfolded form of a normal host protein (PrP).
  • Same amino acid sequence, different conformation: α-helix → β-sheet, a change in secondary structure.
  • PrPSc templates PrPC into PrPSc; infectious without nucleic acid; β-sheet aggregates are protease resistant, so they cannot be cleared.
  • Diseases: Creutzfeldt-Jakob (sporadic, familial, iatrogenic: cadaver tissue, growth hormone), mad cow, kuru (New Guinea cannibalism), scrapie. Rapidly progressive dementia (death within about a year), spongiform vacuolated neurons.
q247's stem mentions neurofibrillary tangles (an Alzheimer finding), but the key is prion disease, chosen for the rapid one-year course.

Practice Q571Vignette never names it
A 56-year-old pathologist was taken to his family doctor by his son for he was showing mood changes, minor loss of memory, and decreased motor skills. During the patient history, it became clear that over the course of his career he had, on occasion, cut himself using the instruments he had been using on the cadavers he had been working on. A potential explanation for his symptoms is abnormal aggregation of which of the following proteins?

  2. B. Fibrillin in the extracellular compartments of the brain

  5. E. A truncated extracellular protein
AnswerD. A misfolded form of a normal protein

  5. E. Irregular amino acid sequence and greater sensitivity to heat and pH
AnswerE. Irregular amino acid sequence and greater sensitivity to heat and pH
WhyGlobular proteins are rounded, soluble, functional (transport, catalysis), with irregular sequences, and are more sensitive to heat and pH. The other four options all describe fibrous proteins.
Key fact
  • Fibrous (collagen, keratin, elastin, myosin, actin, fibrin): long and narrow; structural (strength, support); insoluble; repetitive sequence; less sensitive to heat and pH.
  • Globular (hemoglobin, catalase, insulin, immunoglobulins, enzymes): rounded and compact; functional (transport, catalysis); soluble; irregular sequence; more sensitive to heat and pH.
  • So fibrous-protein defects weaken tissues (lax joints, fragile vessels); globular-protein defects lose function (anemia, hypoxia).
q504 is keyed only 'irregular sequence', but the course table also makes 'less stable to heat and pH' a globular property (the key note accepts B and C).

What it lets you eliminate

  • Bohr effect, heme groups and O2 transport belong to globular Hb, never to collagen.

Which statement correctly contrasts myoglobin with hemoglobin?
  1. A. Myoglobin has a sigmoidal curve; hemoglobin has a hyperbolic curve
  2. B. Myoglobin is a tetramer with four hemes; hemoglobin is a monomer with one
  3. C. Myoglobin is a muscle monomer that stores O2 with higher affinity (lower P50) and a hyperbolic curve
  4. D. They differ mainly in secondary and tertiary structure
  5. E. Hemoglobin binds O2 with higher affinity than myoglobin
AnswerC. Myoglobin is a muscle monomer that stores O2 with higher affinity (lower P50) and a hyperbolic curve
WhyMyoglobin: monomer, one heme, in muscle, stores O2, high affinity (P50 about 1 mm Hg), hyperbolic. Hemoglobin: tetramer, four hemes, in RBCs, transports O2, P50 about 26 mm Hg, sigmoidal. They share their primary-to-tertiary fold and differ in quaternary structure, so E is the trap.
Key fact
  • Myoglobin: monomer (~17 kDa), 1 heme, 1 O2; cardiac and skeletal muscle; O2 storage for ATP generation during contraction; hyperbolic curve; higher affinity (P50 ≈ 1 mm Hg); no cooperativity.
  • Hemoglobin: tetramer (~64 kDa; 2 α-like + 2 β-like), 4 hemes, 4 O2; in RBCs; O2 transport lungs → tissues; sigmoidal (cooperative); lower affinity (P50 ≈ 26 mm Hg).
  • Similar primary, secondary and tertiary structure; they differ in quaternary structure. Both use Fe2+ heme. In tissues O2 passes from Hb to Mb.

A mutant hemoglobin tetramer binds O2 at every heme, but O2 binding at one subunit no longer changes the affinity of the others. Its O2-binding curve will most resemble which?
  1. A. Sigmoidal and shifted left
  2. B. Hyperbolic like myoglobin, with poor unloading to tissues
  3. C. Flat, binding no O2
  4. D. Sigmoidal and shifted right, with better unloading
  5. E. The normal hemoglobin curve
AnswerB. Hyperbolic like myoglobin, with poor unloading to tissues
WhyThe sigmoidal shape comes from positive cooperativity. Without it the tetramer behaves like four myoglobins: hyperbolic, high affinity, little O2 released at tissue PO2. A shifted sigmoid is the trap; shifts come from effectors, not from losing cooperativity.
Key fact
  • Positive cooperativity: O2 binding to one subunit shifts the tetramer from T toward R and raises the affinity of the remaining subunits, so affinity increases as saturation rises → sigmoidal curve.
  • Requires quaternary structure (4 interacting subunits); monomeric Mb cannot cooperate → hyperbolic. Lose cooperativity → hyperbolic, poor unloading.
  • Payoff: the steep middle releases a lot of O2 over the tissue PO2 range; the flat top protects loading (alveolar PO2 104 → 60 mm Hg drops saturation only 97% → 89%).

T and R states: shifting the curve

10unlocks 153 not obvious
Which of the following shifts the hemoglobin–O2 dissociation curve to the LEFT?
  1. A. Carbon monoxide poisoning
  2. B. Decreased pH
  3. C. Strenuous exercise
  4. D. Increased 2,3-BPG
  5. E. Fever
AnswerA. Carbon monoxide poisoning
WhyCO locks the tetramer in the high-affinity R state → left shift. Exercise, ↑2,3-BPG, fever and ↓pH all stabilize the T state → right shift.
Key factT (taut) = deoxy, low affinity; R (relaxed) = oxy, high affinity.
  • Right shift (stabilize T, unload O2): ↑H+ (↓pH), ↑CO2, ↑2,3-BPG, ↑temperature → exercise, altitude adaptation, acidosis, shock.
  • Left shift (stabilize R, hold O2): ↑O2 itself, CO, ↓H+ (↑pH, alkalosis), ↓CO2 (hyperventilation), ↓2,3-BPG, ↓temperature, HbF (α2γ2).

  4. D. Decreased O2-carrying capacity of hemoglobin
  5. E. Increased affinity of hemoglobin for O2

WhyA right shift means lower affinity, so a higher PO2 is needed for 50% saturation: ↑P50 and easier unloading. Carrying capacity depends on how much Hb there is, so a shift never changes it.
Key fact
  • P50 = the PO2 at which Hb is 50% saturated (read it at half of the curve's maximum: plateau 20 mL/dL → 10 mL/dL point).
  • Right shift = ↓affinity = ↑P50 = more unloading in tissues (T state).
  • Left shift = ↑affinity = ↓P50 = harder unloading (R state).
  • O2-binding capacity (≈1.34 mL O2 per g Hb) is not changed by curve shifts or by PO2.

The Bohr effect and CO2

12unlocks 14TA ×22 not obvious
During vigorous exercise, CO2 and H+ rise in skeletal muscle capillaries. What happens to hemoglobin there?
  1. A. Increased H+ stabilizes the T state, lowering O2 affinity and releasing O2
  2. B. CO2 binds the heme iron and displaces O2
  3. C. Increased pH stabilizes the R state, promoting O2 release
  4. D. Decreased pH increases hemoglobin's O2 affinity
  5. E. H+ prevents hemoglobin from releasing O2
AnswerA. Increased H+ stabilizes the T state, lowering O2 affinity and releasing O2
WhyBohr effect: H+ (made from CO2 by carbonic anhydrase) protonates Hb side chains (histidine) and stabilizes T → right shift → O2 is released where metabolism is high. CO2 binds globin N-terminal amino groups, never the heme iron.
Key fact
  • Bohr effect = Hb O2 affinity falls as pH falls and CO2 rises (temperature shifts the curve too, but it is not part of the Bohr effect).
  • Tissues: CO2 → carbonic acid → H+ binds histidines (pKa near blood pH), and CO2 forms carbamino-Hb → both stabilize T → right shift → O2 unloading.
  • Lungs (higher pH, lower CO2): the reverse → R → left shift → O2 loading.
  • Reciprocal: H+ binding lowers O2 affinity, and O2 binding lowers H+ affinity (oxyHb releases H+; deoxyHb is the better buffer). H+ and O2 bind different sites.

  • 'Which statement about the Bohr effect is INCORRECT?' → 'O2 binding increases Hb's affinity for H+'; 'which amino acid accepts H+?' → histidine; 'which factors make up the Bohr effect?' → low pH, high CO2

What it lets you eliminate

Practice Q398Trap: the obvious answer is wrong
Why is deoxygenated hemoglobin a better buffer for H⁺ than oxygenated hemoglobin?
  1. A. Because it binds CO₂ more strongly
  2. B. Because it has more available histidine residues
  3. C. Because oxygenation reduces hemoglobin’s buffering capacity
  4. D. Because it prevents carbonic anhydrase activity
AnswerC. Because oxygenation reduces hemoglobin’s buffering capacity
WhyReleasing O₂ shifts Hb to the T conformation, which raises the pKa of key histidines (such as β-His146) so they bind H⁺. Oxygenation reverses this and releases those protons (the Haldane effect), so oxyHb is the poorer buffer. The number of histidines does not change, only their pKa.
Explanation from the source
Deoxygenated Hb binds H⁺ more effectively, stabilizing pH and facilitating CO₂ uptake; oxygenation reverses this.
How it follows from the main questionReciprocal Bohr: O2 binding lowers H+ affinity, so oxygenation reduces buffering capacity. 'More histidines' is the trap: the number is fixed, only their pKa changes.

The Bohr effect and CO2

13unlocks 3TA ×12 not obvious
Deoxygenated blood from exercising muscle reaches the pulmonary capillaries, where CO2 is exhaled and PO2 is high. As hemoglobin binds O2 there, which change occurs?
  1. A. O2 displaces H+ from the heme iron, where both bind
  2. B. Hb shifts toward the R state and releases H+, which joins HCO3− to re-form CO2 for exhalation
  3. C. Hb shifts toward the T state and takes up more H+
  4. D. OxyHb becomes a better H+ buffer than deoxyHb
  5. E. The rise in pH lowers O2 affinity, shifting the curve right
AnswerB. Hb shifts toward the R state and releases H+, which joins HCO3− to re-form CO2 for exhalation
WhyIn the lungs, ↓CO2 and ↑pH favor the R state (left shift), so Hb loads O2. Binding is reciprocal: O2 binding lowers Hb's H+ affinity, so oxyHb releases H+, which joins HCO3− → H2CO3 → CO2 + H2O (exhaled). H+ binds histidines, not heme iron, and deoxyHb, not oxyHb, is the better buffer.
Key fact
  • The Bohr effect runs both ways. Tissues (↓pH, ↑CO2): T state, right shift, O2 released, H+ taken up by deoxyHb. Lungs (↑pH, ↓CO2): R state, left shift, O2 loaded.
  • Reciprocal binding: H+ binding lowers O2 affinity, and O2 binding lowers H+ affinity. So oxygenation releases H+ (in the lungs it re-forms CO2 from HCO3− for exhalation, with the reverse chloride shift), and deoxyHb is the better H+ buffer, which is why venous pH is only slightly lower than arterial pH.
  • H+ binds globin histidines and CO2 binds N-terminal amino groups, separate from the heme O2 site, yet each changes the others' binding.
  • Higher pH → higher O2 affinity (left shift), never lower.

  • 'Which statement about the Bohr effect is INCORRECT?' → 'O2 binding increases Hb's affinity for H+'
  • 'Venous pH is only slightly more acidic than arterial because…' → H+ is buffered by deoxyHb

What it lets you eliminate

The Bohr effect and CO2

A free diver hyperventilates before a dive and blacks out underwater. What did the hyperventilation do to O2 delivery to the tissues?

  • Hyperventilation → ↓PCO2 → ↓H+ (↑pH, respiratory alkalosis) → reduced Bohr effect → R state → left shift, ↓P50, ↑affinity → less O2 unloaded to tissues.

  • Contrast: exercise, acidosis and altitude acclimatization shift the curve right.

  • Graph: a leftward shift from A to B is most likely from → hyperventilation (vs heat, exercise, altitude, metabolic acidosis)
  • 'Which causes a left shift?' or 'affinity is increased by?' → hyperventilation / decreased CO2
  • Patient breathing off CO2 → P50 decreases, curve shifts left

In venous blood carrying CO2 from the tissues to the lungs, which event occurs?
  1. A. H+ is buffered mainly by oxyhemoglobin
  2. B. The red cells become alkaline
  3. C. HCO3− binds to hemoglobin
  4. D. Carbonic anhydrase in red cells converts CO2 + H2O to H+ + HCO3−
  5. E. HCO3− moves into red cells in exchange for Cl−
AnswerD. Carbonic anhydrase in red cells converts CO2 + H2O to H+ + HCO3−
WhyIn the RBC, carbonic anhydrase catalyzes CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3−. H+ is buffered by deoxyHb, HCO3− leaves the cell in exchange for Cl− (chloride shift), and it is CO2, not HCO3−, that binds Hb as carbamino-Hb.
Key fact
  • Tissue RBC: carbonic anhydrase CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3−.
  • H+ is buffered by deoxyHb (Bohr), so venous pH falls only slightly.
  • HCO3− exits to plasma in exchange for Cl− (chloride shift) → most CO2 travels as HCO3− in plasma.
  • Some CO2 binds globin N-terminal amino groups = carbaminohemoglobin → stabilizes T, promotes O2 unloading.
  • Lungs: everything reverses (reverse chloride shift) and CO2 is exhaled.

Which statement about the human globin genes and the hemoglobins they encode is correct?
  1. A. Every hemoglobin pairs two α-like with two β-like chains: HbA α2β2, HbA2 α2δ2, HbF α2γ2
  2. B. The β-like family (ε, γ, δ, β) lies on chromosome 16

WhyTwo families: α-like (ζ, α; chromosome 16) and β-like (ε, γ, δ, β; chromosome 11). Every Hb takes two of each: HbA α2β2 (most of adult Hb), HbA2 α2δ2, HbF α2γ2. γ is β-like, and α2δ2 is HbA2, not HbF.
Key fact
  • α-like family: ζ, α1, α2 on chromosome 16 (HBA1 + HBA2 on each copy = 4 α genes; α-thalassemia = their deletion). β-like family: ε, Gγ, Aγ, δ, β on chromosome 11 (HBB; 2 β genes).

  • Reading rules: γ chain → HbF; δ chain → HbA2; HbA2 and HbF contain no β, so both rise when β is short (β-thalassemia), and β-chain disease shows up only months after birth.

Which statement about carbon monoxide's effect on hemoglobin is NOT true?
  1. A. It makes the curve more hyperbolic
  2. B. It makes the remaining heme sites bind O2 with lower affinity
  3. C. It shifts hemoglobin toward the relaxed (R) state
  4. D. It binds heme Fe2+ about 220 times more tightly than O2
  5. E. It shifts the O2-binding curve to the left
AnswerB. It makes the remaining heme sites bind O2 with lower affinity
WhyCO on one heme pushes the tetramer to R, so the remaining hemes hold O2 more tightly (left shift, hyperbolic) and do not unload. That double hit (fewer sites plus no release) is why 50% COHb kills while a 50% anemia does not.
Key fact
  • CO binds heme Fe2+ ~220× (sources say 200–250×) more avidly than O2; binding is reversible.
  • Hit 1: occupies sites → ↓O2 content and saturation (curve plateau lowered).
  • Hit 2: shifts Hb to R → remaining O2 held tightly → left shift, curve becomes hyperbolic → little release to tissues.
  • So 50% COHb is fatal but a 50% anemia is not (the remaining normal Hb still unloads). CO binds Mb too, but Hb cooperativity makes delivery especially impaired.
Lecture gives 220×; some faculty answers say 240× or 210–250×.

  • Graph: CO curve = lowered plateau + left shift; 50% CO loss vs 50% anemia

  3. C. Carbon monoxide
  4. D. Carbon dioxide
  5. E. Nitrite
AnswerC. Carbon monoxide
WhyIncomplete combustion in an enclosed space (propane engine or lantern, car in a garage, house fire, heavy indoor smoking) makes CO. Standard pulse oximetry reads COHb as oxyHb, so 99% is falsely reassuring. CO2, the product of complete combustion, is the classic distractor.
Key fact
  • Source: incomplete combustion in a closed space: propane forklift or lantern, running car in a garage, house fire, indoor smoking.
  • Clues: headache, dizziness, nausea, irritability, confusion, seizure, tachycardia, tachypnea, cherry-red skin; pulse oximetry falsely normal (COHb counted as oxyHb); elevated carboxyhemoglobin; lactic acidosis.
  • Mechanism (3 parts): ↓O2 delivery (COHb, left shift), ↓O2 utilization (CO binds Fe2+ of complex IV, cytochrome c oxidase), and ROS with lipid peroxidation. Brain and heart (highest O2 demand) are hit first.
What it unlocks: 20 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Richard F. case (propane forklift): source? mechanism? systems affected? → CO from forklift fumes; brain, heart, lungs
  • Closed tent with a propane lantern → carbon monoxide (distractors CO2, nitrite, nitrate, thiosulfate, methanol)
  • House fire with elevated carboxyHb and metabolic acidosis; couple who smoke indoors and improve on 100% O2 → carboxyhemoglobin
  • 'Mechanism of toxicity?' → impaired delivery, impaired utilization and ROS (all of the above); 'what did the patient present with?' → normal O2 saturation

What it lets you eliminate

  • Cross out CO2 (complete combustion), thiosulfate and nitrite (cyanide antidotes), and rotenone, DNP or oligomycin (no exposure source).
  • A normal pulse oximeter reading never rules out CO.

A worker recovers in the ER after several hours of breathing 100% O2 for a workplace exposure. Why does this treatment work if the toxin is carbon monoxide?
  1. A. CO is a noncompetitive inhibitor that O2 cannot displace
  2. B. O2 shifts the curve to the left, releasing O2 to tissues
  3. C. O2 converts CO to CO2 in the blood
  4. D. O2 reduces Fe3+ heme back to Fe2+
  5. E. CO binds the same heme site reversibly, so high O2 competes it off and shortens the COHb half-life
AnswerE. CO binds the same heme site reversibly, so high O2 competes it off and shortens the COHb half-life
WhyCO and O2 compete for the same Fe2+ heme site, and CO is not covalently bound, so it is a competitive, reversible inhibitor: flooding with 100% O2 (hyperbaric if severe) displaces it. Reducing Fe3+ is methylene blue's job in methemoglobinemia.
Key fact
  • CO = competitive inhibitor (same heme site on Hb and on complex IV), reversible (noncovalent).
  • Treatment: 100% O2; hyperbaric O2 if severe (seizure, coma). COHb half-life ≈ 4–6 h on room air → ≈ 80 min on 100% O2 → ≈ 20 min hyperbaric.
  • Not CO treatment: nitrites and thiosulfate (cyanide), methylene blue (metHb), CO2 rebreathing, ferrous sulfate, hyperventilation.

Carbon monoxide

27unlocks 117 not obvious
A worker exposed to nitrites has cyanosis that does not improve with supplemental O2. Which value is most likely normal?
  1. A. O2 delivery to peripheral tissue
  2. B. Arterial O2 content
  3. C. Arterial PO2
  4. D. O2-carrying capacity of arterial blood
  5. E. Bound fraction (saturation) of arterial O2
AnswerC. Arterial PO2
WhyPaO2 measures only O2 dissolved in plasma, set by lung gas exchange, which is intact. Methemoglobin (like COHb) cannot carry O2, so saturation, content, capacity and delivery fall. Extra O2 raises PaO2 but not the Hb-bound O2.
Key fact
  • PaO2 = dissolved O2 (alveolar gas exchange). Saturation = % of heme sites holding O2. Content ≈ 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 (plus a tiny dissolved part).
  • CO poisoning and methemoglobinemia: PaO2 (and alveolar PO2) normal; true SaO2, content and delivery ↓; supplemental O2 raises PaO2 but does not fix the cyanosis of metHb.
  • Anemia: PaO2 and saturation normal, content ↓. Low V/Q, shunt and hypoventilation lower PaO2 itself.
  • Raising PO2 raises % saturation; raising Hb raises content, not % saturation; neither PO2 nor curve shifts change binding capacity per gram.
What it unlocks: 11 questions

The 7 questions you might not expect it to answer are in the dropdown at the bottom.

How it shows up

  • Nitrite worker with O2-resistant cyanosis: which value is most likely normal → PaO2 (5 near-identical copies)

  • 'Which lowers saturation without lowering O2 tension?' → CO poisoning
  • Explain why raising FiO2 raised PaO2 but not the cyanosis; which changes alter binding capacity → none

What it lets you eliminate

  • In CO or metHb, when asked what is normal, cross out everything except PaO2 or alveolar PO2.
  • Anemia does not lower saturation; low V/Q, shunt and hypoventilation lower PaO2.

Practice Q409Trap: the obvious answer is wrong
252. The percentage of hemoglobin saturated with oxygen will increase if
  1. A. The arterial PCO2 is increased
  2. B. The hemoglobin concentration is increased
  3. C. The temperature is increased
  4. D. The arterial PO2 is increased
  5. E. The arterial pH is decreased
AnswerD. The arterial PO2 is increased
WhySaturation follows the curve: raising arterial PO₂ moves up the curve and raises % saturation (if not already near 100%). Higher PCO₂, temperature or acidity shift the curve right and lower saturation; more Hb raises O₂ content, not percent saturation.
Explanation from the source
252. The answer is d. (Guyton, pp 466-469.) The percentage of hemoglobin saturated with oxygen depends on the level of PO2 in the blood and on other factors that affect the position of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve. Factors that shift the curve to the left, such as a decrease in PCO2, an increase in pH, or a decrease in temperature, would increase the percentage of hemoglobin saturated with oxygen as would an increase in PO2, provided that the percentage of saturation was not already at 100%. At a given PO2, increasing the concentration of hemoglobin would not affect the percentage of saturation but would increase the oxygen content of the blood.
How it follows from the main questionMore Hb raises content, not % saturation (the trap). Higher PCO2, heat and acid shift right and lower it → arterial PO2 increased.
Practice Q405Asked from the other direction
222. Which of the following conditions causes a decrease in arterial O2 saturation without a decrease in O2 tension?
  1. A. Anemia
  2. B. Carbon monoxide poisoning
  3. C. A low V/Q ratio
  4. D. Hypoventilation
  5. E. Right-to-left shunt
AnswerB. Carbon monoxide poisoning
WhyCO occupies heme sites, so Hb saturation falls while dissolved O₂ and therefore PaO₂ stay normal. A low V/Q ratio, hypoventilation and right-to-left shunt all lower PaO₂ itself, and anemia lowers O₂ content but leaves saturation normal.
Explanation from the source
222. The answer is b. (Rhoades, pp 391-398.) A rise or fall in the oxygen saturation of hemoglobin is caused by a decrease in the arterial O2 tension, which can result from a low V/Q ratio, hypoventilation, or an anatomical right-to-left shunt. Because carbon monoxide (CO) competes with O2 on the hemoglobin molecule, CO poisoning can cause a decrease in hemoglobin's saturation even when the PO2 is normal. In anemia, oxygen saturation is unchanged but the concentration of hemoglobin is less than normal, reducing the oxygen content.
How it follows from the main question'O2 tension' = PaO2. V/Q mismatch, hypoventilation and shunt lower PaO2; anemia keeps saturation normal → CO poisoning (saturation ↓, PaO2 normal).

28unlocks 5TA ×12 not obvious
A 4-month-old has cyanosis, dyspnea and lethargy. Drawn blood is chocolate-brown, and testing shows more hemoglobin with oxidized (Fe3+) iron. Which is the diagnosis?

  2. B. Methemoglobinemia
  3. C. Sickle cell anemia
  4. D. Carbon monoxide poisoning
  5. E. Iron deficiency anemia
AnswerB. Methemoglobinemia
WhyFe3+ heme cannot bind O2 = methemoglobin: cyanosis not corrected by O2 and chocolate-brown blood. CO poisoning keeps the iron Fe2+ and gives cherry-red, not brown, blood.
Key fact
  • Methemoglobin = heme iron oxidized Fe2+ → Fe3+ → cannot bind O2.
  • Causes: oxidizing drugs and chemicals: nitrites/nitrates (isosorbide dinitrate, nitroglycerin, contaminated water), local anesthetics (benzocaine), nitroprusside; or inherited NADH–methemoglobin reductase deficiency or HbM (lifelong cyanosis that runs in families).
  • Signs: cyanosis unresponsive to O2, chocolate-brown blood, headache, anxiety, dyspnea; PaO2 normal.
  • Treatment: methylene blue (reduces Fe3+ → Fe2+ via the reductase).
  • Made on purpose: nitrites create metHb, which binds cyanide (cyanmethemoglobin) and pulls it off complex IV, then thiosulfate. Cyanide = O2 delivered but not used; CO = O2 not delivered (100% O2).

Qualitative vs quantitative hemoglobinopathies

29unlocks 5TA ×12 not obvious
A child with sickle cell disease has β-globin mRNA of normal amount and length. A cousin with β-thalassemia makes β chains of normal structure, but too few of them. Which statement correctly classifies the two disorders?
  1. A. Both result from defective heme synthesis rather than a globin defect
  2. B. Both are qualitative, because each changes the shape of hemoglobin
  3. C. Sickle cell: frameshift mutation; β-thalassemia: increased synthesis of both α and β chains
  4. D. Sickle cell: qualitative, from a missense point mutation; β-thalassemia: quantitative, with too few β chains for the α chains made
  5. E. Sickle cell: quantitative, from a nonsense mutation; β-thalassemia: qualitative
AnswerD. Sickle cell: qualitative, from a missense point mutation; β-thalassemia: quantitative, with too few β chains for the α chains made
WhyQualitative = a normal amount of a structurally abnormal chain; one base change swapping one amino acid (β6 Glu→Val) is a missense mutation, so mRNA size and level stay normal. Thalassemia is quantitative: a normal chain made in reduced amounts → α:β imbalance. Nonsense and frameshift mutations change the product's length; heme synthesis is not involved.
Key fact
  • Qualitative (structural variants): normal amount of an abnormal chain from a point (missense) mutation: HbS β6 Glu→Val (polymerizes), HbC β6 Glu→Lys (crystallizes), HbM (heme iron stays Fe3+). mRNA level and size normal; protein function altered.
  • Quantitative = thalassemias: decreased synthesis of a structurally normal α or β chain (mutations or gene deletions) → chain imbalance; autosomal recessive, microcytic, hemolytic.
  • Mutation words: missense = one amino acid swapped (sickle cell); nonsense = premature stop → truncated chain (a cause of β0-thalassemia); frameshift or deletion = altered length or no product; trinucleotide repeat = Huntington; ΔF508 Phe deletion = cystic fibrosis.
Lecture slides 35, 40 and 42 print HbC as 'E6L'; the change is E6K (Glu→Lys), as the TA key and the case session state.

  • Trap: 'microcytic hypochromic anemia' in a patient with lifelong pain crises is still sickle cell → point mutation, not deletion

Key fact
  • Thalassemia = quantitative hemoglobinopathy: ↓synthesis of α or β chains → chain imbalance; autosomal recessive; microcytic, hemolytic. (Qualitative = structurally abnormal chain: HbS, HbC.)
  • β-thal: excess unpaired α chains aggregate and precipitate → premature erythroid cell death.
  • Labs: ↑HbA2 (α2δ2) and ↑HbF (α2γ2), because neither contains β.
  • Minor (β+/β or β0/β): mild microcytic anemia. Intermedia (β+/β+ or β+/β0). Major, Cooley (β0/β0): no HbA, severe anemia, splenomegaly, bone deformities, regular transfusions → iron overload → iron chelators. Mediterranean, Asian, Middle Eastern.

31unlocks 4TA ×22 not obvious
In a child with β-thalassemia major, many erythroid precursors die in the bone marrow before they mature. Which mechanism best explains this?
  1. A. Spare α chains bind 2,3-BPG and block O2 release
  2. B. Spare α chains raise hemoglobin's O2 affinity and starve the precursors of O2
  3. C. Spare α chains shut off γ-globin synthesis and prevent HbF formation
  4. D. The mutant β chains form a hydrophobic patch that polymerizes deoxyhemoglobin
  5. E. Spare α chains have too few β partners, so they aggregate and precipitate inside the cells
AnswerE. Spare α chains have too few β partners, so they aggregate and precipitate inside the cells
Whyα and β are normally made 1:1. With too little β, the unpaired α chains aggregate and precipitate in erythroid precursors and red cells → premature cell death and hemolysis. A sticky patch that polymerizes deoxyHb is sickle cell (an abnormal chain, not too little chain); spare α does not bind 2,3-BPG or block HbF.
Key fact
  • α and β chains are normally made 1:1, so none are left over; thalassemia breaks this balance and the spare chains do the damage.
  • β-thalassemia (β short → spare α): free α chains aggregate and precipitate in erythroblasts and RBCs → premature erythroid cell death (ineffective erythropoiesis) + hemolysis → microcytic anemia. Some spare α pairs with δ and γ → ↑HbA2, ↑HbF.
  • α-thalassemia (α short → spare β, or γ in the fetus): β4 = HbH (3 genes lost; unstable, Heinz bodies, hemolytic anemia, compatible with life); γ4 = Hb Bart (4 genes lost; holds O2 too tightly → hydrops fetalis, fetal death).
  • Hb Bart is built of γ chains but means α is missing. Losing both β genes does not kill the fetus: HbF (α2γ2) needs no β.

Sickle cell disease

33unlocks 17TA ×15 not obvious
Which correctly describes the mutations of hemoglobin S and hemoglobin C?
  1. A. Both are α-globin mutations
  2. B. Both reduce β-globin synthesis
  3. C. HbS: Val→Glu; HbC: Lys→Glu, both at β6
  4. D. HbS: Glu→Val; HbC: Glu→Lys, both at position 6 of β-globin
  5. E. HbS: Glu→Lys; HbC: Glu→Val, both at β6
AnswerD. HbS: Glu→Val; HbC: Glu→Lys, both at position 6 of β-globin
WhyBoth are single-base missense changes at β6 that replace negatively charged glutamate: HbS → valine (hydrophobic, polymerizes) and HbC → lysine (charged, crystallizes, no sickling). Reversing the direction (Val→Glu) is the most common trap.
Key fact
  • HbS: β-globin (HBB) codon 6 GAG → GTG, Glu → Val (E6V); a missense point mutation (mRNA level and size normal, protein function altered); HbSS = both β chains mutant; autosomal recessive (about 1 in 500 African Americans).
  • HbC: β6 Glu → Lys (charged, hydrophilic) → no hydrophobic patch, no polymerization; forms crystals → mild chronic hemolytic anemia without pain crises. HbSC = milder sickle disease.
  • Not: ΔF508 phenylalanine deletion (CF), α-chain changes, nonsense, frameshift or deletion (would change mRNA or truncate), reduced synthesis (thalassemia).
Lecture slides F1269:35, :40 and :42 print HbC as 'E6L'; the correct change, used by every practice and TA key, is E6K (Glu→Lys). q567's stem says 'microcytic, hypochromic', which fits thalassemia better than sickle cell; the keyed answer (point mutation) is unaffected.

  • Direction traps: Val→Glu, Glu→Gly, Glu→Lys, 'valine for lysine'; both β chains vs one
  • Mutation type: missense or point mutation (vs nonsense, frameshift, deletion, trinucleotide repeat, trisomy)
  • TA: HbS vs HbC substitutions; short answer: why is HbC nonsickling → Lys is polar, not hydrophobic

What it lets you eliminate

Sickle cell disease

34unlocks 18TA ×14 not obvious
What is the primary structural consequence of the β6 Glu→Val substitution?
  1. A. Formation of α4 tetramers
  2. B. Polymerization of deoxyHbS through hydrophobic contacts between molecules
  3. C. Oxidation of heme iron to Fe3+
  4. D. Increased affinity of the 2,3-BPG pocket
  5. E. Decreased O2 binding by each heme
AnswerB. Polymerization of deoxyHbS through hydrophobic contacts between molecules
WhyValine forms a hydrophobic protrusion that docks into a hydrophobic pocket on another HbS molecule, exposed only in deoxy (T) Hb, so deoxyHbS polymerizes into rigid fibers that sickle the RBC. O2 binding and BPG handling are essentially normal; Fe3+ is methemoglobin.
Key fact
  • Val at β6 = sticky hydrophobic patch → binds a hydrophobic pocket on a neighboring deoxy HbS → deoxyHbS aggregates and polymerizes into insoluble rope-like fibers (↑hydrophobic interactions; quaternary and secondary structure and O2 binding essentially unchanged).
  • Fibers distort RBCs into sickles → vaso-occlusion (ischemia, microinfarcts, pain crises in bone, chest, abdomen) and chronic hemolytic anemia (fragile cells destroyed early, removed by the spleen; jaundice).
  • Case-session summary: deoxyHbS aggregates, mutant β chains sticky, vascular occlusion, chronic anemia, periodic pain.

How can acidosis precipitate a crisis in a patient with sickle cell disease?
  1. A. It decreases 2,3-BPG binding to HbS
  2. B. It favors the R form of HbS

WhyAcid → Bohr effect → more HbS in the deoxy T state, which is far less soluble and polymerizes. Every other option runs the Bohr effect backward.
Key fact
  • Only deoxy (T) HbS polymerizes, so anything that stabilizes T or lowers saturation increases sickling: hypoxia (altitude, exertion, lung disease), acidosis, ↑2,3-BPG, ↑CO2.
  • Anything that favors R (more O2, even the first O2 bound) decreases sickling.
  • Acidosis → ↓solubility of HbS (not ↑affinity, not R, not a left shift).

A patient with sickle cell disease flies to Denver and has a pain crisis after a night of heavy drinking. Which best explains how the drinking contributed?

WhyAlcohol is a diuretic → dehydration → higher [HbS] inside RBCs (faster polymerization) and ↑blood viscosity → sickled cells stick and occlude vessels. Denver's PO2 is lower, and the labs show metabolic acidosis, not alkalosis.
Key fact
  • High altitude (Denver, 5,300 ft) → PO2 17–20% lower → more HbS in the deoxy T state → polymerization.

  • Alcohol metabolism → lactic acid → acidosis → T state (the case labs: high anion gap metabolic acidosis, AG 21; tachypnea is compensation).
  • Common triggers: dehydration, infection (the earlier influenza crisis), high altitude, strenuous exercise, cold or heat, smoking, stress.

A child swallows a bottle of aspirin. The ED changes the urine pH to increase salicylate excretion. Which change and mechanism are correct?
  1. A. Alkalinization, converting salicylate to HA
  2. B. No change in urine pH; dialysis is the first step
  3. C. Alkalinization, converting salicylate to A−, which cannot diffuse back
  4. D. Acidification, converting salicylate to HA
  5. E. Acidification, converting salicylate to A−
AnswerC. Alkalinization, converting salicylate to A−, which cannot diffuse back
WhyIV NaHCO3 raises urine pH above the pKa of salicylic acid, so it is ionized (A−), cannot be reabsorbed across the tubule and is excreted: ion trapping. Acidifying would keep it as HA, which is reabsorbed.
Key factWeak-acid poison (salicylate) → alkalinize the urine (IV NaHCO3, urine pH ≥ 8) → A− trapped in urine → excreted.
Course order after ABCs: 1) activated charcoal to stop absorption; 2) urine alkalinization (NaHCO3 or KCl, with volume and electrolytes corrected).
It helps only when urine pH is above plasma pH.

A patient begins breathing rapidly and exhales more CO2 than normal. Using CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−, what happens to blood pH?
  1. A. pH falls because H+ rises
  2. B. pH is unchanged because the kidneys compensate at once
  3. C. pH falls because HCO3− rises
  4. D. pH rises because H+ falls
  5. E. pH falls because carbonic acid accumulates
AnswerD. pH rises because H+ falls
WhyBlowing off CO2 pulls the reaction to the left, using up H+, so pH rises (respiratory alkalosis). Retaining CO2 pushes it right, making more H+, so pH falls. Kidneys need days, not seconds.
Key factCO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3− (carbonic anhydrase).
↑PCO2 → ↑H+ → ↓pH; ↓PCO2 → ↓H+ → ↑pH.
So in acidemia, lowering PCO2 (hyperventilation) raises pH.

WhypH = 6.1 + log(HCO3− / (0.03 × PCO2)). 7.22 − 6.1 = 1.12, so the ratio is 10^1.12 ≈ 13.2; multiply by 0.03 × 20 = 0.6 → 7.9 mEq/L. 13.2 is the ratio before multiplying.
Key factpH = 6.1 + log [HCO3−] / (0.03 × PCO2)
0.03 converts PCO2 in mm Hg to dissolved CO2 in mM; don't apply it to a CO2 already given in mEq/L.
Normal: 24 / (0.03 × 40 = 1.2) = 20; log 20 = 1.3 → pH 7.4.
Use 6.1 (Lecture 23), not 6.4 from the primer table.
q173 is keyed 8.7 by applying 0.03 to a CO2 already given as 20 mEq/L. By the lecture the factor converts only PCO2 in mm Hg: the answer is pKa + log(30/20) ≈ 7.18 with the slide's pKa 7 (6.28 with 6.1).

ABG: pH 7.33, PCO2 55 mm Hg, HCO3− 25 mEq/L. What is the primary disorder?
  1. A. Metabolic acidosis
  2. B. Respiratory alkalosis

  4. D. No disorder; the values are near normal
  5. E. Respiratory acidosis
AnswerE. Respiratory acidosis
WhyStep 1: pH below 7.40 → acidosis. Step 2: which value explains it? PCO2 above 40 explains the acidemia, while HCO3− 25 is normal (a metabolic acidosis needs a low HCO3−). So this is respiratory acidosis.
Key factReference points: pH 7.40 (7.35–7.45), PCO2 40 (33–44), HCO3− 24 (22–28).
1) pH below 7.40 = acidosis; above = alkalosis.
2) The value that explains the pH is primary:
  • ↓pH + ↓HCO3− = metabolic acidosis
  • ↓pH + ↑PCO2 = respiratory acidosis
  • ↑pH + ↑HCO3− = metabolic alkalosis
  • ↑pH + ↓PCO2 = respiratory alkalosis
The other value, if it moves the opposite way to the pH, is compensation.
q932 (pH 8.1, HCO3 35, PCO2 24) is keyed "metabolic alkalosis with compensation". The low PCO2 is not compensation (that would raise PCO2), so the gas is really a mixed metabolic and respiratory alkalosis. Pick the only metabolic-alkalosis option.

An ED gas is reported only as arrows: pH ↓↓, HCO3− ↓↓, PCO2 ↓. What is the most likely disorder?
  1. A. Respiratory acidosis

  5. E. Metabolic alkalosis
AnswerD. Metabolic acidosis
WhyIn metabolic disorders pH, HCO3− and PCO2 all move the same way, and HCO3− is the bigger change; the smaller PCO2 fall is compensation. A low PCO2 by itself would raise pH, so it can't be primary here.
Key fact
  • Metabolic: pH, HCO3− and PCO2 all move in the same direction; HCO3− is the big arrow (PCO2 follows = compensation)
  • Respiratory: PCO2 moves opposite to pH; PCO2 is the big arrow, HCO3− follows
  • HH arrows: metabolic changes the numerator (HCO3−), respiratory the denominator (PCO2)
  • Typical metabolic acidosis profile: low HCO3− and low PCO2

50unlocks 23TA ×18 not obvious
Arterial blood: pH 7.51, PCO2 52 mm Hg, HCO3− 40 mEq/L. Which is the best description?
  1. A. Mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis, because both values are abnormal
  2. B. Metabolic alkalosis with compensatory hypoventilation
  3. C. Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
  4. D. Respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation
  5. E. Respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
AnswerB. Metabolic alkalosis with compensatory hypoventilation
WhyBoth values are high, so one is primary and the other is compensation. The pH is above 7.40, and only the high HCO3− explains an alkalosis, so it is a metabolic alkalosis; the PCO2 of 52 is the expected hypoventilation (40 + 0.6–0.75 × 16 ≈ 50–52, under 55). The tempting "respiratory acidosis" would need a pH below 7.40, and two abnormal values alone do not make it mixed.
Key factWhen PCO2 and HCO3− move the same way, one is primary and one is compensation. The pH side decides which.
  • Both high + pH below 7.40 → respiratory acidosis with renal compensation (COPD, emphysema, MS, obesity hypoventilation)
  • Both high + pH above 7.40 → metabolic alkalosis with compensatory hypoventilation (vomiting, hyperemesis in early pregnancy)
  • Both low + pH below 7.40 → metabolic acidosis with compensatory hyperventilation
  • Both low + pH above 7.40 → respiratory alkalosis with renal compensation (anxiety, ventilator)
A high PCO2 alone never proves respiratory acidosis. Think "mixed" only when the pH sits at 7.40 or on the wrong side, or a value is outside the expected compensation (PCO2 above 55 can't be compensation for a metabolic alkalosis).
q907 (pH 7.38, PCO2 59, HCO3− 14) is left out: its HCO3− contradicts the keyed chronic respiratory acidosis.

Which set of arterial blood values describes a heavy smoker with a history of emphysema and chronic bronchitis who is becoming increasingly somnolent?

AnswerD. pH 7.32 | HCO3− (mEq/L) 30 | Pco2 (mm Hg) 60
WhyCOPD with somnolence (CO₂ narcosis) is respiratory acidosis: high PCO₂ (60) and low pH, with HCO₃⁻ raised to 30 by renal compensation.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D [IX D 3; Tables 5.8 and 5.9]. The history strongly suggests chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) as a cause of respiratory acidosis. Because of the COPD, the ventilation rate is decreased and CO2 is retained. The [H+] and [HCO3−] are increased by mass action. The [HCO3−] is further increased by renal compensation for respiratory acidosis (increased HCO3− reabsorption by the kidney is facilitated by the high PCO2).
How it follows from the main questionTwo sets are "both high": 7.65 / 48 / 45 is alkalemic → metabolic alkalosis; 7.32 / 30 / 60 is acidemic → respiratory acidosis with renal compensation, the CO2 retainer.
Practice Q669Answered by elimination
A patient has the following arterial blood values: pH = 7.52 PCO2 = 20 mm Hg [HCO3−] = 16 mEq/L Which of the following statements about this patient is most likely to be correct?
  1. A. He is hypoventilating
  2. B. He has decreased ionized [Ca2+] in blood
  3. C. He has almost complete respiratory compensation
  4. D. He has an acid–base disorder caused by overproduction of fixed acid
  5. E. Appropriate renal compensation would cause his arterial [HCO3−] to increase
AnswerB. He has decreased ionized [Ca2+] in blood
WhyHigh pH with low PCO₂ is respiratory alkalosis; with less H⁺ bound to plasma albumin, more Ca²⁺ binds, so ionized Ca²⁺ falls (tingling, tetany). The low HCO₃⁻ is renal compensation.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B [IX D 4; Table 5.8]. First, the acid–base disorder must be diagnosed. Alkaline pH, low PCO2, and low HCO3− are consistent with respiratory alkalosis. In respiratory alkalosis, the [H+] is decreased and less H+ is bound to negatively charged sites on plasma proteins. As a result, more Ca2+ is bound to proteins and, therefore, the ionized [Ca2+] decreases. There is no respiratory compensation for primary respiratory disorders. The patient is hyperventilating, which is the cause of the respiratory alkalosis. Appropriate renal compensation would be decreased reabsorption of HCO3−, which would cause his arterial [HCO3−] to decrease and his blood pH to decrease (become more normal).
How it follows from the main questionBoth low + pH above 7.40 → respiratory alkalosis; the low HCO3− is renal compensation. That kills hypoventilation, fixed acid and rising HCO3−; pH 7.52 isn't near-complete. Left: ↓ionized Ca2+.

Explanation from the source
C) Patients with chronic lung disease develop hypercapnia secondary to chronic ventilation. They are expected to have chronic respiratory acidosis with metabolic compensation. A and B) These values include a normal bicarbonateD) These values are consistent with a mixed respiratory acidosis and metabolic alkalosis E) These values are consistent with a chronic respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation.
How it follows from the main questionChronic CO2 retention → both high with pH still below 7.40: 7.30 / 50 / 29. Normal HCO3− sets are acute; pH 7.40 with both high implies a second process; 7.50 / 30 is alkalosis.
Practice Q670Answered by elimination
A patient arrives at the emergency room with low arterial pressure, reduced tissue turgor, and the following arterial blood values: pH = 7.69 [HCO3−] = 57 mEq/L PCO2 = 48 mm Hg Which of the following responses would also be expected to occur in this patient?
  1. A. Hyperventilation
  2. B. Decreased K+ secretion by the distal tubules
  3. C. Increased ratio of H2PO4− to HPO4−2 in urine
  4. D. Exchange of intracellular H+ for extracellular K+
AnswerD. Exchange of intracellular H+ for extracellular K+
WhypH 7.69 with HCO₃⁻ 57 is metabolic alkalosis (with hypoventilation as compensation); low ECF H⁺ draws H⁺ out of cells in exchange for K⁺ moving in, producing hypokalemia.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D [IX D 2; Table 5.8]. First, the acid–base disorder must be diagnosed. Alkaline pH, with increased HCO3− and increased PCO2, is consistent with metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation. The low blood pressure and decreased turgor suggest extracellular fluid (ECF) volume contraction. The reduced [H+] in blood will cause intracellular H+ to leave cells in exchange for extracellular K+. The appropriate respiratory compensation is hypoventilation, which is responsible for the elevated PCO2. H+ excretion in urine will be decreased, so less titratable acid will be excreted. K+ secretion by the distal tubules will be increased because aldosterone levels will be increased secondary to ECF volume contraction.
How it follows from the main questionBoth high + pH above 7.40 → metabolic alkalosis, PCO2 48 = compensatory hypoventilation, so cross out hyperventilation. In alkalosis cells release H+ and take up K+ → H+ out, K+ in.
Practice Q862Asked from the other direction
Question 4 A 60 year old patient comes into clinic with a respiratory rate of 8 bpm. He denies taking any drugs, but has a 55 pack year history. What might his pH, pCO2, and bicarb levels be? (explanation on next slide)
  1. A. pH 7.54, PCO2 21, HCO3- 19
  2. B. pH 7.40, PCO2 40, HCO3- 24
  3. C. pH 7.24, PCO2 25, HCO3- 12
  4. D. pH 7.34, PCO2 60, HCO3- 38
AnswerD. pH 7.34, PCO2 60, HCO3- 38
WhyBradypnea in a heavy smoker (COPD) retains CO₂, so pH ↓ and PCO₂ ↑; chronic retention lets the kidneys raise HCO₃⁻ (38) as compensation for respiratory acidosis.
Explanation from the source
The patient has COPD, which indicates respiratory acidosis. The patient has a low respiratory rate, which means he’s keeping in the carbon dioxide (“keeping in acid”). This will (very quickly) bring down his pH. As there’s more carbon dioxide in the blood, the pCO2 will go up. To compensate, the kidneys will start saving/ making more bicarbonate to try to bring the pH back to normal. Respiratory acidosis is compensated by metabolic alkalosis.
How it follows from the main questionSlow breathing in a smoker = CO2 retention, chronic. Only one set has both values high with pH below 7.40: 7.34 / 60 / 38, respiratory acidosis with renal compensation.

Causes of the four disorders

51unlocks 6TA ×12 not obvious
Which patient is most likely to have a primary respiratory acidosis?
  1. A. A patient on a ventilator set to too high a rate
  2. B. A 16-year-old having a panic attack
  3. C. A hiker newly arrived at 8,000 ft
  4. D. A patient with an acute pulmonary embolism
  5. E. A heroin user found with a respiratory rate of 6/min and pinpoint pupils
AnswerE. A heroin user found with a respiratory rate of 6/min and pinpoint pupils
WhyRespiratory acidosis = hypoventilation, so CO2 is retained. Opioids depress the respiratory center. Panic, altitude (hypoxemia), pulmonary embolism and an over-set ventilator all hyperventilate and cause respiratory alkalosis.
Key factRespiratory acidosis = ↓ alveolar ventilation → ↑PCO2 (pH below 7.40):
  • chronic lung disease: COPD, emphysema, chronic bronchitis (somnolence = CO2 narcosis); severe asthma (FEV1 under 40%)
  • central depression: opioids, morphine (respiratory rate 5–9)
  • nerve and muscle: myasthenia gravis, MS, Guillain–Barré; obesity hypoventilation
  • rarely ↑CO2 production (malignant hyperthermia)
Hypoventilation gives ↑PCO2 and ↓PO2.
q647 calls HCO3− 30 "adequately compensated" in an acute opioid overdose; by the lecture's acute rule (+1–2 per 10 mm Hg) about 26–28 is expected, so 30 hints at an added metabolic alkalosis. The primary disorder, respiratory acidosis, is right.

• An FEV1 75% of normal means Jonathan has mild pulmonary obstruction • With RR at 46/min, Jonathan would most likely have respiratory alkalosis
• IF Jonathan’s FEV1 was <40% of normal, this means Jonathan has severe pulmonary obstruction and would then more likely have respiratory acidosis (usually the case with chronic asthma and COPD)
WhyYes: hypoxia and anxiety drive hyperventilation (RR 46) while obstruction is only mild (FEV1 75%), so CO₂ is blown off, giving acute respiratory alkalosis; severe obstruction (FEV1 under 40%) would instead retain CO₂ and cause respiratory acidosis.
How it follows from the main questionAsthma suggests CO2 retention, but that needs severe obstruction (FEV1 under 40%). At 75% with RR 46, CO2 is blown off → respiratory alkalosis.

Practice Q669Asked from the other direction
A patient has the following arterial blood values: pH = 7.52 PCO2 = 20 mm Hg [HCO3−] = 16 mEq/L Which of the following statements about this patient is most likely to be correct?
  1. A. He is hypoventilating
  2. B. He has decreased ionized [Ca2+] in blood
  3. C. He has almost complete respiratory compensation
  4. D. He has an acid–base disorder caused by overproduction of fixed acid

AnswerB. He has decreased ionized [Ca2+] in blood
WhyHigh pH with low PCO₂ is respiratory alkalosis; with less H⁺ bound to plasma albumin, more Ca²⁺ binds, so ionized Ca²⁺ falls (tingling, tetany). The low HCO₃⁻ is renal compensation.
Explanation from the source
The answer is B [IX D 4; Table 5.8]. First, the acid–base disorder must be diagnosed. Alkaline pH, low PCO2, and low HCO3− are consistent with respiratory alkalosis. In respiratory alkalosis, the [H+] is decreased and less H+ is bound to negatively charged sites on plasma proteins. As a result, more Ca2+ is bound to proteins and, therefore, the ionized [Ca2+] decreases. There is no respiratory compensation for primary respiratory disorders. The patient is hyperventilating, which is the cause of the respiratory alkalosis. Appropriate renal compensation would be decreased reabsorption of HCO3−, which would cause his arterial [HCO3−] to decrease and his blood pH to decrease (become more normal).
How it follows from the main question↑pH with ↓PCO2 = respiratory alkalosis, which lowers ionized Ca2+ (B). Not hypoventilation, not a fixed acid, and renal compensation lowers HCO3−.

  • High altitude (low inspired PO2)
Asthma flips to respiratory acidosis only when obstruction is severe (FEV1 under 40%); chronic lung disease (COPD, emphysema) retains CO2 → respiratory acidosis. So "lung disease" is not automatically acidosis: read the breathing rate and the severity.
The lecture slide (F1275:22) lists airway disorders such as asthma under respiratory acidosis; the practice keys and the CV faculty answer (Jonathan) treat an acute, non-severe attack as respiratory alkalosis and reserve acidosis for severe obstruction (FEV1 under 40%) or chronic disease. Practice Q682Answered by elimination
Which of the following conditions causes hypoventilation?
  1. A. Strenuous exercise
  2. B. Ascent to high altitude
  3. C. Anemia
  4. D. Diabetic ketoacidosis
  5. E. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
AnswerE. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
WhyCOPD limits alveolar ventilation, so CO₂ is retained (hypoventilation). Exercise, high altitude (hypoxemia) and DKA (compensatory Kussmaul breathing) all increase ventilation; anemia lowers O₂ content but not PaO₂, so it does not cause hypoventilation.
Explanation from the source
The answer is E [Chapter 4, IX A, B; Chapter 5 IX D]. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) causes hypoventilation. Strenuous exercise increases the ventilation rate to provide additional oxygen to the exercising muscle. Ascent to high altitude and anemia cause hypoxemia, which subsequently causes hyperventilation by stimulating peripheral chemoreceptors. The respiratory compensation for diabetic ketoacidosis is hyperventilation.
How it follows from the main questionAltitude (hypoxemia) and DKA (Kussmaul compensation) and exercise all increase ventilation; anemia leaves PaO2 normal. Only chronic obstruction retains CO2 → COPD.

  • Respiratory acidosis — chronic lung disease
  • Respiratory alkalosis — hyperventilation; drug toxicity (analeptics, salicylates)
  • Metabolic acidosis — ↑ketogenesis (DKA), diarrhea, kidney failure; also salicylate, ethylene glycol, acetazolamide
  • Metabolic alkalosis — vomiting, salts of metabolic acids (lactate, ketoanions), NaHCO3 or antacids, loop and thiazide diuretics, hyperaldosteronism, hypokalemia
TA31 keys "Metabolic acidosis — DKA", but the COPD and panic-attack pairings in that question are also correct; only "metabolic alkalosis — severe diarrhea" is wrong. Drug-induced toxicity is matched to respiratory alkalosis (salicylates); opioids would cause respiratory acidosis.

A 30-year-old has had profuse watery diarrhea for 4 days. Blood pressure is low and skin turgor is poor. Arterial blood: pH 7.29, PCO2 29 mm Hg, HCO3− 14 mEq/L; serum K+ 2.8 mEq/L; anion gap normal. Which best explains the low serum K+?
  1. A. Buffering of the excess H+ by HCO3− consumes K+
  2. B. Decreased ADH lets K+ escape in a dilute urine
  3. C. Volume depletion raises aldosterone, which drives renal K+ secretion (on top of K+ lost in stool)
  4. D. Acidosis drives K+ into cells in exchange for H+ leaving them
  5. E. Hypoventilation retains CO2, which carries K+ into red cells
AnswerC. Volume depletion raises aldosterone, which drives renal K+ secretion (on top of K+ lost in stool)
WhyDiarrhea loses HCO3− and K+ in stool, and the volume loss raises aldosterone, which makes the distal tubule reabsorb Na+ and secrete K+ and H+. The tempting shift answer (D) runs the wrong way: in acidosis H+ moves into cells and K+ moves out, which would raise serum K+.
Key factK+ and H+ trade places across cell membranes, and aldosterone wastes both
  • Acidosis: H+ enters cells, K+ leaves → serum K+ ↑ (DKA can show normal or high K+ despite total-body loss)
  • Alkalosis: intracellular H+ is exchanged for extracellular K+ (H+ out, K+ in) → serum K+ ↓
  • Volume depletion (diarrhea, vomiting, diuretics) → renin–angiotensin → ↑aldosterone → distal tubule reabsorbs Na+, secretes K+ and H+ → hypokalemia (and in vomiting it keeps the alkalosis going)
  • Lecture cases: diarrhea → normal-gap acidosis with K+ 2.9; bulimia (vomiting) → metabolic alkalosis with K+ 2.6
The mechanism is renal physiology; the biochemistry lecture shows the low K+ in its diarrhea and bulimia cases without explaining it.

Practice Q668Trap: the obvious answer is wrong
Questions 3 and 4 A 45-year-old woman develops severe diarrhea while on vacation. She has the following arterial blood values: pH = 7.25 PCO2 = 24 mm Hg [HCO3−] = 10 mEq/L Venous blood samples show decreased blood [K+] and a normal anion gap. Which of the following statements about this patient is correct?
  1. A. She is hypoventilating
  2. B. The decreased arterial [HCO3−] is a result of buffering of excess H+ by HCO3−
  3. C. The decreased blood [K+] is a result of exchange of intracellular H+ for extracellular K+
  4. D. The decreased blood [K+] is a result of increased circulating levels of aldosterone
  5. E. The decreased blood [K+] is a result of decreased circulating levels of antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
AnswerD. The decreased blood [K+] is a result of increased circulating levels of aldosterone
WhyDiarrhea contracts ECF volume, activating renin–angiotensin–aldosterone, which increases distal K⁺ secretion and causes hypokalemia. Acidemia would shift K⁺ out of cells (raising it), and she is hyperventilating, not hypoventilating.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D [IX D 1 a–c; Tables 5.8 and 5.9]. The decreased arterial [HCO3−] is caused by gastrointestinal (GI) loss of HCO3− from diarrhea, not by buffering of excess H+ by HCO3−. The woman is hyperventilating as respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis. Her hypokalemia cannot be the result of the exchange of intracellular H+ for extracellular K+, because she has an increase in extracellular H+, which would drive the exchange in the other direction. Her circulating levels of aldosterone would be increased as a result of extracellular fluid (ECF) volume contraction, which leads to increased K+ secretion by the distal tubule and hypokalemia.
How it follows from the main questionAcidosis pushes K+ out of cells and would raise it, so the H+/K+ swap (C) is wrong; volume loss → ↑aldosterone → distal K+ secretion (D). ADH handles water.

  1. A. Hyperventilation

  3. C. Increased ratio of H2PO4− to HPO4−2 in urine
  4. D. Exchange of intracellular H+ for extracellular K+
AnswerD. Exchange of intracellular H+ for extracellular K+
WhypH 7.69 with HCO₃⁻ 57 is metabolic alkalosis (with hypoventilation as compensation); low ECF H⁺ draws H⁺ out of cells in exchange for K⁺ moving in, producing hypokalemia.
Explanation from the source
The answer is D [IX D 2; Table 5.8]. First, the acid–base disorder must be diagnosed. Alkaline pH, with increased HCO3− and increased PCO2, is consistent with metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation. The low blood pressure and decreased turgor suggest extracellular fluid (ECF) volume contraction. The reduced [H+] in blood will cause intracellular H+ to leave cells in exchange for extracellular K+. The appropriate respiratory compensation is hypoventilation, which is responsible for the elevated PCO2. H+ excretion in urine will be decreased, so less titratable acid will be excreted. K+ secretion by the distal tubules will be increased because aldosterone levels will be increased secondary to ECF volume contraction.
How it follows from the main questionSevere metabolic alkalosis: H+ leaves cells as K+ enters → D. The lungs hypoventilate (not A), and volume loss raises aldosterone, increasing K+ secretion.

A patient with ethylene glycol poisoning has a high-AG metabolic acidosis. What is the body's first compensation?
  1. A. Breathing slows
  2. B. PCO2 rises
  3. C. PCO2 falls through hyperventilation
  4. D. The kidneys increase HCO3−
  5. E. HCO3− decreases further
