WhyCompensation uses the other system: metabolic problems → lungs (fast, minutes); respiratory problems → kidneys (slow, days). Low pH stimulates chemoreceptors → hyperventilation, ↓PCO2 (Kussmaul breathing). Renal HCO3− regeneration is real but slow.
Key fact
  • Metabolic acidosis → hyperventilation, ↓PCO2 (the lecture calls it compensatory respiratory alkalosis); the extra carbonic acid leaves as CO2 through the lungs
  • Metabolic alkalosis → hypoventilation, ↑PCO2
  • Respiratory acidosis → kidneys retain and make HCO3− (↑PCO2 → more H+ secreted → more HCO3− reabsorbed)
  • Respiratory alkalosis → kidneys excrete HCO3−
Lungs act in minutes; kidneys over days. Vomiting and diarrhea are never compensation.

Why does adding lactic acid raise the anion gap, while losing HCO3− in stool does not?
  1. A. Lactic acid raises the plasma Cl−
  2. B. Lactic acid raises the plasma Na+
  3. C. Diarrhea adds unmeasured cations to plasma

AnswerE. Lactate is an unmeasured anion that replaces the HCO3− it uses up; stool HCO3− loss is replaced by Cl−
WhyAn added acid's H+ uses up HCO3−, and its anion (lactate, ketoacids, salicylate, formate, glycolate) is unmeasured, so the gap rises with a normal Cl− (normochloremic). Lost HCO3− is replaced by Cl− (hyperchloremic), so the gap stays normal.
Key factThe AG is used to sort metabolic acidosis:
  • Gain of acid → unmeasured anion accumulates → high AG, normochloremic
  • Loss of base (HCO3−) → replaced by Cl− → normal AG, hyperchloremic
A high AG means a metabolic acidosis is present, even when pH is normal.
AG = unmeasured anions − unmeasured cations.
TA33 and TA34 have no key marked in the TA file; by the lecture the answers are C (decreased HCO3− reflects either chloride replacement or unmeasured anions) and B (patient 1 accumulated chloride, patient 2 unmeasured anions).

RTA, diarrhea and acetazolamide are normal-gap.

A 22 year-old female presents to the Emergency Dept. where you are rotating at as a 4th year student (manifest!). She is brought in by her college roommate and shows signs of confusion, dehydration, and overall low level of consciousness. After getting the patient stable and situated, you get a ABG (arterial blood gas) and receive the following labs. | pH | 7.26 | | HCO3- | 18 | | PCO2 | 40 | | Na+ | 138 | | K+ | 4.7 | | Cl- | 97 | Bonus Question: Do you recognize what might be going on with this patient? Answer/explanation in the speaker notes!
Answeraspirin overdose
WhyA young woman with confusion and dehydration and a high-AG (23) metabolic acidosis fits salicylate overdose (the S in MUDPILES), salicylate being an unmeasured anion. Note: PCO₂ 40 exceeds Winter's expected ≈ 35, so the typical salicylate respiratory alkalosis is absent; other MUDPILES causes fit too.
Explanation from the source
This patient is likely suffering from an aspirin overdose. Asprin is composed of acetylsalicylic acid, which when broken down turns into Salicylic acid. Salicylates are one of the many causes of metabolic acidosis (the S in MUDPILES)! Initially, they cause a respiratory alkalosis because they stimulate your brain’s respiratory center, causing you to hyperventilate and increase your pH. However, in the late stage, your liver can’t break down salicylic acid into its active component, so you begin to have an accumulation of salicylates in the blood, which DON’T come up on a routine ABG. When you go to calculate your Anion Gap, the “gap” is explained by the unmeasured acid from aspirin. The pH tells you “the patient is acidotic” but your labs initially say different.
How it follows from the main questionAG = 138 − (97 + 18) = 23 in a confused young patient → the course answer is aspirin overdose. Caveat: PCO2 40 lacks aspirin's usual respiratory alkalosis. Also asked as Q737.

Toxic and hypoxic acidoses

An unresponsive 17-year-old who may have swallowed either aspirin or antifreeze has a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. Which finding points to ethylene glycol rather than aspirin?
  1. A. A high serum salicylate level
  2. B. Calcium oxalate crystals in the urine with a low serum Ca2+
  3. C. Hyperglycemia with ketonuria
  4. D. Tinnitus with an early respiratory alkalosis
  5. E. A normal anion gap with a high Cl−
AnswerB. Calcium oxalate crystals in the urine with a low serum Ca2+
WhyAlcohol dehydrogenase turns ethylene glycol into glycolic, glyoxylic and finally oxalic acid; oxalate binds Ca2+ → calcium oxalate crystals in urine and a low serum Ca2+. A high salicylate level and tinnitus with early respiratory alkalosis point to aspirin; hyperglycemia with ketonuria is DKA; both poisons give a high gap.
Key factWhy a suicide threat matters (Tisha): the ingested toxin may be causing the high-AG metabolic acidosis, and knowing which one sets the treatment.
  • Aspirin: serum salicylate high; tinnitus, early respiratory alkalosis. After ABCs: 1) activated charcoal; 2) alkalinize the urine (IV NaHCO3, urine pH ≥ 8)
  • Ethylene glycol (antifreeze, sweet, often blue): alcohol dehydrogenase → glycolaldehyde → glycolic, glyoxylic, oxalic acid → urine calcium oxalate crystals, low serum Ca2+. Treat with fomepizole to block alcohol dehydrogenase (ethanol historically, as a competing substrate)
  • Either: psychiatry referral before discharge
Both are high-AG; the first compensation is hyperventilation (↓PCO2) unless the patient's breathing is depressed (RR 6 → ↑PCO2, ↓PO2).

Toxic and hypoxic acidoses

A patient in cardiogenic shock after a myocardial infarction is hypotensive with cool extremities. Which best explains the expected acid–base change?
  1. A. Lactate from anaerobic glycolysis → high-AG metabolic acidosis
  2. B. CO2 retention → respiratory acidosis only
  3. C. Loss of ketones in urine → metabolic alkalosis
  4. D. HCO3− retention by the kidneys → metabolic alkalosis
  5. E. Chloride gain → normal-AG acidosis
AnswerA. Lactate from anaerobic glycolysis → high-AG metabolic acidosis
WhyPoor perfusion = tissue hypoxia → pyruvate is reduced to lactate (LDH regenerates NAD+) → high-AG metabolic acidosis, tracked by serum lactate; hyperventilation compensates. The same logic covers CO poisoning, sickle crisis and heavy drinking.
Key factLactic acidosis = high-AG metabolic acidosis (↑lactate, ↓pH):
  • Tissue hypoxia: shock, MI, CO poisoning (blocks O2 delivery and cytochrome c oxidase; pulse oximetry falsely about 99%), sickle crisis
  • Alcohol: ↑NADH/NAD+ → pyruvate → lactate, plus ketone bodies
  • PDH deficiency (Farrah, Hosni): high lactate, pyruvate and alanine with normal glucose → lactic acidosis, not ketoacidosis
Tachypnea = compensatory hyperventilation (not CO2 retention). Measure serum lactate.
q794 (student note) calls Jasmine hyperchloremic with no compensation; AG 21 and PCO2 29 make it high-AG metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation, as the page's key note says. q795's student reasoning (CO2 retention; lower pH raises O2 affinity) is wrong; use the faculty answer.

A warehouse worker who drives a propane forklift indoors has a worsening headache, then a seizure. HR 120, RR 30/min, pulse oximetry 99%. What acid–base status is expected when paramedics arrive?
  1. A. Metabolic alkalosis with compensatory hypoventilation
  2. B. Respiratory acidosis from CO2 retention
  3. C. Metabolic acidosis (lactic, high anion gap) with compensatory hyperventilation
  4. D. No disorder, because the oxygen saturation is normal
  5. E. Primary respiratory alkalosis from the fast breathing
AnswerC. Metabolic acidosis (lactic, high anion gap) with compensatory hyperventilation
WhyIndoor propane = carbon monoxide. CO blocks O2 release from Hb and inhibits cytochrome c oxidase, so cells turn to anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acid → high-AG metabolic acidosis. RR 30 is CNS hypoxia plus compensation, not the primary problem (E) and not CO2 retention (B); pulse oximetry is falsely normal (D).
Key factCO poisoning (propane or gasoline engine, heater or lantern in a closed space; headache, confusion, seizure):
  • CO binds Hb about 220× more tightly than O2 and holds it in the R state → O2 is not unloaded; CO also inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (complex IV)
  • → anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acid → high-AG metabolic acidosis
  • RR 30 = ↓O2 delivery to the CNS stimulating the respiratory center + compensatory hyperventilation (↓PCO2). Board wording: "metabolic acidosis with compensatory respiratory alkalosis"
  • Pulse oximetry reads falsely normal (about 99%): it can't tell COHb from O2Hb
q795's printed student answer (CO2 retention, lower pH raises O2 affinity) and q661's "more CO2 in tissues" reasoning are wrong; the faculty answer is lactic metabolic acidosis with compensatory hyperventilation, and acidosis lowers Hb's O2 affinity (Bohr effect).

KEY-L24 Lipid digestion and absorption

Mouth and stomach: the acid lipases

73unlocks 4TA ×2
A 4-week-old exclusively breastfed infant digests much of the fat in milk even though pancreatic lipase output is still low. Which feature describes the enzymes responsible?
  1. A. They need bile salts to become active in the stomach
  2. B. They are secreted as zymogens and activated by trypsin
  3. C. They cut the C2 ester of phospholipids to give lysophospholipids
  4. D. They need colipase and work mainly in the duodenum
  5. E. They are acid stable (pH 4–6) and prefer TAG with short- and medium-chain fatty acids
AnswerE. They are acid stable (pH 4–6) and prefer TAG with short- and medium-chain fatty acids
WhyLingual and gastric lipases are acid stable (pH 4–6), start TAG digestion in the mouth and stomach, and prefer short- and medium-chain TAG (milk, butter, coconut oil); they matter most in newborns and in pancreatic insufficiency such as cystic fibrosis. Colipase, bile salts and trypsin activation belong to the pancreatic phase in the duodenum, and cutting C2 is phospholipase A2.
Key factLingual (mouth) + gastric (stomach) lipase = the acid lipases
  • Start TAG digestion: TAG is the only dietary lipid whose digestion begins in the mouth (then stomach, then duodenum)
  • Acid stable, optimum pH 4–6; no colipase, no bile salts, not zymogens
  • Prefer TAG with short- and medium-chain FA (under 12 C): milk fat, butter, coconut oil
  • Significant in newborns (milk fat) and pancreatic insufficiency / cystic fibrosis → a patient with no pancreatic lipase can still digest short-chain (dairy) TAG

Which statement about pancreatic lipase is correct?

WhyPancreatic lipase is the main TAG-digesting enzyme; in the duodenum it cuts the C1 and C3 esters of long-chain TAG, giving 2-MAG + 2 free FA, the form that enters enterocytes. Key factPancreatic lipase = the main TAG enzyme, acting in the duodenum
  • Most lipid digestion: duodenum + pancreatic lipase (the acid lipases add only a little)

  • Secreted active (not a zymogen) into the duodenum; needs colipase. CF: it never reaches the gut → long-chain TAG undigested
  • Destroyed by acid: gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison) floods the duodenum with HCl → lipase inactivated → steatorrhea

  • CCK: I cells (duodenum/jejunum); trigger = fat + protein in the duodenum → gallbladder contraction + sphincter of Oddi relaxation (bile release), pancreatic acinar enzymes, slower gastric emptying

  • Order after a fatty meal: fat enters duodenum → I cells release CCK → gallbladder contracts, Oddi relaxes → bile emulsifies fat into microdroplets
  • No CCK → tight sphincter, little bile, fewer micelles → steatorrhea; more CCK improves fat digestion (never a steatorrhea cause)

Bile: composition, emulsification, bile acids

Bile is collected from the gallbladder of a healthy volunteer. According to the lecture, which statement about it is correct?

  4. D. Bile salts are its main lipid (about 85%), and bile salts plus phospholipid keep its cholesterol dissolved
  5. E. Its bile salts are made from bilirubin
AnswerD. Bile salts are its main lipid (about 85%), and bile salts plus phospholipid keep its cholesterol dissolved
WhyBile is made by hepatocytes, then stored and concentrated 10–20x in the gallbladder; its lipids are about 85% bile salts, 10% free cholesterol, 5% phospholipid (lecture numbers), and bile salts + phospholipid solubilize cholesterol, preventing stones. Bile has no fatty acids, it is released on CCK, and bile salts come from cholesterol (bilirubin, from heme, is the pigment).
Key factBile: where it is made, what it contains, what it does
  • Made by hepatocytes; stored and concentrated 10–20x in the gallbladder; released on CCK
  • Lipids: 85% bile salts, 10% free cholesterol, 5% phospholipid (lecture); also water, electrolytes, bilirubin; no fatty acids
  • Bile acids are made from cholesterol in the liver (rate-limiting enzyme 7α-hydroxylase)
  • Four functions: (1) main route to excrete excess cholesterol; (2) bile acids + phospholipids keep cholesterol in solution (no stones); (3) emulsify TAG for pancreatic lipase; (4) help absorb fat-soluble vitamins
  • The bile component that matters for fat digestion and absorption is the bile salts (not cholesterol, lecithin or bilirubin)

A patient with cirrhosis makes very little bile and has steatorrhea, although their pancreatic enzyme output is normal. What does bile normally do for fat digestion?
  1. A. Activates pancreatic lipase from its zymogen
  2. B. Carries intact micelles across the enterocyte membrane

  4. D. Converts dietary lipids into cholesterol

AnswerC. Emulsifies fat into small droplets, increasing the surface area for pancreatic lipase
WhyBile salts are amphipathic detergents; with peristalsis they emulsify fat in the duodenum into small, stable droplets that do not coalesce, giving water-soluble lipase more surface area. They never hydrolyze TAG, and lipase is not a zymogen. Less bile → less emulsification → maldigestion.
Key factBile salts emulsify; they do not digest
  • Emulsification happens in the duodenum (not mouth, stomach or colon) by bile salts (detergent) + peristalsis (mixing)
  • Result: smaller, stable droplets kept from coalescing → ↑ surface area for pancreatic lipase
  • Bile salts do not hydrolyze TAG, activate lipase or enter the enterocyte; after digestion they form mixed micelles
  • Liver disease / bile obstruction → ↓ emulsification → fat less accessible to lipase → steatorrhea (course: maldigestion)

Researchers compare cholic acid with glycocholate. Why is the glycine-conjugated form the better emulsifier in the duodenum?
  1. A. Conjugation lowers its pKa, so it stays ionized and more amphipathic at intestinal pH
  2. B. Conjugation lets it hydrolyze TAG ester bonds
  3. C. Conjugation raises its pKa, so it stays protonated
  4. D. Conjugation happens in the gut and lets it diffuse across the enterocyte membrane
  5. E. Conjugation makes it more hydrophobic, so it dissolves inside the fat droplet
AnswerA. Conjugation lowers its pKa, so it stays ionized and more amphipathic at intestinal pH
WhyIn the liver, bile acids are joined by an amide bond to glycine or taurine. This lowers the pKa (to about 2–4), so at intestinal pH they are ionized Na+/K+ bile salts, more amphipathic and better detergents. Lower pKa means a better emulsifier, and ionized salts do not diffuse across membranes.
Key factConjugation: glycine/taurine → lower pKa → bile salt → better detergent
  • Done in the liver; amide bond with glycine or taurine only (not cholesterol, not other amino acids)
  • Lowers pKa (about 2–4) → ionized at intestinal pH → bile salt (Na+/K+ salt) = the ionized, conjugated form of a bile acid
  • More amphipathic and water soluble → more effective emulsifier: lower pKa = better
  • Ionized bile salts do not cross membranes passively (the ileum uses a Na+ cotransporter); secreted bile acids are conjugated
  • Cannot conjugate → poor emulsification and micelles → steatorrhea

Enterohepatic circulation and bile acid drugs

82unlocks 9TA ×11 not obvious
A 30-year-old with Crohn disease has their terminal ileum resected. Months later they have watery diarrhea and greasy stools. Which lost process explains both findings?
  1. A. Bile acid synthesis in the liver
  2. B. Gallbladder storage of bile

  5. E. Cholesterol uptake by NPC1L1
AnswerD. Bile salt reabsorption, so bile acids spill into the colon and the bile salt pool shrinks
WhyAbout 95–98% of bile salts are reabsorbed in the terminal ileum by a Na+ cotransporter and return to the liver in portal blood (enterohepatic circulation). Without the ileum, bile acids reach the colon (diarrhea, bile in stool) and the shrinking pool cannot make enough micelles (steatorrhea, fat-soluble vitamin loss); liver synthesis, gallbladder storage and pancreatic lipase are intact.
Key factEnterohepatic circulation
  • 95–98% of bile salts reabsorbed in the terminal (distal) ileum via Na+ cotransport → portal vein → liver; each molecule recycles about 10x/day
  • Only about 5% is lost in feces and replaced by new synthesis, so secreted bile is mostly recycled bile salt, not new
  • Ileal resection or Crohn ileitis → bile acids lost → ↑ bile in stool (diarrhea), ↓ pool → steatorrhea + ↓ A, D, E, K (and B12)
  • Bile's job is to solubilize and absorb lipids; it is reabsorbed in the terminal ileum (not duodenum or colon)
Lecture slide 23 says 98% recycling; practice keys say 95%. Either is accepted.

Enterohepatic circulation and bile acid drugs

83unlocks 123 not obvious
A patient with an LDL of 190 mg/dL starts a positively charged resin that is not absorbed from the gut. What is its main mechanism, and which side effect should they be warned about?
  1. A. Binds bile acids and blocks their ileal reabsorption; vitamin K malabsorption
  2. B. Replaces dietary fat with a nondigestible sucrose polyester; gallstones
  3. C. Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase; myopathy
  4. D. Inhibits pancreatic lipase; oily stools
  5. E. Blocks NPC1L1 cholesterol uptake; vitamin B12 deficiency
AnswerA. Binds bile acids and blocks their ileal reabsorption; vitamin K malabsorption
WhyCholestyramine (and colesevelam) are anion-exchange resins that bind negatively charged bile acids and block the enterohepatic circulation; the liver diverts more cholesterol into bile acids, LDL receptors rise and serum LDL falls. Binding bile acids also impairs micelles, so fat-soluble vitamins (K) are lost. Lipase inhibition is orlistat; NPC1L1 blockade is ezetimibe.
Key factDrugs that act on fat digestion and absorption
  • Cholestyramine / colesevelam (bile acid sequestrant, positively charged resin): binds bile acids in the gut → blocks enterohepatic reabsorption → more cholesterol made into bile acids → ↑ LDL receptors → ↓ LDL. Side effect: ↓ fat-soluble vitamins (vitamin K); space other drugs
  • Orlistat: inhibits gastric + pancreatic lipase → TAG not hydrolyzed (about 1/3 of fat lost) → oily, foul steatorrhea
  • Ezetimibe: blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1)
  • Olestra: nondigestible fat substitute (sucrose + 6–8 FA). Ursodeoxycholic / chenodeoxycholic acid: dissolve cholesterol gallstones
q1027: the answer slide bolds C, but its explanation describes lipase inhibition; the page key B (inhibition of triglyceride hydrolysis) is correct by the lecture.

Gallstones (cholelithiasis)

84unlocks 8TA ×32 not obvious
A 44-year-old obese woman with three children has RUQ pain after fatty meals, and ultrasound shows cholesterol stones. Which change in bile directly causes them?
  1. A. Increased bilirubin from hemolysis
  2. B. Low calcium in bile
  3. C. More cholesterol than bile salts and phospholipid can keep in solution
  4. D. Increased pancreatic lipase secretion
  5. E. More bile salt and phospholipid relative to cholesterol
AnswerC. More cholesterol than bile salts and phospholipid can keep in solution
WhyCholesterol stones form when bile is supersaturated: either more cholesterol enters bile (obesity, estrogen, pregnancy, diabetes, fibrates) or there are fewer bile acids (low 7α-hydroxylase, ileal disease, biliary obstruction, liver failure). Excess bilirubin from hemolysis gives black pigment stones instead.
Key factCholelithiasis
  • Mechanism: more cholesterol enters bile than bile salts + phospholipid can solubilize → cholesterol precipitates (most common stone)
  • ↓ Bile acids: ileal disease (bile acid malabsorption), biliary obstruction, liver failure, ↓ 7α-hydroxylase (fibrates such as fenofibrate inhibit it)
  • ↑ Biliary cholesterol: obesity, estrogen/contraceptives, pregnancy, diabetes, fibrates. Decreased cholesterol excretion is never a cause
  • 5 Fs: fat, female, fertile, forty, fair (age 30 and below is not a risk)
  • Black pigment stones: chronic hemolysis (e.g., hereditary spherocytosis)
  • Clinic: RUQ pain after a fatty meal (CCK) radiating under the right shoulder; ultrasound; jaundice + clay stool = duct blocked; after cholecystectomy, limited tolerance for fatty food

Gallstones (cholelithiasis)

85unlocks 3TA ×13 not obvious
A 17-year-old with sickle cell disease has recurrent right upper quadrant pain, and ultrasound shows several small gallstones. Which stone type and mechanism are most likely?
  1. A. Cholesterol stones; bile holds more cholesterol than bile salts and phospholipid can dissolve
  2. B. Uric acid stones; increased purine turnover from red cell breakdown
  3. C. Mixed stones; low 7α-hydroxylase activity reduces bile acid synthesis
  4. D. Calcium oxalate stones; increased oxalate absorption from the gut
  5. E. Black pigment stones; excess bilirubin from chronic hemolysis precipitates with calcium salts
AnswerE. Black pigment stones; excess bilirubin from chronic hemolysis precipitates with calcium salts
WhyChronic hemolysis (sickle cell, hereditary spherocytosis) floods bile with bilirubin, which precipitates with calcium salts as black pigment stones, even in a young male. Cholesterol stones need supersaturated bile and fit the 5 Fs patient. Calcium oxalate and uric acid stones are kidney stones, even though red cell turnover sounds like it fits uric acid.
Key factGallstone type follows the cause
  • Cholesterol stones (most common; cholesterol is insoluble): bile has more cholesterol than bile salts + phospholipid can hold. Who: 5 Fs, estrogen/pregnancy, diabetes, ileal disease, fibrates (↓ 7α-hydroxylase → ↓ bile acid synthesis)
  • Pigment stones (about 10%): mostly bile pigment (bilirubin) with calcium salts and a little cholesterol. Main risk = chronic hemolysis → black pigment stones (hereditary spherocytosis, sickle cell), even in a teenager or a man. (Brown pigment stones come from biliary infection.) Mixed stones = cholesterol + pigment
  • No hemolysis and a normal bilirubin in a 5 Fs or fibrate patient → cholesterol stone, not bilirubin precipitation
  • Jaundice + clay stool after a fatty meal = a stone blocking the duct so bilirubin cannot leave; it is still cholelithiasis, not a 'bilirubin stone'
  • Ursodeoxycholic / chenodeoxycholic acid dissolve cholesterol stones only; cholecystectomy is preferred
  • Calcium oxalate and uric acid stones are kidney stones (nephrolithiasis), never gallstone types
The lecture (slide 27) says only 'pigment stones' with chronic hemolysis as the most important risk factor; TA45 keys 'black pigment stones'. Brown pigment stones from biliary infection are textbook, not on the slides.

Micelles and absorption

86unlocks 11TA ×12 not obvious
A patient has a common bile duct stone, and no bile reaches the gut. Which dietary component will still be absorbed normally?
  1. A. Stearic acid (C18)
  2. B. Octanoic acid (C8)
  3. C. Retinol
  4. D. Cholesterol
  5. E. Vitamin K
AnswerB. Octanoic acid (C8)
WhyShort- and medium-chain FA (under 12 C, e.g., C8) enter enterocytes without mixed micelles and go straight to portal blood. Long-chain FA (C18), 2-MAG, cholesterol and vitamins A, D, E, K must ride in bile-salt micelles, so they fail when bile is absent.
Key factMixed micelles and what needs them
  • Structure: bile salts and other amphipathic lipids with hydrophilic groups outside, hydrophobic inside; core = 2-MAG, LCFA, cholesterol, lysophospholipid, vitamins A D E K
  • Job: the hydrophilic, water-soluble surface carries hydrophobic lipids through the watery lumen to the brush border (jejunum)
  • Micelles are not absorbed intact: their contents enter the enterocyte; bile salts stay in the lumen for the ileum
  • Need micelles: LCFA, 2-MAG, cholesterol, fat-soluble vitamins. Do not: short/medium-chain FA (under 12 C) → directly to portal blood, not lymph; glycerol, amino acids, B12 (intrinsic factor), bile acids (ileal transporter)
  • Sequence: micelles → FFA + 2-MAG enter the cell → chylomicrons → lymph
Lecture slide 14 has a garbled line ('short and medium chain fatty acid-lymphatic-portal circulation'); its meaning, and q1033/q1139, is that short/medium chains go to portal blood, not lymph.

  • 'Micelle formation is needed for the absorption of...' → vitamin A

  • Triglycerides are never inside the micelle or crossing the brush border intact

Micelles and absorption

87unlocks 8TA ×22 not obvious
After a fatty meal, 2-monoacylglycerol and long-chain fatty acids have just entered a jejunal enterocyte from mixed micelles. What happens to them next, and why?
  1. A. They are oxidized in the enterocyte to power further absorption
  2. B. They are split further into glycerol and fatty acids before entering the lacteal
  3. C. They are converted into bile salts and returned to the liver
  4. D. They are re-esterified to triacylglycerol in the ER so they can be packaged with apoB-48 for transport
  5. E. They are rebuilt into mixed micelles and released into portal blood
AnswerD. They are re-esterified to triacylglycerol in the ER so they can be packaged with apoB-48 for transport
WhyAbsorbed lipids move to the ER and are re-esterified (2-MAG + 2 acyl-CoA → TAG; cholesterol → CE by ACAT). The purpose is to remake complex lipids for repackaging and transport in the chylomicron. Micelles never enter the cell or the blood, and nothing is broken down further or turned into bile salts or glucose.
Key factLipid absorption step by step, and what each step is for
  • 1. Lumen → mixed micelle: 2-MAG, LCFA, cholesterol, lysophospholipid + vitamins A D E K packed with bile salts. Its hydrophilic surface carries hydrophobic lipids through the watery lumen to the brush border (jejunum); it does not dissolve them in blood or digest them
  • 2. Brush border: the contents (FFA + 2-MAG, never intact TAG) enter the cell; the micelle itself is not absorbed, and bile salts stay behind for the ileum
  • 3. Enterocyte ER = re-esterification: FA + ATP → acyl-CoA; 2-MAG + 2 acyl-CoA → TAG; cholesterol → CE (ACAT); lysophospholipid → PL. Purpose: resynthesize complex lipids for repackaging and transport (not breakdown, not bile salts, not glucose)
  • 4. Package: TAG + CE + PL + apoB-48 → nascent chylomicron (made inside the enterocyte)
  • 5. Exit: lacteal → lymph → thoracic duct → blood, bypassing the portal vein and liver
  • Order to memorize: micelles → FFA/2-MAG → chylomicrons → lymph

How it shows up

  • TA style: the primary purpose of ER re-esterification (repackaging for transport) vs breaking TAG down, making bile salts or glucose
  • TA style: what the hydrophilic micelle surface does (carries lipids through the aqueous lumen to the brush border)
  • Put the steps in order (micelles, FFA/MAG, chylomicrons, lymph); true/false 'micelles are absorbed with the fat'
  • Surgery vignette: thoracic duct blocked → absorbed fat cannot reach the blood

What it lets you eliminate

  • Any option where micelles enter the cell, the blood or the tissues → wrong; chylomicrons do the transport
  • TAG crossing the brush border intact, or being broken down again after entry → wrong
  • Chylomicrons are made inside the enterocyte, never by lipase in the lumen
  • Bile recirculation runs through the portal vein, so a thoracic duct block does not touch it

How it follows from the main questionChylomicrons go lacteal → lymph → thoracic duct → blood, so absorbed fat is stranded → decreased lipid absorption into the bloodstream. Bile returns by portal vein, unaffected.

Chylomicrons and apoproteins

88unlocks 18TA ×12 not obvious
A child with abetalipoproteinemia has fat-laden enterocytes, steatorrhea and almost no plasma chylomicrons. Which step is defective?
  1. A. Micelle formation by bile salts
  2. B. Hydrolysis of TAG by pancreatic lipase
  3. C. Loading of re-esterified lipid onto apoB-48 by microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP)
  4. D. Activation of lipoprotein lipase by apoC-II
  5. E. Esterification of cholesterol by LCAT
AnswerC. Loading of re-esterified lipid onto apoB-48 by microsomal triglyceride transfer protein (MTP)
WhyIn the enterocyte ER, fatty acids (as acyl-CoA) are re-esterified with 2-MAG into TAG (cholesterol → CE by ACAT), and MTP loads these lipids onto apoB-48 to build the chylomicron, which leaves via lacteals. Without MTP, fat stays in the enterocyte. Lipase and micelles act in the lumen, LPL in capillaries, LCAT on HDL.
Key factRe-esterification and the chylomicron
  • Enterocyte ER: FA → acyl-CoA; 2-MAG + 2 acyl-CoA → TAG; cholesterol → CE (ACAT); lysophospholipid → PL. Purpose: re-make complex lipids for packaging and transport
  • MTP loads them onto apoB-48 → nascent chylomicron (needs protein synthesis). MTP loss = abetalipoproteinemia; chylomicron retention disease → fat + A D E K malabsorption
  • Chylomicron = made by the intestine, most TAG (85–90%), largest, lowest density, carries dietary (exogenous) TAG to muscle and adipose
  • Too big for capillaries → lacteal → lymph → thoracic duct → blood (chyle richest in intestinal lymph); plasma lipemic after a fatty meal; ↑ in fed state
  • Compare: VLDL = liver TAG; LDL = cholesterol to tissues; HDL = reverse cholesterol transport

Chylomicrons and apoproteins

89unlocks 22
Hours after a fatty meal, a patient's plasma stays milky. Their chylomicrons contain normal apoB-48, but fatty acids are not released from them in capillaries. Which apoprotein is most likely missing?
  1. A. ApoC-II
  2. B. ApoA-I
  3. C. ApoE
  4. D. Apo(a)
  5. E. ApoB-100
AnswerA. ApoC-II
WhyApoC-II, picked up from HDL, activates capillary lipoprotein lipase, which frees fatty acids from chylomicron and VLDL TAG; without it TAG-rich particles persist. ApoB-100 binds the LDL receptor, apoE mediates remnant uptake by the liver and apoA-I activates LCAT.
Key factApoprotein table
  • ApoB-48: made only in enterocytes (apoB mRNA editing → stop codon, 48% length, no LDL-receptor domain); unique to chylomicrons; required to assemble and secrete them
  • ApoB-100: full length, liver; VLDL/LDL; ligand for the LDL receptor
  • ApoC-II: from HDL; activates lipoprotein lipase → deficiency = hypertriglyceridemia (chylomicrons persist)
  • ApoE: from HDL; remnant uptake by hepatocytes. ApoA-I: HDL, activates LCAT
  • LPL (capillary wall): chylomicron TAG → FA to muscle/adipose, glycerol to liver; chylomicrons lose FA as they circulate and become remnants
q971 distractors misstate apoB mRNA editing (the change is C→U in the intestine, creating a stop codon); the keyed answer (apoB-48 belongs to the intestine) is still right.

  • ApoE does not bind pneumocytes; apoB-100 binds the LDL (not HDL) receptor; apoA-I is the main HDL (not LDL) protein

Steatorrhea and malabsorption

A 3-year-old with recurrent pneumonia, a positive sweat chloride test and bulky, floating stools has a stool fat analysis. Which pattern is expected?

  2. B. Maldigestion; mostly lactose and sucrose in stool

WhyIn cystic fibrosis, thick secretions plug the pancreatic ducts, so lipase (and amylase and proteases) never reach the duodenum: maldigestion with TAG in stool. Key factSteatorrhea = frothy, foul-smelling, floating stool with excess fat
  • Maldigestion → TAG in stool: pancreatic insufficiency (cystic fibrosis, chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer), Zollinger-Ellison (acid kills lipase), liver disease / ↓ bile (↓ emulsification)
  • Malabsorption → fatty acids in stool: intestinal disease (Crohn, celiac, bacterial or parasitic disease)
  • CF: lung infections + steatorrhea + failure to thrive + ↑ sweat Cl- (or meconium ileus) → pancreatic ducts plugged → no pancreatic lipase, amylase or proteases (starch, TAG, protein undigested; lactose/sucrose fine); treat with oral enzymes
  • Chronic pancreatitis → steatorrhea + diabetes
  • Not causes: obesity, ↑ CCK, kidney stones

CASE 4: HYPOGLYCEMIA, HYPERKETONEMIA, AND LIVER DYSFUNCTION Patient Presentation: AK, a 59-year-old male with slurred speech, ataxia (loss of skeletal muscle coordination), and abdominal pain, was dropped off at the Emergency Department (ED). Focused History: AK is known to the ED staff from previous visits. He has a 6-year history of chronic, heavy alcohol consumption. He is not known to take illicit drugs. At this ED visit, AK reports that he has been drinking heavily in the past day or so. He cannot recall having eaten anything in that time. There is evidence of recent vomiting, but no blood is apparent. Physical Examination (Pertinent Findings): The physical examination was remarkable for the emaciated appearance of the patient. (His body mass index was later determined to be 17.5, which put him in the underweight category.) The cheeks of his face were erythematous (red in color) due to dilated blood vessels in the skin (telangiectasia). Eye movement was normal. Neither icterus (jaundice) nor edema (swelling due to fluid retention) was seen. The liver was slightly enlarged. Bedside tests revealed hypoglycemia and hyperketonemia (as acetoacetate). Blood was drawn and sent to the clinical laboratory. Pertinent Test Results: Additional Tests: Complete blood count (CBC) and blood smear revealed a macrocytic anemia (right Image). Folate and B12 levels were ordered. Diagnosis: Alcoholism Treatment (Immediate): Thiamine and glucose were given intravenously. Prognosis: Alcoholism (alcohol dependence) is the third most common cause of preventable death in the United States. People with alcoholism are at increased risk for liver cirrhosis, pancreatitis, gastrointestinal bleeding, and some cancers. Chronic, excessive consumption of alcohol is a leading cause of acute pancreatitis, a painful inflammatory condition that results from autodigestion of the gland by premature activation of pancreatic enzymes. Which of the following statements concerning the pancreas is correct?
  1. A. Autodigestion of the pancreas would be expected to result in a decrease in pancreatic proteins in the blood.
  2. B. In individuals who progress from acute to chronic pancreatitis, with the characteristic structural changes that result in decreased pancreatic function, diabetes and steatorrhea are expected findings.
  3. C. In response to secretin, the exocrine pancreas secretes protons to lower the pH in the intestinal lumen.
  4. D. Pancreatitis may also be seen in individuals with hypercholesterolemia.
AnswerB. In individuals who progress from acute to chronic pancreatitis, with the characteristic structural changes that result in decreased pancreatic function, diabetes and steatorrhea are expected findings.
WhyChronic pancreatitis destroys both exocrine and endocrine tissue: losing lipase causes steatorrhea, and losing β cells causes diabetes. Autodigestion raises serum amylase/lipase, secretin triggers HCO₃⁻, and pancreatitis follows hypertriglyceridemia, not hypercholesterolemia.
Explanation from the source
Answer = B. The exocrine pancreas secretes enzymes required for the digestion of dietary carbohydrate, protein, and fat. The endocrine pancreas secretes the peptide hormones insulin and glucagon. Damage that affects the functions of the pancreas would lead to diabetes (decreased insulin) and steatorrhea (fatty stool), with the latter the consequence of maldigestion of dietary fat. As was seen with the rise of troponins in a myocardial infarction and transaminases in liver damage, loss of cellular integrity (as would be seen in autodigestion of the pancreas) results in proteins that normally are intracellular being found in higher-than-normal concentrations in the blood. Secretin causes the pancreas to release bicarbonate to raise the pH of the chyme coming to the intestine from the stomach. Pancreatic enzymes work best at neutral or slightly alkaline pH. Pancreatitis is seen in individuals with hypertriglyceridemia as a result of a deficiency in lipoprotein lipase or its coenzyme, apolipoprotein C-II.
How it follows from the main questionIgnore the ketone setup: it is a pancreas question. Chronic pancreatitis destroys exocrine tissue (lipase → steatorrhea) and islets (diabetes), so B is correct.

Steatorrhea and malabsorption

91unlocks 13TA ×14 not obvious
A 2-year-old with recurrent pneumonia, a positive sweat chloride test and bulky, foul-smelling stools is evaluated. Which digestive process is still normal?
  1. A. Hydrolysis of long-chain triacylglycerol to 2-monoacylglycerol
  2. B. Hydrolysis of lactose and sucrose at the brush border
  3. C. Release of cholesterol from dietary cholesteryl esters
  4. D. Activation of trypsinogen to trypsin in the duodenal lumen
  5. E. Hydrolysis of starch by pancreatic α-amylase
AnswerB. Hydrolysis of lactose and sucrose at the brush border
WhyCF plugs the pancreatic ducts, so every pancreatic enzyme (amylase, lipase, proteases, cholesterol esterase) fails to reach the duodenum. Lactase and sucrase sit on the brush border, so disaccharides are still split. Enteropeptidase is present, but no trypsinogen arrives, so trypsin activation (D) still fails.
Key factCystic fibrosis = pancreatic duct plug, not a mucosal or hormone defect
  • Recognize it, often unnamed: recurrent lung infections + steatorrhea + failure to thrive + ↑ sweat Cl- (meconium ileus in a newborn)
  • Lost (everything pancreatic): lipase/colipase → long-chain TAG in stool (maldigestion); amylase → starch; proteases (trypsinogen etc.) → protein in stool; PLA2 and cholesterol esterase. Thick secretions can plug bile ducts too. The enzyme blamed for the steatorrhea = pancreatic lipase
  • Spared: brush-border enzymes (lactase, sucrase, enteropeptidase, aminopeptidases) → lactose and sucrose digested normally; lingual/gastric lipase → short/medium-chain (dairy) TAG still digested; CCK and secretin release; the mucosa itself (not celiac, not an amino acid transporter defect)
  • Consequences: vitamins A, D, E, K lost, poor growth. Treat with oral pancreatic enzymes
The lecture names CF only as pancreatic lipase insufficiency (slides 7 and 35); the brush-border and protease points come from the practice questions (q1129, q1131) and standard physiology.

The fed state and insulin

93unlocks 9TA ×12 not obvious
Two hours after a large pasta dinner, which set of changes is expected in a person's hepatocytes?
  1. A. Glucagon is high, PEPCK is induced and ketogenesis increases
  2. B. Hormone-sensitive lipase is phosphorylated and fatty acid oxidation increases
  3. C. The low-insulin state drives fatty acid synthesis in the mitochondrial matrix
  4. D. Insulin-activated protein phosphatase dephosphorylates glycogen synthase, pyruvate kinase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase, all of which are active
  5. E. Glycogen phosphorylase is phosphorylated and active, and CPT-I activity rises
AnswerD. Insulin-activated protein phosphatase dephosphorylates glycogen synthase, pyruvate kinase and acetyl-CoA carboxylase, all of which are active
WhyAfter a meal the insulin/glucagon ratio is high; insulin activates protein phosphatase, so the storage enzymes (glycogen synthase, pyruvate kinase, PFK-2, ACC) sit in their active dephosphorylated form. Phosphorylase, CPT-I, PEPCK, HSL and ketogenesis are fasting events, and fatty acid synthesis is cytosolic and needs high insulin.
Key factFatty acid synthesis = well-fed, high-insulin, high-ATP state.
  • Where: cytosol; mainly liver and lactating mammary gland, less so adipose.
  • Insulin → protein phosphatase → dephosphorylated = active storage enzymes: glycogen synthase, pyruvate kinase, PFK-2, acetyl-CoA carboxylase. Insulin is the hormone that promotes lipogenesis.
  • The fed state switches OFF: lipolysis (HSL), β-oxidation (CPT-I), ketogenesis, gluconeogenesis (pyruvate carboxylase, PEPCK, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase), glycogenolysis, muscle proteolysis.
  • A low-insulin state never promotes fatty acid synthesis (true or false: false).
  • Lecture summary table: rate-limiting enzyme ACC; needs ATP; activator citrate; inhibitor long-chain acyl-CoA; clinical link alcoholic fatty liver.

WhyFructokinase and aldolase B split fructose-1-phosphate into DHAP and glyceraldehyde, which enter glycolysis below PFK-1, so hepatic flux is fast and unregulated and supplies glycerol 3-phosphate and acetyl-CoA for TAG. Which statement correctly pairs the phases of fatty acid synthesis with their enzymes?
  1. A. Phase I: ATP-citrate lyase makes cytosolic acetyl-CoA; Phase II: ACC makes malonyl-CoA; Phase III: fatty acid synthase builds palmitate
  2. B. Phase I: carboxylation of 3C acetyl-CoA to 2C malonyl-CoA; Phase II: citrate export; Phase III: fatty acid synthase
  3. C. Phase I: ACC makes malonyl-CoA in mitochondria and exports it; Phase II: ATP-citrate lyase; Phase III: thioesterase II
  4. D. Phase I: fatty acid synthase; Phase II: elongase; Phase III: desaturase
  5. E. Phase I: cytosolic pyruvate dehydrogenase; Phase II: malic enzyme; Phase III: ACC
AnswerA. Phase I: ATP-citrate lyase makes cytosolic acetyl-CoA; Phase II: ACC makes malonyl-CoA; Phase III: fatty acid synthase builds palmitate
WhyThe course scheme is I citrate out and cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase, II ACC carboxylates 2C acetyl-CoA to 3C malonyl-CoA, III FAS adds 2C units and thioesterase releases palmitate. Malonyl-CoA is never made in mitochondria, and the reversed carbon counts (3C acetyl, 2C malonyl) are a planted trap.
Key factThree phases
  • I Production of cytosolic acetyl-CoA: citrate exported, cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase.
  • II Carboxylation: ACC, 2C acetyl-CoA → 3C malonyl-CoA (committed, rate-limiting).
  • III Chain building on fatty acid synthase → palmitate (16:0), released by thioesterase.
Regulated at three enzymes: ATP-citrate lyase (induced by glucose/insulin), ACC (allosteric, covalent, gene expression), FAS (gene expression: insulin, feeding ↑; PUFA, fasting ↓). Not regulators: thioesterase, NADPH (a substrate). Blocking ATP-citrate lyase → less cytosolic acetyl-CoA for ACC.

Practice Q1331Looks like another topic
CASE 2: SEVERE FASTING HYPOGLYCEMIA Patient Presentation: Jason S. is a 4-month-old boy whose mother is concerned about the “twitching” movements he makes just before feedings. She tells the pediatrician that the movements started about 1 week ago, are most apparent in the morning, and disappear shortly after eating. Focused History: Jason is the product of a normal pregnancy and delivery. He appeared normal at birth. He has been at the 30th percentile for both weight and length since birth. His immunizations are up to date. Jason last ate a few hours ago. Physical Examination (Pertinent Findings): Jason appears sleepy and feels clammy to the touch. His respiratory rate is elevated. His temperature is normal. Jason has a protuberant, firm abdomen that appears to be nontender. His liver is palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin and is smooth. His kidneys are enlarged and symmetrical. Pertinent Test Results: Jason is sent to the regional children’s hospital for further evaluation. Ultrasound studies confirm hepatomegaly and renomegaly and show no evidence of tumors. A liver biopsy is performed. The hepatocytes are distended. Staining reveals large amounts of lipid (primarily triacylglycerol) and carbohydrate. Liver glycogen is elevated in amount and normal in structure. Enzyme assay using liver homogenate treated with detergent reveals less than 10% of the normal activity of glucose 6-phosphatase, an enzyme of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane in the liver and the kidneys. Diagnosis: Glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency (glycogen storage disease [GSD] type Ia, von Gierke disease) Treatment (Immediate): Jason was given glucose intravenously, and his blood glucose level rose into the normal range. However, as the day progressed, it fell to well below normal. Administration of glucagon had no effect on blood glucose levels but increased blood lactate. Jason’s blood glucose levels were able to be maintained by constant infusion of glucose. Prognosis: Individuals with glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency develop hepatic adenomas starting in the second decade of life and are at increased risk for hepatic carcinoma. Kidney glomerular function is impaired and can result in kidney failure. Patients are at increased risk for developing gout, but this rarely occurs before puberty. A. Why are triacylglycerols and cholesterol elevated? Hint: Glucose is the primary carbon source for their synthesis.
Show figure
AnswerIncreased glycolysis results in increased availability of glycerol 3-phosphate for hepatic TAG synthesis. Additionally, some of the pyruvate generated in glycolysis will be oxidatively decarboxylated to acetyl coenzyme A (CoA). However, the tricarboxylic acid cycle is inhibited by the rise in NADH, and the acetyl CoA is transported to the cytosol as citrate. The rise of acetyl CoA in the cytosol results in increased fatty acid synthesis. Recall that citrate is an allosteric activator of acetyl CoA carboxylase (ACC). The malonyl product of ACC inhibits fatty acid oxidation at the carnitine palmitoyltransferase I step. Because mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation generates the acetyl CoA substrate for hepatic ketogenesis, ketone body levels do not rise. The fatty acids get esterified to the glycerol backbone, resulting in an increase in TAGs that get sent out of liver as components of very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDLs). [Note: The hypoglycemia results in release of epinephrine and the activation of TAG lipolysis with release of free fatty acids into the blood. The fatty acids are used in hepatic TAG synthesis.] The acetyl CoA is also a substrate for cholesterol synthesis. Thus, the increase in glycolysis results in the hyperlipidemia seen in the patient (see Figure).
WhyGlucose 6-phosphatase deficiency traps G6P, driving glycolysis: more glycerol 3-phosphate and acetyl-CoA, exported as citrate for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis. Malonyl-CoA blocks CPT I, so the fatty acids are esterified into TAG and secreted as VLDL rather than oxidized to ketones.
How it follows from the main questionLooks like a glycogen question. Trapped G6P → ↑ glycolysis → acetyl-CoA; high NADH stalls the TCA, so citrate is exported and cleaved → cytosolic acetyl-CoA for fat and cholesterol; citrate also activates ACC.
Practice Q1275Trap: the obvious answer is wrong
Q1. Dr. Panini is treating a patient who is chronically malnourished and exhibits signs of impaired fatty acid synthesis. Laboratory tests show low levels of NADPH and acetyl-CoA in the cytosol. Given these findings, which metabolic pathway is most likely compromised in this patient, and how does it affect fatty acid biosynthesis?
  1. A. Glycolysis
  2. B. Pentose phosphate pathway
  3. C. Citrate shuttle
  4. D. Beta-oxidation
  5. E. Glycogenolysis
AnswerC. Citrate shuttle
WhyThe citrate shuttle exports mitochondrial acetyl units as citrate, which ATP-citrate lyase splits into cytosolic acetyl-CoA; the oxaloacetate returns via malate → pyruvate through malic enzyme, generating NADPH. A shuttle defect lowers both.
Explanation from the source
Explanation: The citrate shuttle is crucial for transporting acetyl-CoA from the mitochondria to the cytosol, where it can be used for fatty acid synthesis. In the cytosol, citrate is cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase to regenerate acetyl-CoA. This process also indirectly supplies NADPH via malic enzyme, which is necessary for the reduction steps in fatty acid synthesis. (A) is incorrect because glycolysis provides pyruvate for acetyl-CoA production but does not directly regulate fatty acid synthesis. (B) is incorrect because although the pentose phosphate pathway generates NADPH, the issue in this case seems to be with acetyl-CoA availability in the cytosol. (D) is incorrect because beta-oxidation breaks down fatty acids rather than synthesizing them. (E) is incorrect because glycogenolysis is related to glucose release, not fatty acid synthesis
How it follows from the main questionPentose phosphate explains only the NADPH. The citrate shuttle explains both: ATP-citrate lyase gives acetyl-CoA, and its OAA → malate → malic enzyme gives NADPH.

  3. C. Isocitrate leaves the mitochondrion and is cleaved in the cytosol, with NADH supplying the reducing power
  4. D. Acetyl-CoA released from exported citrate is the immediate carbon source, and dietary glucose is the ultimate source
  5. E. Glycerol from adipose TAG supplies the carbons through hepatic glycerol kinase
AnswerD. Acetyl-CoA released from exported citrate is the immediate carbon source, and dietary glucose is the ultimate source
WhyDietary carbohydrate is the ultimate source: glucose → pyruvate → PDH → acetyl-CoA in the mitochondria, which leaves as citrate. In the cytosol ATP-citrate lyase frees acetyl-CoA, the immediate building block; citrate is only the carrier (and ACC activator), and glycerol, ketones, isocitrate and NADH are not inputs.
Key factWhat fatty acids are made from
  • Ultimate carbon source = dietary carbohydrate (glucose): glycolysis → pyruvate → PDH (mitochondria) → acetyl-CoA. Not dietary protein, ketone bodies, cholesterol or glycerol.
  • Immediate carbon source = acetyl-CoA, the principal building block (all 16 C of palmitate; malonyl-CoA's added CO2 is lost again). It reaches the cytosol only as citrate (PDH → citrate synthase → citrate export); citrate is the carrier and ACC activator, pyruvate and OAA are upstream.
  • Directly required: acetyl-CoA, ATP, NADPH (plus biotin and CO2 at ACC). Lecture list: dietary carbohydrate, acetyl-CoA, ATP, NADPH, insulin. Not inputs: AMP (an inhibitor via AMPK), isocitrate, GTP, NADH, FADH2, propionyl-CoA. Palmitate and palmitoyl-CoA are products.
  • One shuttle, two inputs: exported citrate gives cytosolic acetyl-CoA, and its OAA returns as malate → pyruvate (malic enzyme) making NADPH. A citrate-shuttle defect lowers both; a PPP defect lowers only NADPH.
  • More glucose flux (e.g. glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency trapping G6P) → more acetyl-CoA and glycerol 3-P → ↑ TAG and cholesterol.
Amino acids can contribute some acetyl-CoA, but the lecture (F1270:7, F1270:12) names dietary carbohydrate as the source, and the TA key follows it.

Practice Q1331Looks like another topic
CASE 2: SEVERE FASTING HYPOGLYCEMIA Patient Presentation: Jason S. is a 4-month-old boy whose mother is concerned about the “twitching” movements he makes just before feedings. She tells the pediatrician that the movements started about 1 week ago, are most apparent in the morning, and disappear shortly after eating. Focused History: Jason is the product of a normal pregnancy and delivery. He appeared normal at birth. He has been at the 30th percentile for both weight and length since birth. His immunizations are up to date. Jason last ate a few hours ago. Physical Examination (Pertinent Findings): Jason appears sleepy and feels clammy to the touch. His respiratory rate is elevated. His temperature is normal. Jason has a protuberant, firm abdomen that appears to be nontender. His liver is palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin and is smooth. His kidneys are enlarged and symmetrical. Pertinent Test Results: Jason is sent to the regional children’s hospital for further evaluation. Ultrasound studies confirm hepatomegaly and renomegaly and show no evidence of tumors. A liver biopsy is performed. The hepatocytes are distended. Staining reveals large amounts of lipid (primarily triacylglycerol) and carbohydrate. Liver glycogen is elevated in amount and normal in structure. Enzyme assay using liver homogenate treated with detergent reveals less than 10% of the normal activity of glucose 6-phosphatase, an enzyme of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane in the liver and the kidneys. Diagnosis: Glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency (glycogen storage disease [GSD] type Ia, von Gierke disease) Treatment (Immediate): Jason was given glucose intravenously, and his blood glucose level rose into the normal range. However, as the day progressed, it fell to well below normal. Administration of glucagon had no effect on blood glucose levels but increased blood lactate. Jason’s blood glucose levels were able to be maintained by constant infusion of glucose. Prognosis: Individuals with glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency develop hepatic adenomas starting in the second decade of life and are at increased risk for hepatic carcinoma. Kidney glomerular function is impaired and can result in kidney failure. Patients are at increased risk for developing gout, but this rarely occurs before puberty. A. Why are triacylglycerols and cholesterol elevated? Hint: Glucose is the primary carbon source for their synthesis.
Show figure
AnswerIncreased glycolysis results in increased availability of glycerol 3-phosphate for hepatic TAG synthesis. Additionally, some of the pyruvate generated in glycolysis will be oxidatively decarboxylated to acetyl coenzyme A (CoA). However, the tricarboxylic acid cycle is inhibited by the rise in NADH, and the acetyl CoA is transported to the cytosol as citrate. The rise of acetyl CoA in the cytosol results in increased fatty acid synthesis. Recall that citrate is an allosteric activator of acetyl CoA carboxylase (ACC). The malonyl product of ACC inhibits fatty acid oxidation at the carnitine palmitoyltransferase I step. Because mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation generates the acetyl CoA substrate for hepatic ketogenesis, ketone body levels do not rise. The fatty acids get esterified to the glycerol backbone, resulting in an increase in TAGs that get sent out of liver as components of very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDLs). [Note: The hypoglycemia results in release of epinephrine and the activation of TAG lipolysis with release of free fatty acids into the blood. The fatty acids are used in hepatic TAG synthesis.] The acetyl CoA is also a substrate for cholesterol synthesis. Thus, the increase in glycolysis results in the hyperlipidemia seen in the patient (see Figure).
WhyGlucose 6-phosphatase deficiency traps G6P, driving glycolysis: more glycerol 3-phosphate and acetyl-CoA, exported as citrate for fatty acid and cholesterol synthesis. Malonyl-CoA blocks CPT I, so the fatty acids are esterified into TAG and secreted as VLDL rather than oxidized to ketones.
How it follows from the main questionGlucose is the carbon source: trapped G6P → ↑ glycolysis → ↑ acetyl-CoA (exported as citrate) and ↑ glycerol 3-P → more fatty acids, TAG and cholesterol.
Practice Q1275Trap: the obvious answer is wrong
Q1. Dr. Panini is treating a patient who is chronically malnourished and exhibits signs of impaired fatty acid synthesis. Laboratory tests show low levels of NADPH and acetyl-CoA in the cytosol. Given these findings, which metabolic pathway is most likely compromised in this patient, and how does it affect fatty acid biosynthesis?
  1. A. Glycolysis
  2. B. Pentose phosphate pathway
  3. C. Citrate shuttle
  4. D. Beta-oxidation
  5. E. Glycogenolysis
AnswerC. Citrate shuttle
WhyThe citrate shuttle exports mitochondrial acetyl units as citrate, which ATP-citrate lyase splits into cytosolic acetyl-CoA; the oxaloacetate returns via malate → pyruvate through malic enzyme, generating NADPH. A shuttle defect lowers both.
Explanation from the source
Explanation: The citrate shuttle is crucial for transporting acetyl-CoA from the mitochondria to the cytosol, where it can be used for fatty acid synthesis. In the cytosol, citrate is cleaved by ATP-citrate lyase to regenerate acetyl-CoA. This process also indirectly supplies NADPH via malic enzyme, which is necessary for the reduction steps in fatty acid synthesis. (A) is incorrect because glycolysis provides pyruvate for acetyl-CoA production but does not directly regulate fatty acid synthesis. (B) is incorrect because although the pentose phosphate pathway generates NADPH, the issue in this case seems to be with acetyl-CoA availability in the cytosol. (D) is incorrect because beta-oxidation breaks down fatty acids rather than synthesizing them. (E) is incorrect because glycogenolysis is related to glucose release, not fatty acid synthesis
How it follows from the main questionPPP explains only NADPH. The citrate shuttle delivers acetyl-CoA and, via malate → pyruvate (malic enzyme), NADPH, so it alone lowers both.
Practice Q1193Trap: the obvious answer is wrong
In a well-fed individual with high insulin levels, which of the following molecules provides the immediate carbon source for de novo fatty acid synthesis in the cytosol?
  1. A. Pyruvate
  2. B. Citrate
  3. C. Acetyl-CoA
  4. D. Oxaloacetate
AnswerC. Acetyl-CoA
WhyAcetyl-CoA is the direct carbon source: citrate carries it out of the mitochondria and ATP-citrate lyase releases it in the cytosol, where ACC converts it to malonyl-CoA.
Explanation from the source
Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the cytosol and requires Acetyl-CoA as the immediate precursor. Acetyl-CoA is derived from glucose metabolism via pyruvate oxidation in the mitochondria and transported as citrate into the cytosol. In the cytosol, ATP-citrate lyase converts citrate back to acetyl-CoA for fatty acid synthesis. The process requires ATP, NADPH (from the HMP shunt and malic enzyme), and insulin stimulation in well-fed states.
How it follows from the main questionCitrate only carries the acetyl unit out; ATP-citrate lyase frees it, so the immediate carbon source is acetyl-CoA.

A mouse lacking cytosolic malic enzyme has reduced hepatic fatty acid synthesis. Which reaction normally supplies the missing cofactor, and where is it used?
  1. A. Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA; NADPH for ATP-citrate lyase
  2. B. Malate → pyruvate + CO2; NADPH for the two reduction steps on fatty acid synthase
  3. C. Isocitrate → α-ketoglutarate (NAD+-linked); NADH for fatty acid synthase
  4. D. Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate → 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; NADPH for thioesterase
  5. E. Oxaloacetate → malate; NADH for acetyl-CoA carboxylase
AnswerB. Malate → pyruvate + CO2; NADPH for the two reduction steps on fatty acid synthase
WhyMalic enzyme oxidatively decarboxylates malate to pyruvate + CO2 and reduces NADP+ to NADPH, which FAS uses for its two reductions per cycle. ACC needs no NADPH, and glycolysis, PDH and NAD+-isocitrate dehydrogenase make NADH, not NADPH.
Key factNADPH sources
  • Pentose phosphate pathway (HMP shunt; oxidative phase: G6PD, 6-phosphogluconate DH; glucose 6-P → ribulose 5-P) = the chief source.
  • Malic enzyme: malate → pyruvate + CO2 + NADPH (about half the NADPH for FA synthesis); its malate comes from the OAA released by ATP-citrate lyase (OAA → malate by malate DH, using NADH).
  • Used by FAS's two reductases (14 per palmitate) and by cholesterol synthesis; ACC uses none.
  • NOT NADPH sources: glycolysis, TCA, ETC/oxidative phosphorylation, β-oxidation, gluconeogenesis, hexokinase, urea cycle. Glutathione reductase and FA synthesis consume NADPH.
  • G6PD deficiency or inhibition → less NADPH → less fatty acid synthesis.
q1201 keys the HMP shunt as the major NADPH source over malic enzyme; the lecture calls the pentose phosphate pathway the chief source and also says malic enzyme supplies about 50%, so take PPP only when 'major' is asked.

Practice Q1278Trap: the obvious answer is wrong
Q4. A researcher studying fatty acid metabolism knocks out the gene encoding malic enzyme in a mouse model. This enzyme provides NADPH, a critical cofactor for fatty acid synthesis. Dr. Panini is asked how this knockout will impact fatty acid synthesis in the liver, particularly the role of NADPH. Which of the following consequences is most likely to result from this knockout?
  1. A. Increased activity of the citric acid cycle
  2. B. Decreased formation of malonyl-CoA
  3. C. Reduced elongation of palmitic acid
  4. D. Enhanced activity of fatty acid synthase
  5. E. Impaired reduction reactions in fatty acid synthesis
AnswerE. Impaired reduction reactions in fatty acid synthesis
WhyMalic enzyme is a major cytosolic source of NADPH, and fatty acid synthase uses NADPH for its two reduction steps (β-ketoacyl and enoyl reductases) in each cycle; malonyl-CoA formation by ACC does not need NADPH.
Explanation from the source
Explanation: Impaired reduction reactions in fatty acid synthesis are the most likely result of knocking out malic enzyme. Fatty acid synthase requires NADPH for the reduction of carbon-carbon double bonds during the synthesis of palmitic acid. Without malic enzyme, which generates NADPH from malate, the supply of NADPH would be limited, hindering the reductive steps in the fatty acid synthesis pathway. (A) is incorrect because this knockout would not increase the activity of the citric acid cycle; in fact, citrate may accumulate due to impaired lipogenesis. (B) is incorrect because malonyl-CoA formation is dependent on ACC, not NADPH. (C) is incorrect because the elongation of palmitic acid is a downstream process that would be affected after fatty acid synthesis is reduced, but this is not the primary effect. (D) is incorrect because fatty acid synthase activity is dependent on NADPH; without sufficient NADPH, its activity would not be enhanced
How it follows from the main question'Decreased malonyl-CoA formation' is the trap: ACC uses no NADPH. Less NADPH hits FAS's two reductases → impaired reduction reactions in fatty acid synthesis.

Which reaction is the committed and rate-limiting step of fatty acid synthesis, with its correct requirements?
  1. A. Acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA by acetyl-CoA carboxylase; needs NADPH, ATP and biotin
  2. B. Palmitoyl-ACP → palmitate by thioesterase; needs water
  3. C. Pyruvate → oxaloacetate by pyruvate carboxylase; needs biotin and ATP
  4. D. Citrate → acetyl-CoA + oxaloacetate by ATP-citrate lyase; needs ATP and CoA
  5. E. Acetyl-CoA (2C) → malonyl-CoA (3C) by acetyl-CoA carboxylase; needs biotin, ATP and CO2
AnswerE. Acetyl-CoA (2C) → malonyl-CoA (3C) by acetyl-CoA carboxylase; needs biotin, ATP and CO2
WhyAcetyl-CoA carboxylase carboxylates acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA using biotin, ATP and CO2 (HCO3−); this is the committed, rate-limiting step. NADPH belongs to fatty acid synthase, and pyruvate carboxylase also uses biotin but serves gluconeogenesis.
Key factAcetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) = committed and rate-limiting step.
  • Acetyl-CoA (2C) + HCO3−/CO2 + ATP → malonyl-CoA (3C) + ADP + Pi, in the cytosol.
  • Cofactors: biotin (B7), ATP, CO2. Two half-reactions: ATP carboxylates biotin, then biotin hands CO2 to acetyl-CoA.
  • No NADPH and no AMP (NADPH is used by FAS; AMP inhibits ACC through AMPK).
  • Not rate-limiting: ATP-citrate lyase, fatty acid synthase, malic enzyme, PDH, citrate synthase, malate DH, thioesterase, pyruvate or propionyl-CoA carboxylase.

A 26-year-old bodybuilder who eats a dozen raw egg whites daily develops periorificial dermatitis, alopecia and fasting hypoglycemia. Which pair of enzymes is impaired?
  1. A. PEPCK and fatty acid synthase
  2. B. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase and ATP-citrate lyase
  3. C. Glucose-6-phosphatase and malic enzyme
  4. D. Pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase
  5. E. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase and pyruvate carboxylase
AnswerE. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase and pyruvate carboxylase
WhyEgg-white avidin binds biotin (B7), the CO2 carrier of the carboxylases: acetyl-CoA carboxylase (no malonyl-CoA) and pyruvate carboxylase (first step of gluconeogenesis, hence fasting hypoglycemia). PDH and α-KG DH use thiamine, and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase uses B12.
Key factBiotin = vitamin B7, covalently attached to a lysine (biotinylation) of three carboxylases:
  • Acetyl-CoA carboxylase: acetyl-CoA → malonyl-CoA (fatty acid synthesis).
  • Pyruvate carboxylase: pyruvate → OAA, first step of gluconeogenesis → deficiency gives fasting hypoglycemia.
  • Propionyl-CoA carboxylase: odd-chain catabolism.
Causes: raw egg-white avidin, bacterial streptavidin, biotinidase deficiency (cannot recycle biotin). Signs: periorificial dermatitis, alopecia, brittle nails, paresthesias. Not biotin: PDH (B1), transaminases (B6), methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12), CoA (B5).

A mutation makes acetyl-CoA carboxylase resistant to phosphorylation. During a 24-hour fast, what is expected in the liver?
  1. A. Glucagon dephosphorylates ACC, raising fatty acid synthesis only in muscle
  2. B. ACC is inactivated by AMPK, malonyl-CoA falls, and β-oxidation rises normally
  3. C. Malonyl-CoA activates hormone-sensitive lipase, increasing lipolysis
  4. D. ACC stays active, malonyl-CoA stays high, CPT-I is inhibited, and β-oxidation and ketogenesis fall
  5. E. ACC stays active, and malonyl-CoA activates CPT-I, raising ketogenesis
AnswerD. ACC stays active, malonyl-CoA stays high, CPT-I is inhibited, and β-oxidation and ketogenesis fall
WhyFasting signals (glucagon, epinephrine, AMP → AMPK) normally phosphorylate and inactivate ACC; if ACC cannot be switched off, malonyl-CoA stays high and inhibits CPT-I, so fatty acids cannot enter mitochondria and β-oxidation and ketogenesis fall. Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I; it never activates it.
Key factCovalent (short-term) control of ACC
  • Insulin → ↓cAMP, protein phosphatase → dephosphorylated ACC = active.
  • Glucagon, epinephrine (cAMP/PKA) and AMP → AMPK → phosphorylated ACC = inactive (exercise, fasting, low energy, insulin deficiency).
  • Malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-I, so synthesis and β-oxidation never run together.
    ACC on → malonyl-CoA ↑ → CPT-I blocked → ↓ β-oxidation, ↓ ketones.
    ACC off → malonyl-CoA ↓ → CPT-I free → ↑ β-oxidation (marathon runner).
  • Inhibitors of fatty acid synthesis: glucagon, epinephrine, AMP. Activators: insulin, citrate.

Which statement about mammalian fatty acid synthase is correct?
  1. A. It is a dimer of identical multifunctional polypeptides, each with seven activities and an ACP; each cycle is condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction
  2. B. It builds the chain from the carboxyl (α) end toward the methyl (ω) end
  3. C. Its monomer is fully active, with the intermediates free in solution
  4. D. Each cycle is dehydration, oxidation, condensation, oxidation, using NAD+
  5. E. It is a filamentous polymer activated by citrate
AnswerA. It is a dimer of identical multifunctional polypeptides, each with seven activities and an ACP; each cycle is condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction
WhyFAS is a head-to-tail dimer of identical polypeptides, each with all seven activities plus an ACP; only the dimer works. Each turn is condensation → reduction → dehydration → reduction (both reductions use NADPH), and the first acetyl becomes the ω end, so the chain grows ω → α. The citrate-activated filament is ACC.
Key factFatty acid synthase (FAS)
  • Dimer of identical polypeptides, head to tail; each has all 7 activities + ACP (phosphopantetheine arm carries the chain). Only the dimer is active.
  • Each 2C cycle: condensation (−CO2) → reduction (NADPH) → dehydration → reduction (NADPH).
  • The primer acetyl becomes the methyl (ω) end; new 2C units go on at the carboxyl end → chain grows ω → α. The α end (C1) is the carboxyl group.

Hepatocytes convert palmitate (16:0) into oleate (18:1 Δ9). Which description of the two steps is correct?
  1. A. Palmitoyl-CoA is elongated in the smooth ER with acetyl-CoA and FADH2, and elongase introduces the C9–C10 double bond
  2. B. Fatty acid synthase elongates free palmitate in the cytosol using acetyl-CoA and NADH, and a mitochondrial desaturase then acts
  3. C. Stearate is desaturated between C12 and C13 in the cytosol, then shortened to 18 carbons
  4. D. Acyl-CoA synthetase elongates palmitate in the rough ER, and acetyl-CoA carboxylase inserts the double bond
  5. E. Palmitate is activated to palmitoyl-CoA and elongated in the smooth ER with malonyl-CoA and NADPH; Δ9 (stearoyl-CoA) desaturase in the ER then places a double bond between C9 and C10
AnswerE. Palmitate is activated to palmitoyl-CoA and elongated in the smooth ER with malonyl-CoA and NADPH; Δ9 (stearoyl-CoA) desaturase in the ER then places a double bond between C9 and C10
WhyPalmitate is first activated to palmitoyl-CoA; ER elongase adds 2 C from malonyl-CoA using NADPH (→ stearate 18:0), and Δ9-desaturase in the ER places the first double bond at C9–C10 (→ oleate). Acetyl-CoA is the donor only for mitochondrial elongation, and FAS, elongase and ACC never make double bonds.
Key factAfter palmitate: activate, elongate, desaturate
  • Step 0: palmitate → palmitoyl-CoA (activation comes first).
  • Elongation by elongase, mainly in the smooth ER (2C donor malonyl-CoA) and also in mitochondria (2C donor acetyl-CoA). Each round adds 2 carbons (malonyl's third carbon leaves as CO2). NADPH is the reductant.
  • Desaturation by desaturases in the ER (not mitochondria, not cytosol). Δ9 = stearoyl-CoA desaturase places the first double bond between C9 and C10: stearate 18:0 → oleate 18:1 Δ9 (so oleic acid is made by humans).
  • PUFAs = elongation plus desaturation. FAS stops at palmitate in the cytosol; FAS, elongase and ACC never insert double bonds.

Which sequence describes hepatic triacylglycerol synthesis?
  1. A. Fatty acyl-CoA is converted to free fatty acids by acyl-CoA synthetase before GPAT acts
  2. B. Free fatty acids are joined directly to glycerol 3-P by lipoprotein lipase
  3. C. Fatty acids → fatty acyl-CoA; glycerol 3-P → lysophosphatidic acid (GPAT) → phosphatidic acid (AGPAT) → DAG (phosphatidic acid phosphatase) → TAG (DGAT)

WhyThe first step is activation of fatty acids to fatty acyl-CoA (ATP); acyl groups are then added one at a time: GPAT makes lysophosphatidic acid, AGPAT phosphatidic acid, a phosphatase removes the phosphate to give DAG, and DGAT makes TAG. Key factTAG synthesis order
  • Step 1: activate fatty acids: fatty acid → fatty acyl-CoA (fatty acyl-CoA synthetase, ATP).
  • Step 2: make glycerol 3-phosphate.
  • Step 3: acylate one at a time: G3P → lysophosphatidic acid (GPAT) → phosphatidic acid (AGPAT) → DAG (phosphatidic acid phosphatase) → TAG (DGAT). Intestine: 2-monoacylglycerol route via MGAT.

Key factRegulation of the TAG acylation enzymes

A 50-year-old man who drinks heavily has hepatomegaly with macrovesicular steatosis. Which change in the patient's hepatocytes drives the fat accumulation?

  2. B. Increased LCAT activity loads cholesterol ester into VLDL
  3. C. High NADPH from ethanol activates hormone-sensitive lipase in the liver

WhyAlcohol and acetaldehyde dehydrogenases make NADH; the high NADH/NAD+ pushes DHAP → glycerol 3-phosphate and inhibits β-oxidation, so fatty acids are esterified into TAG faster than the liver can export it as VLDL.   • Fatty liver (steatosis) = hepatic TAG synthesis exceeds VLDL secretion (alcohol, obesity, diabetes, NAFLD).

    ↓ gluconeogenesis (pyruvate → lactate, OAA → malate) → hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis (not alkalosis)
    ↓ VLDL export
  • The deficient process is 'export of TAGs from the liver as VLDL'; the apoprotein involved is apoB-100.

During a 24-hour fast, a 30-year-old has rising plasma free fatty acids. Which change in the adipocyte best explains this?
  1. A. Increased lipoprotein lipase activity on adipose capillaries
  2. B. Glucagon directly hydrolyzing stored triacylglycerol
  3. C. Insulin-stimulated dephosphorylation of hormone-sensitive lipase
  4. D. Glucagon-stimulated rise in cAMP, PKA phosphorylation and activation of hormone-sensitive lipase
  5. E. Phosphodiesterase activation lowering cAMP, which activates hormone-sensitive lipase
AnswerD. Glucagon-stimulated rise in cAMP, PKA phosphorylation and activation of hormone-sensitive lipase
WhyGlucagon and epinephrine (β-receptors) raise cAMP → PKA, which phosphorylates and activates HSL; the freed fatty acids ride albumin. Lipoprotein lipase is the insulin-driven storage enzyme acting on circulating lipoprotein TAG, so it lowers, not raises, plasma FFA.
Key factHormone-sensitive lipase (HSL) releases fatty acids + glycerol from stored adipocyte TAG.
  • ON: glucagon, epinephrine/sympathetic drive (β-receptor) → ↑cAMP → PKA → phosphorylated = active HSL. Active in fasting, exercise, uncontrolled diabetes/DKA, ketogenic diet.
  • OFF: insulin (fed state, after a carbohydrate meal) → phosphodiesterase (↓cAMP) + protein phosphatase → dephosphorylated, inactive HSL.
  • Released fatty acids travel on serum albumin to liver and muscle.
  • Not lipoprotein lipase: insulin-induced, hydrolyzes chylomicron/VLDL TAG for storage (insulinoma → ↑LPL → ↓plasma FFA).
  • Insulin resistance → HSL no longer suppressed → ↑FFA → ↑liver TAG → ↑VLDL, ↓HDL.

Q1: A patient with long-standing insulinoma (excess insulin secretion) presents with decreased plasma free fatty acids (FFA) despite fasting. Which mechanism best explains the low plasma FFA in this patient?

  2. B) Excess insulin increases adipocyte lipoprotein lipase (LPL) activity, increasing uptake of circulating TAG into adipose tissue and lowering plasma FFA.

Explanation from the source
Explanation:
A. Incorrect — insulin does not stimulate HSL. Insulin inhibits HSL; option A states stimulation and an incorrect downstream effect.
B. Correct — insulin increases LPL activity in adipose tissue, promoting uptake of circulating TAG into adipocytes and facilitating storage; that reduces circulating FFA and TAG-derived FFA, explaining low plasma FFA. This is a mechanistic (2nd-order) explanation beyond simply “insulin inhibits lipolysis.”
C. Incorrect — there are no physiologically significant “albumin receptors” that clear FFA via that mechanism; the liver takes up FFA but insulin’s primary effect lowering plasma FFA is adipose LPL stimulation and HSL inhibition.
D. Incorrect — insulin dephosphorylates HSL (via activation of phosphodiesterase and lowered cAMP), thereby reducing HSL activity; the option claims insulin increases phosphorylation causing decreased lipolysis — contradictory and wrong.
E. Incorrect — adipocytes lack glycerol kinase (so down-regulation would not lower plasma FFA); also reduced triglyceride synthesis would increase, not decrease, plasma FFA.
How it follows from the main questionThe HSL-sounding options are wrong: insulin dephosphorylates HSL and never stimulates it. The card's LPL line wins: insulin induces adipose lipoprotein lipase → TAG uptake and storage → ↓plasma FFA.

In a fasting person, glycerol released from adipose tissue is turned into glucose in the liver. Which hepatic sequence is correct?
  1. A. Glycerol → pyruvate by pyruvate kinase → glucose
  2. B. Glycerol → acetyl-CoA → oxaloacetate → glucose
  3. C. Glycerol → glycerol 3-phosphate (glycerol kinase) → dihydroxyacetone phosphate → gluconeogenesis
  4. D. Glycerol → malonyl-CoA → glucose
  5. E. Glycerol is phosphorylated in the adipocyte and released as glucose
AnswerC. Glycerol → glycerol 3-phosphate (glycerol kinase) → dihydroxyacetone phosphate → gluconeogenesis
WhyAdipocytes lack glycerol kinase, so glycerol goes to the liver, where glycerol kinase makes glycerol 3-phosphate and an NAD⁺-dependent dehydrogenase makes DHAP, a gluconeogenic triose. Routes through acetyl-CoA (B) never give net glucose.
Key fact
  • TAG lipolysis → fatty acids + glycerol. Glycerol is the only part of TAG that becomes glucose; even-chain fatty acids → acetyl-CoA → no net glucose.
  • Adipocytes lack glycerol kinase → glycerol travels to the liver: glycerol kinase (ATP) → glycerol 3-P → G3P dehydrogenase (needs NAD⁺) → DHAP → fructose 1,6-bisphosphate → glucose.
  • Alcohol: ↑NADH/NAD⁺ blocks G3P → DHAP → fasting hypoglycemia despite plenty of glycerol.
  • Ketogenic diet or long fast: glycerol (with glucogenic amino acids) becomes the glucose source.
  • Glycerol kinase deficiency → ↑free plasma glycerol → falsely high TAG on a glycerol-based assay.

  1. A. It condenses with oxaloacetate in citrate synthase to make glucose precursors

AnswerE. It allosterically activates pyruvate carboxylase, a biotin- and ATP-dependent enzyme
WhyAcetyl-CoA is the obligatory allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase (biotin, ATP; pyruvate → oxaloacetate), and it inhibits PDH, so pyruvate is pushed toward glucose. Acetyl-CoA itself gives no net glucose, so any 'acetyl-CoA becomes glucose' option is wrong.
Key fact
  • β-Oxidation supports gluconeogenesis in two ways: it supplies ATP/NADH, and its acetyl-CoA regulates pyruvate.
  • Acetyl-CoA activates pyruvate carboxylase (mitochondrial, biotin + ATP, pyruvate → oxaloacetate, first gluconeogenic bypass) and inhibits PDH → pyruvate is carboxylated, not oxidized.
  • Acetyl-CoA is never a net glucose substrate; glycerol is the gluconeogenic carbon from fat.
  • Therefore any block in hepatic β-oxidation (MCAD, carnitine defects, ackee) → ↓gluconeogenesis → fasting hypoglycemia.

  1. A. CPT-2 transfers the acyl group from CoA to carnitine in the cytosol
  2. B. CPT-1 transfers the acyl group from CoA to carnitine
  3. C. Acyl-CoA synthetase in the matrix reactivates it
  4. D. It diffuses across the inner membrane without help
  5. E. The translocase transfers the acyl group back to CoA in the matrix
AnswerB. CPT-1 transfers the acyl group from CoA to carnitine
WhyCPT-1 (outer membrane) makes acylcarnitine, CACT carries it across the inner membrane, and CPT-2 (inner membrane) returns the acyl group to CoA in the matrix. Long-chain acyl-CoA cannot cross the inner membrane on its own; only short and medium chains can.
Key fact
  • Phase I: activation to acyl-CoA in the cytosol (acyl-CoA synthetase on the ER, outer mitochondrial and peroxisomal membranes), then the shuttle.
  • CPT-1 (outer membrane): acyl group from CoA → carnitine. CACT: swaps acylcarnitine across the inner membrane. CPT-2 (inner membrane): acyl group back to CoA in the matrix.
  • Short and medium chains cross the inner membrane without carnitine.
  • Carnitine: mainly diet (meat); limited synthesis in liver and kidney from lysine + SAM; heart and skeletal muscle make none (high-affinity uptake). Vegans/vegetarians → low carnitine.
  • Too little carnitine → CPT-1 can't form acylcarnitine → long-chain fatty acids can't be oxidized.

WhyCPT-1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane is rate-limiting for fatty acid oxidation and is where malonyl-CoA acts. Acetyl-CoA carboxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme of fatty acid synthesis, the usual trap.
Key fact
  • CPT-1 = rate-limiting step of fatty acid oxidation, located on the outer mitochondrial membrane.
  • Inhibited by malonyl-CoA, the product of acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC), so newly made fatty acids are not burned as they are made.
  • Pair: ACC = rate-limiting for synthesis (citrate activates it); CPT-1 = rate-limiting for oxidation (malonyl-CoA inhibits it).
  • So the ACC product modulates fatty acid transport into mitochondria, not 'degradation in the cytosol'.
