Practice Q1473One extra step
A product of the acetyl-CoA carboxylase reaction is an allosteric modulator of which of the following processes?
  1. A. Fatty acid elongation in mitochondria
  2. B. Fatty acid desaturation in cytosol
  3. C. Fatty acid degradation in cytosol
  4. D. Fatty acid activation in cytosol
  5. E. Fatty acid transport into mitochondria
AnswerE. Fatty acid transport into mitochondria
Correct key: E. Fatty acid transport into mitochondria. Malonyl-CoA (ACC product) inhibits CPT I, controlling FA entry into mitochondria; the E key (Canvas 2026 Pre Discussion Week 10, IS slides) is right, the C key in the 2023 Week 9 Interactive file is wrong (degradation is mitochondrial, not cytosolic).
WhyThe ACC product malonyl-CoA allosterically inhibits CPT-1, blocking fatty acid transport into mitochondria; degradation itself happens in mitochondria, not the cytosol.
Explanation from the source
Malonyl-CoA serves as an important regulator of fatty acid metabolism. It acts as an inhibitor of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (CPT-1), which is an enzyme involved in the transport of fatty acids into the mitochondria for β-oxidation (fatty acid degradation). By inhibiting CPT-1, malonyl-CoA reduces the entry of fatty acids into the mitochondria, effectively limiting their degradation. This regulation is crucial for coordinating fatty acid synthesis (which starts with acetyl-CoA carboxylase) and fatty acid degradation in response to cellular energy needs.
How it follows from the main questionTwo steps: the ACC product is malonyl-CoA, and malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-1, the shuttle step. So fatty acid transport into mitochondria; 'degradation in cytosol' is the trap, since β-oxidation is mitochondrial. Also asked as Q1475.

Carnitine shuttle and its control

121unlocks 10TA ×13 not obvious
Shortly after a large carbohydrate meal, insulin rises. What happens to hepatic fatty acid oxidation, and why?
  1. A. It decreases, because insulin activates hormone-sensitive lipase
  2. B. It decreases, because insulin activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, raising malonyl-CoA, which inhibits CPT-1
  3. C. It increases, because insulin dephosphorylates acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
  4. D. It increases, because insulin activates CPT-1 directly
  5. E. It decreases, because insulin lowers malonyl-CoA
AnswerB. It decreases, because insulin activates acetyl-CoA carboxylase, raising malonyl-CoA, which inhibits CPT-1
WhyInsulin turns ACC on → ↑malonyl-CoA → CPT-1 inhibited → ↓β-oxidation. Glucagon, epinephrine and AMP (AMPK) do the reverse: ACC off, malonyl-CoA falls, CPT-1 opens and β-oxidation rises.
Key factACC sets the malonyl-CoA level, and malonyl-CoA sets CPT-1.
  • Insulin (fed) and citrate → ACC on → ↑malonyl-CoA → CPT-1 off → ↓fatty acid oxidation.
  • Glucagon/epinephrine (PKA phosphorylates ACC) and AMP/AMPK (exercise, low energy) → ACC off (AMP also speeds malonyl-CoA breakdown) → ↓malonyl-CoA → CPT-1 on → ↑fatty acid oxidation (and, in liver, ketogenesis).
  • Bottom line: glucagon/epinephrine ↑FA oxidation; insulin ↓FA oxidation.
  • Loss of muscle ACC2 → no malonyl-CoA brake → unregulated FA oxidation and weight loss. Von Gierke disease: extra glycolysis → citrate → malonyl-CoA → CPT-1 shut → ketones do not rise.

Practice Q1658Looks like another topic
CASE 2: SEVERE FASTING HYPOGLYCEMIA Patient Presentation: Jason S. is a 4-month-old boy whose mother is concerned about the “twitching” movements he makes just before feedings. She tells the pediatrician that the movements started about 1 week ago, are most apparent in the morning, and disappear shortly after eating. Focused History: Jason is the product of a normal pregnancy and delivery. He appeared normal at birth. He has been at the 30th percentile for both weight and length since birth. His immunizations are up to date. Jason last ate a few hours ago. Physical Examination (Pertinent Findings): Jason appears sleepy and feels clammy to the touch. His respiratory rate is elevated. His temperature is normal. Jason has a protuberant, firm abdomen that appears to be nontender. His liver is palpable 4 cm below the right costal margin and is smooth. His kidneys are enlarged and symmetrical. Pertinent Test Results: Jason is sent to the regional children’s hospital for further evaluation. Ultrasound studies confirm hepatomegaly and renomegaly and show no evidence of tumors. A liver biopsy is performed. The hepatocytes are distended. Staining reveals large amounts of lipid (primarily triacylglycerol) and carbohydrate. Liver glycogen is elevated in amount and normal in structure. Enzyme assay using liver homogenate treated with detergent reveals less than 10% of the normal activity of glucose 6-phosphatase, an enzyme of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane in the liver and the kidneys. Diagnosis: Glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency (glycogen storage disease [GSD] type Ia, von Gierke disease) Treatment (Immediate): Jason was given glucose intravenously, and his blood glucose level rose into the normal range. However, as the day progressed, it fell to well below normal. Administration of glucagon had no effect on blood glucose levels but increased blood lactate. Jason’s blood glucose levels were able to be maintained by constant infusion of glucose. Prognosis: Individuals with glucose 6-phosphatase deficiency develop hepatic adenomas starting in the second decade of life and are at increased risk for hepatic carcinoma. Kidney glomerular function is impaired and can result in kidney failure. Patients are at increased risk for developing gout, but this rarely occurs before puberty. A. Why are triacylglycerols and cholesterol elevated? Hint: Glucose is the primary carbon source for their synthesis. B. Why are ketone bodies not elevated?
Show figure
AnswerIncreased glycolysis results in increased availability of glycerol 3-phosphate for hepatic TAG synthesis. Additionally, some of the pyruvate generated in glycolysis will be oxidatively decarboxylated to acetyl coenzyme A (CoA). However, the tricarboxylic acid cycle is inhibited by the rise in NADH, and the acetyl CoA is transported to the cytosol as citrate. The rise of acetyl CoA in the cytosol results in increased fatty acid synthesis. Recall that citrate is an allosteric activator of acetyl CoA carboxylase (ACC). The malonyl product of ACC inhibits fatty acid oxidation at the carnitine palmitoyltransferase I step. Because mitochondrial fatty acid oxidation generates the acetyl CoA substrate for hepatic ketogenesis, ketone body levels do not rise. The fatty acids get esterified to the glycerol backbone, resulting in an increase in TAGs that get sent out of liver as components of very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDLs). [Note: The hypoglycemia results in release of epinephrine and the activation of TAG lipolysis with release of free fatty acids into the blood. The fatty acids are used in hepatic TAG synthesis.] The acetyl CoA is also a substrate for cholesterol synthesis. Thus, the increase in glycolysis results in the hyperlipidemia seen in the patient (see Figure).
WhyTrapped G6P drives glycolysis, giving glycerol 3-phosphate and acetyl-CoA (exported as citrate) → TAG, VLDL and cholesterol synthesis. Citrate activates ACC, and malonyl-CoA inhibits CPT-1, so β-oxidation, the acetyl-CoA source for ketogenesis, stays low.
How it follows from the main questionA glycogen-storage case hiding a malonyl-CoA question: extra glycolysis → citrate → ACC on → ↑malonyl-CoA shuts CPT-1 → little β-oxidation → no acetyl-CoA for ketogenesis.

Beta-oxidation and ATP yield

122unlocks 4TA ×1
Each turn of mitochondrial β-oxidation of palmitoyl-CoA follows which sequence, giving which products?
  1. A. Oxidation (FAD) → hydration → oxidation (NAD⁺) → thiolysis; 1 FADH₂, 1 NADH, 1 acetyl-CoA
  2. B. Condensation → reduction → dehydration → reduction; uses NADPH
  3. C. Thiolysis → oxidation → hydration → dehydration; 1 FADH₂ only
  4. D. Hydration → oxidation → thiolysis → oxidation; 2 NADH
  5. E. Oxidation (NAD⁺) → dehydration → oxidation (FAD) → thiolysis; 1 NADH, 1 acetyl-CoA
AnswerA. Oxidation (FAD) → hydration → oxidation (NAD⁺) → thiolysis; 1 FADH₂, 1 NADH, 1 acetyl-CoA
WhyEach cycle is dehydrogenation (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, FAD) → hydration → dehydrogenation (NAD⁺) → thiolysis, giving 1 FADH₂ + 1 NADH + 1 acetyl-CoA. Condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction with NADPH is fatty acid synthesis.
Key fact
  • Phase II cycle: oxidation → hydration → oxidation → thiolysis (dehydrogenation, hydration, dehydrogenation, thiolysis).
  • Step 1: chain-length-specific acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (SCAD, MCAD, LCAD, VLCAD), FAD → FADH₂; its electrons pass to ETF → ETF:CoQ oxidoreductase → CoQ (lose that and step 1 stalls).
  • Step 3: 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase → NADH. Step 4: thiolase releases acetyl-CoA + an acyl-CoA 2 carbons shorter.
  • Each cycle = 1 FADH₂, 1 NADH, 1 acetyl-CoA.
  • Synthesis runs the opposite logic: condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction (NADPH, cytosol).

  • Synthesis-vs-degradation comparison: the repetitive four-step process
  • Mechanism twist: ETF:CoQ oxidoreductase mutation → acyl-CoA dehydrogenase is inhibited first

What it lets you eliminate

  • 'Dehydration' belongs to synthesis; β-oxidation has a hydration
  • Any sequence not starting with an oxidation and ending with thiolysis is wrong
  • NADPH is a synthesis cofactor, never a β-oxidation product

WhyStearate: 8 cycles → 8 FADH₂ (16) + 8 NADH (24) + 9 acetyl-CoA (108) = 148, minus 2 ATP for activation = 146, which is 17 more than palmitate's 129. 148 forgets the activation cost.
Key fact
  • Even chain of n carbons: n/2 − 1 cycles and n/2 acetyl-CoA; each cycle gives 1 FADH₂ + 1 NADH.
  • Lecture values: NADH 3, FADH₂ 2, acetyl-CoA 12 ATP.
  • Palmitate (16:0): 7 cycles, 8 acetyl-CoA → 14 + 21 + 96 = 131 − 2 = 129 ATP (versus 36–38 per glucose).
  • Activation costs 2 ATP equivalents: ATP → AMP + PPi breaks two high-energy bonds; subtracted once per fatty acid.
  • Each extra 2 carbons = +17 ATP (stearate 146). Unsaturated fatty acids give fewer ATP.

Which statement about the pathways of fatty acid oxidation is correct?
  1. A. Unsaturated fatty acids are oxidized only in peroxisomes
  2. B. ω-Oxidation occurs in peroxisomes and is the main route for phytanic acid
  3. C. Oxidation of fatty acids longer than C20 begins in mitochondria
  4. D. α-Oxidation occurs in peroxisomes, handles branched phytanic acid and yields no energy
  5. E. ω-Oxidation in mitochondria releases acetyl-CoA from the β-carbon
AnswerD. α-Oxidation occurs in peroxisomes, handles branched phytanic acid and yields no energy
Whyα-oxidation = peroxisome, phytanic acid, no energy. ω-oxidation is in the ER (cytochrome P450) and makes dicarboxylic acids; very long chains start in peroxisomes; unsaturated fats use mitochondrial β-oxidation plus two extra enzymes.
Key fact
  • β-oxidation: mitochondria of liver and muscle; major pathway for chains below C20; oxidizes the β-carbon → acetyl-CoA.
  • Peroxisomal β-oxidation: VLCFA above C20; less energy than mitochondria.
  • α-oxidation: peroxisomes; branched phytanic acid; minor, no energy yield.
  • ω-oxidation: ER (cytochrome P450); minor (lecture: normally SCFA below C6); makes dicarboxylic acids; rises when β-oxidation fails (MCAD).
  • Unsaturated: mitochondrial β-oxidation plus enoyl-CoA isomerase and an NADPH-dependent reductase → fewer ATP (a bond at an odd position skips one FADH₂; at an even position it also costs NADPH).
Lecture slide F1278:7 says ω-oxidation substrates are normally SCFA below C6 (textbooks say C10–C12); course wording kept.

Atypical fatty acids

125TA ×2
Why does peroxisomal β-oxidation of a C26 fatty acid yield less ATP than mitochondrial β-oxidation?
  1. A. Peroxisomal β-oxidation consumes NADPH
  2. B. Peroxisomes remove only one carbon per cycle
  3. C. The fatty acid is converted to ketone bodies in the peroxisome
  4. D. The fatty acid must first be converted to propionyl-CoA
  5. E. Its first enzyme, acyl-CoA oxidase, passes electrons directly to O₂, forming H₂O₂ instead of FADH₂ for the electron transport chain
AnswerE. Its first enzyme, acyl-CoA oxidase, passes electrons directly to O₂, forming H₂O₂ instead of FADH₂ for the electron transport chain
WhyPeroxisomal acyl-CoA oxidase sends electrons straight to O₂ → H₂O₂, so that step makes no ATP. Peroxisomes only shorten VLCFA to below C20; the shorter acyl-CoA is exported to mitochondria to finish. Removing one carbon is α-oxidation.
Key fact
  • VLCFA (above C20) enter peroxisomes as acyl-CoA via the ABCD1 transporter.
  • First step: acyl-CoA oxidase, electrons go directly to O₂ → H₂O₂ (inhibit it → ↓H₂O₂ and VLCFA build up).
  • Peroxisomes shorten VLCFA; acyl-CoA below C20 is exported to mitochondria to complete β-oxidation. Mitochondria cannot start on VLCFA, so they cannot compensate for a peroxisomal defect.
  • Not α-oxidation (pristanic acid), not propionyl-CoA, not ketones, not isomerase/reductase.
What it unlocks: 2 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Inhibitor of the enzyme that passes electrons to O₂ → what else changes (↓H₂O₂ production)
  • Block VLCFA entry into peroxisomes → why mitochondria can't compensate (VLCFA need initial peroxisomal shortening)
  • Matching: peroxisomal β-oxidation = VLCFA, less energy

What it lets you eliminate

  • Pristanic and phytanic acid belong to α-oxidation, not VLCFA
  • Propionyl-CoA, ketone bodies and enoyl-CoA isomerase come from other pathways

In a healthy hepatocyte, how is a C26:0 fatty acid degraded?
  1. A. Peroxisomal α-oxidation converts it to pristanic acid, which mitochondria then oxidize
  2. B. CPT-1 carries it into mitochondria, where β-oxidation runs to completion
  3. C. Peroxisomes oxidize it completely to acetyl-CoA, sending FADH₂ to the electron transport chain
  4. D. ABCD1 imports it into peroxisomes; β-oxidation there (acyl-CoA oxidase, electrons to O₂ → H₂O₂) shortens it, and acyl-CoA below C20 is exported to mitochondria to finish
  5. E. ω-Oxidation in the endoplasmic reticulum converts it to a dicarboxylic acid that is excreted
AnswerD. ABCD1 imports it into peroxisomes; β-oxidation there (acyl-CoA oxidase, electrons to O₂ → H₂O₂) shortens it, and acyl-CoA below C20 is exported to mitochondria to finish
WhyVLCFA (above C20) can only be started in peroxisomes, entering as acyl-CoA through ABCD1; acyl-CoA oxidase hands electrons to O₂ (H₂O₂, not FADH₂). Peroxisomes only shorten the chain and export acyl-CoA below C20 to mitochondria. Mitochondria can't start on VLCFA, α-oxidation is for branched phytanic acid, and ω-oxidation is a minor ER route.
Key fact
  • Division of labor: peroxisomes start VLCFA (above C20), mitochondria finish. The peroxisome shortens the chain and exports acyl-CoA below C20 to mitochondria for complete β-oxidation.
  • Entry: VLCFA-CoA enters by the ABCD1 transporter (defective in X-ALD).
  • First step: acyl-CoA oxidase, electrons go directly to O₂ → H₂O₂, so less ATP than in mitochondria.
  • So any peroxisomal block (ABCD1, oxidase, biogenesis) → VLCFA accumulate even with normal mitochondria: mitochondria cannot compensate because they can't do the initial shortening. Inhibit the oxidase → ↓H₂O₂ and ↓shortening.
  • Not part of the VLCFA route: α-oxidation/pristanic acid (phytanic acid), propionyl-CoA (odd chains), ketone bodies, isomerase + NADPH reductase (unsaturated chains).

A laboratory technician is studying fatty acid degradation in cultured hepatocytes. A compound is introduced that selectively inhibits the enzyme responsible for transferring electrons directly to molecular oxygen during the first reaction of peroxisomal β-oxidation. Mitochondrial β-oxidation enzymes remain functional. Following treatment, the cells demonstrate impaired degradation of fatty acids containing more than 20 carbon atoms. Which of the following additional metabolic changes would most likely occur?
  1. A. Decreased production of hydrogen peroxide during the first reaction of peroxisomal β-oxidation
  2. B. Increased conversion of VLCFAs into pristanic acid
  3. C. Increased shortening of VLCFAs into fatty acyl-CoAs containing fewer than 20 carbon atoms
  4. D. Increased conversion of propionyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA
  5. E. Increased oxidation of the α-carbon of phytanic acid
AnswerA. Decreased production of hydrogen peroxide during the first reaction of peroxisomal β-oxidation
How it follows from the main questionAcyl-CoA oxidase makes H₂O₂ as it starts shortening VLCFA, so blocking it gives ↓H₂O₂ (answer) and less, not more, shortening; pristanic, propionyl and phytanic options belong to other routes.

Atypical fatty acids

127unlocks 7TA ×11 not obvious
A 25-year-old has night blindness, hearing loss, an unsteady gait and numb feet. Plasma phytanic acid is high and VLCFA are normal. Which step is defective?
  1. A. ω-Oxidation in the endoplasmic reticulum
  2. B. ABCD1 transport of VLCFA-CoA into peroxisomes
  3. C. Mitochondrial oxidation of medium-chain acyl-CoA
  4. D. Assembly of peroxisomes
  5. E. Peroxisomal α-oxidation by phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase
AnswerE. Peroxisomal α-oxidation by phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase
WhyPhytanic acid has a methyl group on its β-carbon that blocks β-oxidation, so peroxisomal α-oxidation (phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase) first removes one carbon to make pristanic acid. Losing it = adult Refsum disease. Normal VLCFA rule out X-ALD and Zellweger.
Key fact
  • Phytanic acid (from chlorophyll; dairy, ruminant fat, some fish): methyl branch on the β-carbon → β-oxidation can't proceed.
  • α-oxidation in peroxisomes: phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase → removes C1 → pristanic acid → then β-oxidation. No energy yield.
  • Adult Refsum disease = phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase deficiency: ↑phytanic acid, ↓pristanic acid formation; retinitis pigmentosa (night blindness), cerebellar ataxia, peripheral polyneuropathy, hearing loss (short metacarpals); adolescent/adult onset; single-enzyme peroxisomal defect.

  • Phytanic acid is not handled by mitochondria, ER ω-oxidation or the carnitine shuttle
  • Normal VLCFA argue against X-ALD and Zellweger

Atypical fatty acids

128unlocks 4TA ×1
The last thiolysis of a 17-carbon fatty acid releases a 3-carbon acyl-CoA. Which enzyme and cofactor act on it first?
  1. A. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase; biotin
  2. B. Enoyl-CoA isomerase; no cofactor
  3. C. Pyruvate dehydrogenase; thiamine
  4. D. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase; vitamin B12
  5. E. Methylmalonyl-CoA racemase; vitamin B6
AnswerA. Propionyl-CoA carboxylase; biotin
WhyOdd chains end with propionyl-CoA, which propionyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin, ATP, CO₂) converts to D-methylmalonyl-CoA; a racemase makes the L form and the B12-dependent mutase makes succinyl-CoA. B12 works at the last step, not the first.
Key fact
  • Odd-chain fatty acids (and Val, Ile, Met, Thr) → propionyl-CoA (3C).
  • Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (biotin, ATP, adds CO₂) → D-methylmalonyl-CoA → racemase → L-methylmalonyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12) → succinyl-CoA.
  • Succinyl-CoA is a TCA intermediate → oxaloacetate → glucose, so the propionyl end of odd chains is glucogenic (even chains are not).
  • Carboxylase or biotin block → propionyl-CoA accumulates → metabolic acidosis.
Lecture slide F1278:21 says propionyl-CoA metabolism 'needs vitamin B6'. That is a slide error: the cofactors are biotin (carboxylase) and B12 (mutase), as the review slides and every practice key say.

  • Which atypical fatty acid yields succinyl-CoA (odd-chain); why odd chains can feed gluconeogenesis

What it lets you eliminate

  • B12 belongs to the mutase step, not the carboxylase
  • Lactate/Cori cycle, glucogenic amino acids or 'glucose in the fat' are not why odd chains are glucogenic
  • Unsaturated, VLCFA and phytanic acid do not end in succinyl-CoA

An infant has vomiting, metabolic acidosis and high urine methylmalonic acid with normal propionic acid, and improves with a vitamin. The defective enzyme belongs to which class and uses which cofactor?
  1. A. Dehydrogenase; riboflavin (FAD)
  2. B. Hydroxylase; pyridoxine (B6)
  3. C. Isomerase (mutase); adenosylcobalamin (vitamin B12)
  4. D. Kinase; ATP
  5. E. Carboxylase; biotin
AnswerC. Isomerase (mutase); adenosylcobalamin (vitamin B12)
WhyMethylmalonic acid builds up behind methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, which rearranges L-methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA using B12; a mutase is an isomerase. Normal propionic acid places the block after the biotin carboxylase.
Key fact
  • L-methylmalonyl-CoA → succinyl-CoA by methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (intramolecular rearrangement = isomerase class), cofactor adenosyl-B12.
  • Mutase or B12 defect → methylmalonic acidemia/aciduria: high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, ketosis, vomiting, lethargy, hypotonia, hyperammonemia, hepatomegaly, developmental delay; B12-responsive forms improve with cobalamin.
  • Adult B12 deficiency: ↑methylmalonic acid + neuropathy (numbness, gait trouble).
  • ↑Propionic acid → think biotin/carboxylase; ↑methylmalonic acid with normal propionic acid → mutase/B12.

A patient presents with vomiting, lethargy, altered mental status and hepatomegaly. On bloodwork you note ketoacidosis and hyperammonemia. Which of the following is the most likely reason?
  1. A. Build up of succinyl CoA
  2. B. Defective formation of B6
  3. C. Build up of propionyl CoA

AnswerD. Defective methylmalonyl CoA mutase
WhyDefective methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (methylmalonic acidemia) builds up methylmalonic and propionic metabolites, causing ketoacidosis, and propionyl-CoA inhibits N-acetylglutamate synthase, causing secondary hyperammonemia, with vomiting, lethargy and hepatomegaly.

AnswerD. Defective methylmalonyl CoA mutase
WhyDefective methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (methylmalonic acidemia) builds up methylmalonic and propionic metabolites, causing ketoacidosis, and propionyl-CoA inhibits N-acetylglutamate synthase, causing secondary hyperammonemia, with vomiting, lethargy and hepatomegaly.

Practice Q1465One extra step
A newborn experiences lethargy, vomiting, and hypotonia during the first few days of life. Laboratory examination reveals a metabolic acidosis with a large anion gap, ketosis, and hypoglycemia. The concentration of methylmalonic acid is markedly increased in the plasma and urine. The step most likely defective in the newborn is catalysed by:
  1. A. Carboxylase
  2. B. Dehydrogenase
  3. C. Kinase
  4. D. Isomerase
  5. E. Hydroxylase
AnswerD. Isomerase
WhyMethylmalonic acidemia blocks methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B12-dependent), which only rearranges the carbon skeleton of methylmalonyl-CoA into succinyl-CoA. Mutases are intramolecular-transfer enzymes in the isomerase class.
Explanation from the source
Correct answer: D. Isomerase
1. What reaction are we talking about? The blocked step in methylmalonic acidemia is:
Methylmalonyl-CoA → Succinyl-CoA
Enzyme: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (B₁₂-dependent).
2. What does this enzyme actually do? It does not add or remove anything big. It just rearranges the carbon skeleton of the molecule so that the same atoms are connected in a different way:
Same formula, different arrangement → isomer.
Enzymes that only rearrange atoms within a molecule (no CO₂ added, no phosphate added, no electrons removed) are classified as isomerases (mutases are a subtype).
So methylmalonyl-CoA mutase is an isomerase, and when it fails, methylmalonic acid accumulates → methylmalonic acidemia.
Why the other options are wrong (briefly)
A. Carboxylase Would fit propionyl-CoA carboxylase (propionyl-CoA → methylmalonyl-CoA), which causes propionic acidemia, not isolated MMA.
B. Dehydrogenase Oxidation/reduction steps (e.g., acyl-CoA dehydrogenases in β-oxidation), not the MMA → succinyl-CoA step.
C. Kinase Adds phosphate using ATP (e.g., hexokinase); not involved in this part of the pathway.
E. Hydroxylase Adds an –OH group (e.g., phenylalanine hydroxylase, tyrosine hydroxylase), unrelated to MMA conversion.
So: defective isomerase (methylmalonyl-CoA mutase) → methylmalonic acidemia.
How it follows from the main questionThe block is methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, but the options are enzyme classes. A mutase is an intramolecular rearrangement, so the class is isomerase, not carboxylase.

Disorders of fat degradation

130unlocks 7TA ×11 not obvious
A boy has adrenal insufficiency and progressive loss of cerebral white matter. Plasma VLCFA are high; phytanic acid is normal. Which defect is most likely?
  1. A. Phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase deficiency
  2. B. X-linked ABCD1 transporter that carries VLCFA-CoA into peroxisomes
  3. C. CPT-2 deficiency
  4. D. Peroxin defect preventing peroxisome formation
  5. E. Medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
AnswerB. X-linked ABCD1 transporter that carries VLCFA-CoA into peroxisomes
WhyX-linked adrenoleukodystrophy is an ABCD1 defect: VLCFA-CoA can't enter peroxisomes, so only VLCFA rise. A biogenesis defect (Zellweger spectrum) would raise both VLCFA and phytanic acid.
Key fact
  • X-ALD: X-linked ABCD1 transporter (VLCFA-CoA into peroxisomes) → ↑VLCFA only; α-oxidation intact.
  • Zellweger spectrum: defects in peroxisome biogenesis (peroxins) → every peroxisomal function fails → ↑VLCFA and ↑phytanic/pristanic acid; infant with hypotonia, seizures, hepatomegaly, craniofacial signs, high serum iron and copper.
  • Infantile Refsum: peroxin (assembly) defect → ↓cerebral myelination, hearing and vision loss.
  • Adult Refsum: one enzyme (phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase) in an otherwise normal peroxisome → phytanic acid only.
  • CPT-1, CPT-2, CACT and MCAD defects are mitochondrial, not peroxisomal.

How it shows up

  • Two patients: X-linked VLCFA-entry defect vs peroxisome-formation defect → transport vs biogenesis
  • Matching tables: adult Refsum, X-ALD, Zellweger, infantile Refsum
  • Infant with seizures, hypotonia, ↑phytanic and pristanic acid → biogenesis defect, not single enzyme
  • Why Zellweger raises VLCFA and phytanic acid while X-ALD raises only VLCFA
  • Infant with hepatomegaly, high iron/copper, vision problems → can't oxidize VLCFA

What it lets you eliminate

  • X-ALD is not mitochondrial; CPT defects are not peroxisomal
  • Adult Refsum and the infantile form are not distinguished by β- vs α-oxidation or by dominance; it's single enzyme vs biogenesis
  • Ketogenesis, ω-oxidation and propionyl-CoA metabolism are unrelated distractors

Disorders of fat degradation

131unlocks 9TA ×21 not obvious
A 4-month-old has fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia, high plasma free fatty acids, and low free carnitine and low acylcarnitines. Which defect fits best?
  1. A. CPT-2 deficiency
  2. B. Plasma-membrane carnitine transporter (primary carnitine deficiency)
  3. C. Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase deficiency
  4. D. Hormone-sensitive lipase deficiency
  5. E. MCAD deficiency
AnswerB. Plasma-membrane carnitine transporter (primary carnitine deficiency)
WhyPrimary carnitine deficiency (transporter, renal wasting) lowers both free carnitine and acylcarnitines, so long chains can't enter mitochondria and FFA rise. MCAD, CPT-2 and CACT defects raise acylcarnitines; HSL deficiency would lower FFA.
Key fact
  • Primary carnitine deficiency (carnitine transporter, diet/vegan, synthesis, renal reabsorption): ↓free carnitine + ↓acylcarnitines, ↑FFA, hypoketotic hypoglycemia, fatty liver, muscle cramps and weakness.
  • Secondary carnitine deficiency (CPT-2, CACT, MCAD): acylcarnitines accumulate and inhibit renal carnitine reabsorption → free carnitine falls; acyl/free ratio high.
  • So the acylcarnitine level separates carnitine deficiency (low) from CPT-2 deficiency (high long-chain species).
  • CPT-2 (muscle form): exercise- or fast-induced myalgia, rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuria, ↑CK, cardiomyopathy. CPT-1 or CACT defects: lethal young.
  • Treatment of shuttle defects: high-carb/low long-chain fat, add medium-chain fat (bypasses carnitine), carnitine supplements, limit exertion.

  • Known shuttle defect with falling carnitine and ↑acylcarnitines → acylcarnitines inhibit renal carnitine reabsorption
  • Lab pattern (low free carnitine + low acylcarnitines + ↑FFA) → carnitine transporter
  • Which blood test separates carnitine deficiency from CPT-2 deficiency (acylcarnitine)
  • Vegan with carnitine deficiency → high carbohydrate + medium-chain fat + carnitine supplement

What it lets you eliminate

  • Dicarboxylic acids with C6–C10 acylcarnitines point to MCAD, not a shuttle defect
  • Increased renal reabsorption, or carnitine 'consumed' by β-oxidation or α-oxidation, never explain secondary deficiency
  • Medium-chain fat helps shuttle defects but is forbidden in MCAD

Disorders of fat degradation

132unlocks 3TA ×2
A 20-year-old cross-country runner has a third episode of severe muscle pain and cola-colored urine after a long race; CK is very high. Plasma long-chain acylcarnitines are high and free carnitine is low, although their diet and hepatic carnitine synthesis are normal. Why is free carnitine low?
  1. A. Peroxisomal α-oxidation consumes circulating carnitine
  2. B. Low ketone body production increases carnitine consumption
  3. C. Accumulated acylcarnitines inhibit renal reabsorption of carnitine
  4. D. A defective plasma-membrane carnitine transporter wastes carnitine in the urine
  5. E. Carnitine is oxidized to acetyl-CoA during β-oxidation
AnswerC. Accumulated acylcarnitines inhibit renal reabsorption of carnitine
WhyExercise-induced myalgia, rhabdomyolysis and myoglobinuria with ↑long-chain acylcarnitines = muscle CPT-2 deficiency. Acylcarnitines that can't be turned back into acyl-CoA build up and inhibit renal carnitine reabsorption → secondary carnitine deficiency. A transporter defect (primary) would make acylcarnitines low, and carnitine is a carrier, never burned as fuel.
Key fact
  • CPT-2 deficiency, muscle form: young adult or athlete with recurrent muscle pain and weakness after prolonged exercise (or fasting) that resolves with rest; rhabdomyolysis, myoglobinuria, ↑CK; can cause cardiomyopathy. Muscle can't turn acylcarnitine back into acyl-CoA in the matrix, so it can't burn long-chain fat.
  • CPT-2 or CACT block → acylcarnitines accumulate → they inhibit renal resorption of carnitine → free carnitine falls = secondary carnitine deficiency (acyl/free ratio high).
  • Primary carnitine deficiency (transporter, diet/vegan, hepatic synthesis, renal reabsorption defect): free carnitine and acylcarnitines both low.
  • So the test is acylcarnitine: high → CPT-2/CACT (secondary); low → primary.
  • Liver blocks (MCAD, CPT-1, ackee) instead give fasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia; CPT-1 or CACT defects are lethal young.
What it unlocks: 5 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • TA vignette: college athlete with muscle pain, weakness, ↑CK and rhabdomyolysis after workouts, defect in mitochondrial transport of long-chain fatty acids → CPT-2 (traps: ABCD1, phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase, MCAD, methylmalonyl-CoA mutase).
  • Child with recurrent weakness and myoglobinuria after exercise → CPT-2, with CPT-1 and MCAD as the traps.
  • TA mechanism: known shuttle defect, carnitine falling despite good intake and normal synthesis, acylcarnitines up → acylcarnitines inhibit renal carnitine reabsorption.
  • 'Which blood test separates carnitine deficiency from CPT-2 deficiency (or secondary from primary)?' → acylcarnitine.

What it lets you eliminate

  • 'Increased renal reabsorption', carnitine 'converted to acetyl-CoA', 'consumed by α-oxidation' or 'consumed because ketogenesis is low' never explain secondary deficiency.
  • Exercise rhabdomyolysis without fasting hypoglycemia points to muscle CPT-2, not MCAD or CPT-1.
  • Peroxisomal (ABCD1, phytanoyl-CoA hydroxylase) and odd-chain (mutase) defects don't present as exercise rhabdomyolysis.

Three hours after eating unripe fruit on a trip to Jamaica, a traveler has severe vomiting and a blood glucose of 30 mg/dL. The toxin acts by
  1. A. Increasing ketogenesis
  2. B. Inhibiting glycogen phosphorylase
  3. C. Activating CPT-1
  4. D. Sequestering CoA and carnitine, blocking fatty acid β-oxidation
  5. E. Stimulating insulin secretion
AnswerD. Sequestering CoA and carnitine, blocking fatty acid β-oxidation
WhyHypoglycin A metabolites trap carnitine and CoA (and inhibit acyl-CoA dehydrogenases), so β-oxidation stops; without its ATP and acetyl-CoA, gluconeogenesis fails → severe hypoglycemia within 2–6 h.
Key fact
  • Jamaican vomiting sickness: unripe ackee fruit → hypoglycin A.
  • Its metabolites sequester carnitine and CoA (impairing fatty acid entry into mitochondria) and inhibit acyl-CoA dehydrogenases → β-oxidation blocked.
  • → ↓gluconeogenesis → sudden vomiting within 2–6 h, severe hypoglycemia, weakness, seizures, altered consciousness, death.
  • The process most directly inhibited is fatty acid breakdown; gluconeogenesis fails secondarily.
What it unlocks: 5 questions

  • 'Name that disease': hypoglycin A, vomiting in 2–6 h, hypoglycemia
  • Traveler or cook ate unripe ackee → mechanism (sequesters carnitine/CoA, blocks β-oxidation)
  • 'Which process do the toxins most directly inhibit' → fatty acid breakdown / transport into mitochondria

What it lets you eliminate

  • Not insulin secretion, glycogenolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway or ACC/malonyl-CoA
  • Ketogenesis falls, it never rises

When brought to the emergency department the man was severely dehydrated and exhibited several seizures. The toxic effects of the fruit were interfering with which of the following?

WhyUnripe ackee contains hypoglycin A, whose metabolite forms CoA and carnitine esters, sequestering carnitine and impairing fatty acid transport into mitochondria; it also inhibits acyl-CoA dehydrogenases. Without β-oxidation, gluconeogenesis fails, giving hypoglycemia, vomiting and seizures.

Q2. A 6-year-old child is brought to Dr. Binstock with symptoms of weakness, lethargy, and vomiting after ingesting unripe ackee fruit while on a family trip to Jamaica.   1. A. Inhibition of the pentose phosphate pathway

  4. D. Impaired production of malonyl-CoA

AnswerE. Inhibition of β-oxidation by hypoglycin A
WhyHypoglycin A in unripe ackee is metabolized to MCPA-CoA, which inhibits acyl-CoA dehydrogenases and blocks β-oxidation; without fatty acid–derived ATP and acetyl-CoA, gluconeogenesis fails and glucose is consumed, causing hypoglycemia.
Explanation from the source
Explanation: Inhibition of β-oxidation by hypoglycin A is the primary mechanism in Jamaican vomiting sickness. Hypoglycin A, found in unripe ackee fruit, inhibits the breakdown of fatty acids by sequestering CoA and carnitine, which are essential for the activation and transport of fatty acids into mitochondria. This inhibition of β-oxidation leads to a reliance on glucose for energy, quickly depleting blood glucose levels and causing hypoglycemia. (A) is incorrect because the pentose phosphate pathway is not directly affected by hypoglycin A. (B) is incorrect because the carnitine shuttle is indirectly affected by the sequestration of carnitine, but it is not the primary block. (C) is incorrect because the sequestration of CoA and carnitine is a result, not the initial cause. (D) is incorrect because malonyl-CoA is involved in fatty acid synthesis, not degradation
How it follows from the main questionCarnitine shuttle blockade and CoA/carnitine sequestration are partial truths. The key wants the whole process the card names: inhibition of β-oxidation by hypoglycin A, with gluconeogenesis failing secondarily.

In prolonged fasting, hepatic β-oxidation is high but citric acid cycle flux is low. Why does acetyl-CoA go to ketone bodies?

  3. C. Acetyl-CoA is low, so the liver stores it as ketones

AnswerE. Oxaloacetate is pulled into gluconeogenesis and high NADH slows the cycle, so acetyl-CoA exceeds TCA capacity
WhyFasting and type 1 diabetes flood the liver with fatty acids; oxaloacetate is diverted to gluconeogenesis and NADH from β-oxidation inhibits the TCA dehydrogenases, so excess acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria becomes ketone bodies for other tissues.
Key fact
  • ↑Lipolysis (fasting, type 1 diabetes) → ↑fatty acids to liver → ↑β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA + ↑NADH.
  • Oxaloacetate drained into gluconeogenesis (↑PC, PEPCK); NADH inhibits the TCA dehydrogenases → the cycle can't take the acetyl-CoA.
  • Excess acetyl-CoA in liver mitochondria → ketone bodies, made from fatty acids, not glucose.
  • Purpose: water-soluble fuel for brain and muscle; the liver itself can't use them.
  • Fat's end product is acetyl-CoA, hence the name 'ketogenic' diet.

  • Cytosolic HMG-CoA → HMG-CoA reductase → mevalonate → cholesterol.
  • A drug to block ketone formation would target HMG-CoA synthase, not the reductase.

AnswerC. More acetoacetate is reduced to β-hydroxybutyrate, which becomes the dominant ketone
Whyβ-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase uses NADH to reduce acetoacetate, so a high NADH/NAD⁺ ratio (DKA, alcohol, long fast) shifts the pair toward β-hydroxybutyrate. Acetone forms spontaneously, and the liver never has thiophorase.
Key fact

  • High NADH/NAD⁺ (β-oxidation in DKA, ethanol oxidation, prolonged fasting) → more β-hydroxybutyrate; ketone production rises, not falls, as NADH/NAD⁺ rises.
  • β-Hydroxybutyrate is the main circulating ketone (after 5 weeks of starvation about 6 mM, several-fold above acetoacetate) and the main brain fuel in a long fast.
  • Alcoholic ketoacidosis: ↑NADH → ↑β-hydroxybutyrate, and oxaloacetate/pyruvate → malate/lactate → hypoglycemia.

During a 2-week fast, which statement correctly contrasts the two fat-derived fuels in plasma?
  1. A. Ketone bodies are made in skeletal muscle and carried to the liver for ATP production
  2. B. Free fatty acids are carried by albumin; ketone bodies dissolve freely and extrahepatic tissues turn them into acetyl-CoA
  3. C. Ketone bodies are converted to glycogen in skeletal muscle
  4. D. Both free fatty acids and ketone bodies must be carried by albumin
  5. E. Free fatty acids cross the blood–brain barrier easily, while ketone bodies cannot
AnswerB. Free fatty acids are carried by albumin; ketone bodies dissolve freely and extrahepatic tissues turn them into acetyl-CoA
WhyLipolysis releases free fatty acids bound to serum albumin to liver and muscle. The liver turns them into ketone bodies, a water-soluble fuel needing no carrier, which brain, heart and muscle convert back to acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle. Albumin-bound fatty acids barely reach the brain, which is why the brain switches to ketones, not fat.
Key factTwo fat fuels, two ways to travel
  • Free fatty acids (released by HSL): insoluble → carried on serum albumin to liver and muscle (not transferrin, apoB or hemoglobin). Albumin-bound fatty acids barely cross the blood–brain barrier → the brain does not burn fat.
  • Ketone bodies (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate): made only in liver mitochondria from fatty-acid acetyl-CoA (not from glucose); water-soluble, no albumin; extrahepatic tissues (brain in starvation, heart, muscle, kidney) convert them to acetyl-CoA → TCA cycle. Never turned into glucose or glycogen.
  • They are organic acids (pKa 3.5) → add H⁺ (ketoacidosis). Acetone, not acetoacetate, gives fruity breath and is not a fuel.
  • The liver makes ketones but cannot use them (no thiophorase).
q1659's explanation gives the ketoacid pKa as about 4 (textbook); the lecture slide says 3.5. Either way they are fully dissociated at blood pH.

Which enzyme allows heart muscle to oxidize acetoacetate but is absent from the liver?
  1. A. β-Hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase
  2. B. Glucose 6-phosphatase
  3. C. Acetoacetyl-CoA thiolase
  4. D. HMG-CoA lyase
  5. E. Succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase)
AnswerE. Succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase (thiophorase)
WhyExtrahepatic tissues activate acetoacetate with thiophorase, taking CoA from succinyl-CoA, and thiolase splits acetoacetyl-CoA into 2 acetyl-CoA for the TCA cycle. The liver lacks thiophorase, so it makes ketones but can't use them; it does have β-hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase and thiolase.
Key fact
  • Ketolysis (brain, heart, skeletal muscle, kidney): β-hydroxybutyrate → acetoacetate (β-HB dehydrogenase) → thiophorase (succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase; CoA donor = succinyl-CoA) → acetoacetyl-CoA → thiolase → 2 acetyl-CoA → TCA.
  • Ketone bodies are a water-soluble fuel (no albumin needed).
  • Liver lacks thiophorase → makes but cannot use ketone bodies and exports them; it fuels itself by β-oxidation of fatty acids.
  • Thiophorase missing in peripheral tissues too → can't make acetoacetyl-CoA from acetoacetate → recurrent ketoacidosis.
  • Lecture yield: acetoacetate 23 ATP, β-hydroxybutyrate 26 ATP.

Key factWho burns what
  • Brain: glucose when fed and early in fasting; never fatty acids (they barely cross the blood–brain barrier); ketone bodies in prolonged fasting (most of its energy by about 3–4 weeks) → less gluconeogenesis from amino acids → muscle protein spared, urea output falls.
  • RBCs: no mitochondria → glucose only → lactate.
  • Liver: glycogenolysis early (stores gone by about 24–36 h), then gluconeogenesis + ketogenesis; fuels itself with fatty acids, not ketones.
  • Muscle: fatty acids and ketones; sends alanine/glutamine for gluconeogenesis. Heart: prefers fatty acids (palmitate) even when fed.
  • Fatty acid oxidation happens only in the mitochondrial matrix.

Liver uses ketone bodies as fuel — cannot use ketone bodies due to the lack of thiophorase. Ketone body synthesis increases. Gluconeogenesis decreases. Urea synthesis decreases.

4. You have been trapped on a remote island for the last 72 hours and have not consumed any dietary calories during this time. Which of the following metabolic processes would not be occurring to support your metabolic needs 72 hours after starvation?
  1. A. Glycogenolysis
  2. B. Ketone Body Synthesis
  3. C. Urea Synthesis
  4. D. Hepatic Gluconeogenesis
  5. E. Renal Gluconeogenesis
AnswerA. Glycogenolysis
WhyLiver glycogen is exhausted within about 24–36 hours of fasting, so by 72 hours glycogenolysis no longer contributes. Ketogenesis, hepatic and renal gluconeogenesis, and urea synthesis from amino acid catabolism are all active.
Explanation from the source
Glycogen stores are depleted roughly 12-24 hours after starvation. Ketone body synthesis from fatty acids begins after 24 hours of starvation and is the primary source of fuel for the brain during prolonged fasting Urea Cycle activity increases during fasting in order to process glucogenic amino acids which are being broken down to generate glucose. Hepatic gluconeogenesis begins as glycogen stores get depleted (within 24 hours of starvation) and does not stop until starvation ends Renal gluconeogenesis plays an important role in long-term starvation (more than 48 hours without food). Renal production of glucose via gluconeogenesis begins to exceed hepatic production of glucose during long-term starvation.
How it follows from the main questionAsked in reverse. Liver glycogen is gone by about 24–36 hours of fasting, so by 72 hours glycogenolysis is the process no longer running; the rest are active.

A healthy adult has taken only water for 3 days. Which set of hepatic activities best fits this point in the fast?
  1. A. Glycogenolysis supplies most blood glucose, and ketogenesis has not yet begun
  2. B. Glycogen is exhausted; gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis and urea synthesis are all active, and the liver burns fatty acids
  3. C. Gluconeogenesis and urea synthesis have fallen to their lowest levels because the brain already runs mostly on ketones
  4. D. Glycogen synthesis is rising because glucagon is high
  5. E. The liver oxidizes ketone bodies for its own ATP
AnswerB. Glycogen is exhausted; gluconeogenesis, ketogenesis and urea synthesis are all active, and the liver burns fatty acids
WhyLiver glycogen lasts only about a day, so by 72 h glycogenolysis has stopped contributing. Glucose now comes from gluconeogenesis (muscle amino acids, so urea output is high, plus glycerol and lactate), and ketogenesis is climbing. The fall in gluconeogenesis and urea synthesis comes only after weeks, once the brain runs mostly on ketones.
Key factFasting clock
  • Hours (overnight): insulin/glucagon ratio falls; liver glycogenolysis holds blood glucose; HSL turns on; brain and RBCs still run on glucose; ketones are not yet a fuel.
  • About 1 day: liver glycogen exhausted (lecture: it maintains glucose up to about a day). After that, no glycogenolysis.
  • Days: gluconeogenesis from muscle amino acids (↑urea), glycerol and lactate, in liver and kidney; ketogenesis rising; the liver burns fatty acids.
  • Weeks: ketones high (β-hydroxybutyrate about 6 mM at 5 weeks) → the brain gets most of its energy from ketones (major share by about 4 weeks) → glucose demand, gluconeogenesis and urea synthesis fall, muscle protein is spared. Ketogenesis does not fall.
  • Throughout: RBCs use only glucose; the liver never uses ketones.
Timing values follow the course: liver glycogen 'up to a day of fasting' (fat-metabolism recap slide), blood ketone table at 3 days and 5 weeks (lecture slide 36). Textbooks give liver glycogen as exhausted by about 24–36 hours.

A toddler with seizures, lactic acidosis, high alanine and a normal lactate:pyruvate ratio has pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency. Why does a ketogenic diet help?

WhyKetone bodies are converted to acetyl-CoA without passing through PDH (thiophorase, then thiolase), so the brain gets a TCA fuel, and the low-carbohydrate diet cuts pyruvate and lactate production.

  • Ketogenic diet: ketone bodies → acetyl-CoA (thiophorase + thiolase) → TCA cycle, bypassing PDH; less carbohydrate → less lactate.
  • A high-carbohydrate diet worsens it.

Diabetic ketoacidosis

143unlocks 9TA ×11 not obvious
A 30-year-old with type 1 diabetes ran out of insulin 3 days ago. Which set of changes is expected?
  1. A. ↑ HSL, ↑ malonyl-CoA, ↓ CPT-1, ↑ ketogenesis
  2. B. ↑ glycolysis, ↓ fatty acid oxidation, ↑ β-hydroxybutyrate
  3. C. ↑ HSL, ↓ malonyl-CoA, ↑ CPT-1, ↓ glycolysis, ↑ ketogenesis
  4. D. ↓ glucagon, ↑ TCA flux, ↓ fatty acid delivery to liver
  5. E. ↓ HSL, ↑ malonyl-CoA, ↓ CPT-1, ↑ glycolysis
AnswerC. ↑ HSL, ↓ malonyl-CoA, ↑ CPT-1, ↓ glycolysis, ↑ ketogenesis
WhyNo insulin + high glucagon: HSL on (fatty acids flood the liver), ACC off → ↓malonyl-CoA → CPT-1 open → ↑β-oxidation, glycolysis (PFK-1) down, gluconeogenesis up, and excess acetyl-CoA → ketones. ↑malonyl-CoA with ↑ketogenesis (A) contradicts itself.
Key factLow insulin / high glucagon (fasting, DKA)
  • Adipose: ↑HSL, ↑lipolysis; ↓LPL, ↓GLUT4.
  • Liver: ↓ACC → ↓malonyl-CoA → ↑CPT-1 → ↑β-oxidation → ↑acetyl-CoA, ↑NADH → ↓TCA; ↑PC, ↑PEPCK, ↑FBPase-1, ↑glycogen phosphorylase; ↓fructose 2,6-bisphosphate → ↓PFK-1, ↓glycolysis; ↑HMG-CoA synthase → ↑ketones (↑3-hydroxybutyrate).
  • Insulin-dependent enzymes fall: glucokinase, ACC, fatty acid synthase, glycogen synthase, LPL, GLUT4.
  • Glucagon acts on liver and adipose (gluconeogenesis, glycogenolysis, lipolysis, ketogenesis), not muscle protein breakdown (muscle has no glucagon receptors).

A 12-year-old has polyuria, vomiting, deep rapid breathing and fruity breath; glucose is 480 mg/dL. Which finding is expected?
  1. A. High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with urine acetoacetate
  2. B. Metabolic alkalosis
  3. C. Normal anion gap
  4. D. Hypervolemia
  5. E. Low serum β-hydroxybutyrate
AnswerA. High-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with urine acetoacetate
WhyAcetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are acids (pKa 3.5) that release H⁺ at blood pH → high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis, Kussmaul breathing and ketonuria. Acetone, formed spontaneously from acetoacetate, gives the fruity breath. Osmotic diuresis causes volume loss, not hypervolemia.
Key fact
  • Acetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are organic acids (pKa 3.5) → H⁺ load → ↑anion gap metabolic acidosis, ↓HCO₃⁻, Kussmaul respiration (respiratory compensation).
  • Acetone: non-enzymatic from acetoacetate, not an acid, not a fuel, exhaled → fruity breath.
  • DKA labs: hyperglycemia + glucosuria, ↑serum β-hydroxybutyrate, urine ketones (acetoacetate), ↑anion gap, dehydration, low C-peptide in type 1.
  • Insulin treatment stops lipolysis and ketogenesis; ketoacids are burned and HCO₃⁻ regenerated → pH rises; glucose and serum K⁺ fall.
  • Nutritional (physiologic) ketosis: ketones up modestly, pH stays normal.
q1386 keys 'bicarbonate solution is a treatment staple' for DKA; standard care is isotonic saline, insulin and K⁺, with bicarbonate only for severe acidosis. Not counted.

CASE 3: HYPERGLYCEMIA AND HYPERKETONEMIA Patient Presentation: A 40-year-old woman was brought to the hospital in a disoriented, confused state by her husband. Focused History: As noted on her medical alert bracelet, the patient has had type 1 diabetes (T1D) for the last 24 years. Her husband reports that this is her first medical emergency in 2 years. Physical Examination (Pertinent Findings): The patient displayed signs of dehydration (such as dry mucous membranes and skin, poor skin turgor, and low blood pressure) and acidosis (such as deep and rapid breathing [Kussmaul respiration]). Her breath had a faintly fruity odor. Her temperature was normal. Pertinent Test Results: Rapid, bedside tests were strongly positive for glucose and acetoacetate and negative for protein. Results on blood tests performed by the clinical laboratory are shown below: Microscopic examination of her urine revealed a urinary tract infection (UTI). Diagnosis: The patient is in diabetic ketoacidosis that was precipitated by a UTI. [Note: Diabetes increases the risk for infections such as UTIs.] Immediate Treatment: The patient was rehydrated with normal saline given intravenously (IV). She also was given insulin IV. Blood glucose, ketone bodies, and electrolytes were measured periodically. The patient was started on an antibiotic for her UTI. Long-term Treatment: Diabetes increases the risk for macrovascular complications (such as coronary artery disease and stroke) and microvascular complications (such as retinopathy, nephropathy, and neuropathy). Ongoing monitoring for these complications will be continued. Prognosis: Diabetes is the sixth leading cause of death by disease in the United States. Individuals with diabetes have a reduced life expectancy relative to those without diabetes. Diabetic ketoacidosis occurs when the rate of ketone body production is greater than the rate of utilization. Which of the following statements concerning ketone body metabolism is correct? Ketone bodies:
Show figure
  1. A. are made in mitochondria from acetyl coenzyme A (CoA) produced by the oxidation of glucose.
  2. B. are utilized by many tissues, particularly the liver, after conversion to acetyl CoA.
  3. C. include acetoacetate, which can impart a fruity odor to the breath.
  4. D. require albumin for transport through the blood.
  5. E. utilized in energy metabolism are organic acids that can add to the proton load of the body.
AnswerE. utilized in energy metabolism are organic acids that can add to the proton load of the body.
WhyAcetoacetate and β-hydroxybutyrate are organic acids (pKa ~4) that dissociate at blood pH, adding H⁺ and causing ketoacidosis. They come from fatty acid (not glucose) oxidation, the liver cannot use them, the fruity odor is acetone, and being water-soluble they need no albumin.
Explanation from the source
Correct answer = E. 3-Hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate are organic acids, and their ionization contributes to the proton load of the body. Ketone bodies are made in the mitochondria of liver cells using acetyl coenzyme A (CoA) generated primarily from the β-oxidation of fatty acids (see Figure below). Because they are water soluble, they do not require a transporter. Liver cannot use them because it lacks the enzyme thiophorase, which moves CoA from succinyl CoA to acetoacetate for conversion to two molecules of acetyl CoA. It is the acetone released in the breath that can impart a fruity odor.
How it follows from the main question'Acetoacetate gives fruity breath' is the trap: the odor is acetone. Ketones come from fat, the liver can't use them, and need no albumin. Answer: organic acids adding to the proton load.

MCAD deficiency (Helga)

A 7-month-old is unrousable after a viral illness with poor feeding. Glucose is low, urine ketones are absent, plasma octanoylcarnitine (C8) is high, and urine has medium-chain dicarboxylic acids. Which step is most directly defective?
  1. A. α-Oxidation of branched fatty acids
  2. B. Peroxisomal oxidation of fatty acids longer than C20
  3. C. Ketone body synthesis by HMG-CoA synthase
  4. D. The first, FAD-linked oxidation of β-oxidation for C6–C12 acyl-CoAs
  5. E. Carnitine uptake into cells
AnswerD. The first, FAD-linked oxidation of β-oxidation for C6–C12 acyl-CoAs
WhyHypoketotic hypoglycemia after a fast + ↑C6–C10 (C8) acylcarnitines + dicarboxylic aciduria = MCAD deficiency, the medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase (first oxidation, C6–C12) of mitochondrial β-oxidation. Carnitine-uptake defects give low acylcarnitines; ketogenesis falls only secondarily.
Key fact
  • MCAD = medium-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, first FAD-linked step of mitochondrial β-oxidation for C6–C12 (SCAD below C6, LCAD C14–C18, VLCAD above C20). Most common fatty acid oxidation disorder (about 1 in 12,000; Northern European ancestry).
  • Fingerprint: infant or toddler, fasting or illness (vomiting, poor feeding) → lethargy or coma, hypoketotic hypoglycemia, hepatomegaly with fatty liver, ↑ammonia, ↑anion gap, ↑C6–C10 acylcarnitines (C8), dicarboxylic aciduria, hexanoyl- and suberylglycine; sibling with a Reye-like death.
  • 'Mom couldn't wake her' = hypoglycemia (the brain has neither glucose nor ketones).
  • Differential for hypoketotic hypoglycemia: carnitine, CPT and LCAD defects, congenital hyperinsulinism (no acylcarnitine rise), Reye syndrome.

  • C8–C10 acylcarnitines → MCAD rather than SCAD, VLCAD, CPT-2 or CACT

What it lets you eliminate

  • 'Hyperketotic', hyperglycemia, increased gluconeogenesis or more ketone use are the opposite of MCAD
  • OTC, PDH and primary carnitine deficiency don't give C8 acylcarnitines with dicarboxylic acids
  • α-oxidation, peroxisomal oxidation, palmitate synthesis and ketone synthesis are the wrong pathway
  • Metabolic alkalosis, sleep apnea and aspiration don't explain the stupor

Questions it helps you answer (1)
Practice Q1616Answered by elimination
A 3-month-old child had her first ear infection and was feeding poorly due to the ear pain. One morning the parents found the child in a nonresponsive state and rushed her to the emergency department. A blood glucose level was 45 mg/dL, and upon receiving intravenous glucose the child became responsive. Further blood analysis displayed the absence of ketone bodies, normal levels of acyl-carnitine, and the presence of the following unusual carboxylic acids shown below. The enzymatic defect in this child is most likely in which of the following enzymes?
  1. A. Fatty acyl-CoA synthetase
  2. B. Carnitine translocase
  3. C. Carnitine acyltransferase I
  4. D. Carnitine acyltransferase II
  5. E. Medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
AnswerE. Medium chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase
WhyFasting hypoketotic hypoglycemia with medium-chain dicarboxylic acids (from ω-oxidation of accumulating C6–C10 fatty acids) after illness and poor feeding points to MCAD deficiency. Carnitine-shuttle defects would not produce dicarboxylic acids.
How it follows from the main questionNormal acylcarnitines seem to argue against MCAD, but the unusual acids are dicarboxylic (ω-oxidation), which shuttle defects never produce. With hypoketotic hypoglycemia after illness: MCAD.

MCAD deficiency (Helga)

146unlocks 29TA ×1
In MCAD deficiency, which pair of hepatic changes explains both the fasting hypoglycemia and the low ketones?
  1. A. ↓ glycogen phosphorylase activity and excess stored glycogen
  2. B. ↓ ATP and ↑ acetyl-CoA
  3. C. ↓ ATP and ↓ acetyl-CoA
  4. D. ↑ ATP and ↑ acetyl-CoA
  5. E. ↑ insulin and ↓ glucagon
AnswerC. ↓ ATP and ↓ acetyl-CoA
WhyBlocked β-oxidation yields less acetyl-CoA (the substrate for ketogenesis and the obligatory activator of pyruvate carboxylase) and less ATP to run gluconeogenesis. Once glycogen runs out, ketones and glucose both fall; insulin and glycogen handling are normal.
Key fact
  • MCAD block → ↓ATP and ↓acetyl-CoA in the fasting liver.
  • Hypoglycemia: gluconeogenesis needs ATP, and acetyl-CoA is the obligatory allosteric activator of pyruvate carboxylase → ↓gluconeogenesis. Tissues that can't burn fat use more glucose, illness raises needs, and an overnight fast empties glycogen (↑glucose demand, ↓gluconeogenesis).
  • Hypoketosis: low acetyl-CoA = low ketone bodies (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate).
  • Same logic for any hepatic β-oxidation block (carnitine, CPT-1, ackee): hypoketotic hypoglycemia.
What it unlocks: 30 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Toddler, poor intake, ↑C8 acylcarnitine → mechanism of hypoglycemia (↓ATP, ↓pyruvate carboxylase activation)
  • Case short answers: account for the hypoglycemia; account for the hypoketosis
  • MCQ: fasting hypoglycemia is a consequence of ↓acetyl-CoA production; 'reduced gluconeogenesis due to low ATP and low acetyl-CoA'
  • Lethargic between feedings: ↑glucose demand but ↓gluconeogenesis; 'insufficient energy for gluconeogenesis'

What it lets you eliminate

  • Excess insulin, glycogen storage defects and poor glucose absorption are not the cause
  • 'Decreased ability to convert acetyl-CoA to glucose' is a trap: acetyl-CoA never makes net glucose anyway
  • No acylcarnitine or dicarboxylic acid inhibition of gluconeogenesis; the problem is too little energy and activator
  • The gluconeogenic enzymes themselves are intact

An infant in an MCAD crisis has plasma ammonia of 100 µmol/L (normal below 20). Which mechanism best explains it?
  1. A. Dicarboxylic acids activating glutaminase
  2. B. Excess dietary protein
  3. C. Ketone bodies inhibiting carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I
  4. D. Accumulated octanoate uncouples mitochondria, lowering the ATP the urea cycle needs
  5. E. Inherited ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency
AnswerD. Accumulated octanoate uncouples mitochondria, lowering the ATP the urea cycle needs
WhyAccumulated octanoic acid (C8) is a mitochondrial toxin that uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, and the fatty liver works poorly, so hepatic ATP falls and the ATP-hungry urea cycle slows. Ketones are low in MCAD, so D can't be right.
Key fact
  • MCAD → medium chains (octanoate, C8) accumulate → uncouple oxidative phosphorylation → ↓ATP → ↓urea synthesis → hyperammonemia.
  • Fatty infiltration also diminishes liver function.
  • So MCAD = ↓fatty acid oxidation + ↓urea synthesis + ↑ammonia (never ↓ammonia).
Course case answer is octanoate uncoupling → ↓ATP → ↓urea cycle; the N-acetylglutamate/CPS-I mechanism some sources add is a textbook extra.

What it lets you eliminate

  • MCAD does not lower ammonia or cause hyperglycemia

The urine of a child with MCAD deficiency contains suberylglycine, a conjugate of a C8 dicarboxylic acid. Where does the dicarboxylic acid come from?
  1. A. Methylmalonyl-CoA mutase
  2. B. ω-Oxidation of backed-up fatty acids by cytochrome P450 in the endoplasmic reticulum
  3. C. Peroxisomal VLCFA transport
  4. D. Peroxisomal α-oxidation
  5. E. Ketone body breakdown
AnswerB. ω-Oxidation of backed-up fatty acids by cytochrome P450 in the endoplasmic reticulum
WhyMedium-chain acyl groups MCAD can't oxidize leave as C6–C10 acylcarnitines or glycine conjugates (hexanoylglycine, C6); some go through ER ω-oxidation (P450) to dicarboxylic acids (suberate, C8 → suberylglycine). These unmeasured acids, not ketones, raise the anion gap.
Key fact
  • Medium-chain acyl-CoA trapped in mitochondria → carnitine acyltransferases → leave as C6, C8, C10 acylcarnitines (blood) or free acids.
  • Hexanoylglycine = C6 monocarboxylic glycine conjugate (β-oxidation intermediate).
  • Suberylglycine = C8 dicarboxylic conjugate from ω-oxidation (ER, cytochrome P450), which increases whenever β-oxidation fails.
  • Anion gap ↑ (20 vs 8–16) from accumulated mono- and dicarboxylic acids, not ketones (ketones are low).
  • Carnitine synthesis, transport and acyltransferases are normal.
What it unlocks: 18 questions

No surprises here: every question it answers asks the fact straight out.

How it shows up

  • Child with medium-chain dicarboxylic acids + glycine and carnitine conjugates → ↑ω-oxidation by P450 in the ER
  • Case: account for ↑hexanoyl/octanoylcarnitine and urinary hexanoyl/suberylglycine
  • Case: account for the plasma anion gap (mono- and dicarboxylic acids)
  • MCQ: why hexanoyl- and octanoylcarnitine are high (medium chains conjugated to carnitine)

What it lets you eliminate

  • Not increased carnitine synthesis, impaired carnitine transport or acyltransferase deficiency
  • In MCAD the gap is not from ketones
  • α-oxidation, methylmalonyl-CoA and VLCFA transport are unrelated

Which test best confirms a suspected diagnosis of MCAD deficiency?
  1. A. ACADM gene analysis (common European Lys304Glu) and/or MCAD activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts
  2. B. Urine ketone dipstick
  3. C. Brain MRI
  4. D. Liver ultrasound
  5. E. Fasting blood glucose
AnswerA. ACADM gene analysis (common European Lys304Glu) and/or MCAD activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts
WhyConfirmation is genetic analysis of ACADM (chromosome 1); the common European mutation Lys304Glu (K304E, 985A→G) impairs assembly of the MCAD homotetramer. MCAD activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts supports it; glucose and ketones only raise suspicion.
Key fact
  • Gene: ACADM (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, medium chain), chromosome 1; MCAD is a homotetramer.
  • Most common mutation in people of European descent: Lys304Glu (K304E), 985A→G → impaired tetramer assembly.
  • Biochemical support: MCAD enzyme activity in leukocytes or fibroblasts; β-oxidation in cultured fibroblasts (C6–C10 acylcarnitines).
  • Imaging, glucose and urine ketones do not confirm it.

Which instruction is appropriate for the parent of an infant with MCAD deficiency?
  1. A. Use a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet
  2. B. Allow a 12-hour overnight fast
  3. C. Use a formula rich in medium-chain triglycerides
  4. D. Start a high-fat ketogenic diet
  5. E. Feed every 3–4 hours with complex carbohydrate, avoid fasting, and give extra glucose during illness
AnswerE. Feed every 3–4 hours with complex carbohydrate, avoid fasting, and give extra glucose during illness
WhyMCAD patients can't burn fat in a fast, so management is avoid fasting: frequent complex-carbohydrate feeds, lower fat, uncooked cornstarch at bedtime later, extra glucose when ill. MCT formulas are contraindicated because medium chains need MCAD; MCT is for carnitine-shuttle defects.
Key fact
  • Avoid fasting; frequent feeds (every 3–4 h) with complex carbohydrates; extra or IV glucose during illness or vomiting.
  • Avoid medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) formulas.
  • As a toddler: relatively low-fat diet (under 30% of calories) and uncooked cornstarch (2 g/kg) at bedtime for slow overnight glucose.
  • Carnitine supplements may replace carnitine lost as acylcarnitines.
  • Ketogenic, high-fat, high-protein/low-carb diets, fasting and glucagon all provoke crises.
